courses.label: Architecture
courses.blurb: How to pick an architecture style, draw service and module boundaries, and keep a distributed system alive under failure. At SDE2 you own significant parts of a design and argue the trade-offs out loud.

chapters.title: Architecture styles
chapters.summary: The handful of shapes a system takes, when each wins, and the 2025-26 pendulum swing back toward the monolith.

lessons.title: Layered architecture
lessons.body:
The oldest, most familiar shape: organise code into horizontal layers — presentation on top, then business/domain, then data access — where each layer only calls the one below it. Most CRUD apps start here, and that is fine.

```flow
dir: TB
pres: Presentation | step
biz: Business logic | step
data: Data access | step
db: Database | store
pres -> biz : calls down
biz -> data : calls down
data -> db : queries
```

**When it wins:** simple domains, small teams, CRUD-heavy apps where the data model closely matches the business model. It is fast to build and easy to onboard onto, because everyone recognises the shape.

**When it hurts:** the data layer tends to leak upward. ORM entities become domain objects become API DTOs, so a schema change ripples through every layer. Business logic ends up smeared across "service" classes that are really procedural scripts sitting on the database. And nothing *enforces* the boundaries — a UI calling the repository directly compiles just fine, so shortcuts accumulate.

The tell that you have outgrown it: you are afraid to change the database schema because you can't predict what it will break three layers up.

```recall
Q: When is a layered architecture the right default?
A: Simple domains, small teams, and CRUD-heavy apps where the data model closely matches the business model; it is fast to build and everyone recognises the shape.
Q: What is the main failure mode of the layered style?
A: The data layer leaks upward: ORM entities become domain objects become API DTOs, so a schema change ripples through every layer and business logic smears across procedural service classes.
Q: What is the concrete signal that you have outgrown layered architecture?
A: You are afraid to change the database schema because you cannot predict what it will break three layers up, since nothing enforces the layer boundaries.
```

lessons.title: Hexagonal / ports and adapters
lessons.body:
Also called ports-and-adapters, and closely related to Clean Architecture. The domain logic sits at the centre with zero knowledge of infrastructure. It exposes **ports** (interfaces like `OrderRepository`) that **adapters** implement — a Postgres adapter, an in-memory adapter for tests, a REST controller adapter that drives the domain from the outside.

Clean Architecture (Robert C. Martin) is the same idea drawn as concentric rings (entities inside use cases inside interface adapters inside frameworks) with one rule: **the dependency rule** — dependencies only ever point inward, never outward. The core never imports the framework.

```flow
dir: LR
rest: REST adapter | tool
core: Domain core | step
port: OrderRepository | gate
pg: Postgres adapter | store
mem: In-memory adapter | store
rest -> core : drives
core -> port : depends on
pg -> port : implements
mem -> port : implements
```

**When it wins:** you need to swap infrastructure without touching business logic (a different DB per environment, adding a queue trigger beside an HTTP one), or you want to unit-test domain logic with no framework mocking. It pays off when the domain is genuinely complex enough to be worth protecting.

**When it hurts:** it is overkill for a thin-logic CRUD app. You pay real ceremony — interfaces everywhere, DTO mapping at every boundary — for flexibility you never use. And nothing enforces the boundary except discipline and code review, so teams new to it build the skeleton correctly and then leak infra concerns into the "core" anyway.

```recall
Q: What does the dependency rule actually forbid?
A: The core importing the framework or infrastructure; dependencies point only inward, so domain logic defines ports as interfaces and adapters on the outside implement them, never the reverse.
Q: Why does hexagonal make domain logic easy to unit-test?
A: The core depends only on port interfaces, so tests supply in-memory adapters instead of a real database or HTTP layer, removing the need to mock a framework.
Q: When is ports-and-adapters the wrong call?
A: For a thin-logic CRUD app where the domain is not complex enough to protect; you pay interface and DTO-mapping ceremony for flexibility you never exercise.
```

lessons.title: Event-driven architecture
lessons.body:
Components communicate by producing and consuming events rather than calling each other directly. Martin Fowler distinguishes several styles — the simplest is **event notification** ("a change happened; I don't care what you do with it"), where the source system genuinely doesn't care about the response.

A typical async workflow, where one event triggers a chain of independent reactions:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Order as Order service
    participant Bus as Event bus
    participant Inv as Inventory
    participant Pay as Payment
    Order->>Bus: publish "OrderPlaced"
    Bus->>Inv: OrderPlaced
    Bus->>Pay: OrderPlaced
    Note over Inv,Pay: each reacts independently
    Inv->>Bus: publish "StockReserved"
    Pay->>Bus: publish "PaymentCharged"
```

**When it wins:** it naturally decouples producers from consumers and supports fan-out — many services react to one event without the producer knowing they exist. It fits workflows with real async/batch semantics.

**When it hurts:** debugging is materially harder. There is no linear call stack to follow, so "why did X happen?" needs correlation IDs and good tracing. Eventual consistency becomes a first-class problem every caller must reason about, and it is easy to build an untraceable "distributed monolith" where every service depends on every event.

```recall
Q: Why does event notification decouple a producer from its consumers so well?
A: The source publishes "a change happened" and does not care who reacts, so consumers can be added or removed without the producer knowing they exist, enabling fan-out.
Q: What is the main debugging cost of going event-driven, and how do you mitigate it?
A: There is no linear call stack to follow "why did X happen"; you mitigate it with correlation IDs and distributed tracing to reconstruct the chain of reactions.
Q: When is event-driven the wrong choice?
A: When the workflow is inherently synchronous and request/response, or when the team cannot absorb eventual consistency and the tracing burden; it then just hides a distributed monolith behind a bus.
```

lessons.title: Microservices vs modular monolith (2025-26)
lessons.body:
**Microservices** (per Chris Richardson / microservices.io, the standard reference): independently deployable services, each owned by a team, communicating over the network, typically each with its own datastore.

**Modular monolith:** a single deployable unit internally partitioned into modules with enforced boundaries — the same discipline about boundaries as microservices, but the calls are in-process, without the distributed-systems tax.

The current discourse is an actively-forming trend, not settled doctrine, but it clearly leans back toward the monolith:

- Amazon's own Prime Video audio/video monitoring team moved from a distributed serverless/microservices design to a single-process monolith and **cut infrastructure cost by 90%** — per-service orchestration and S3 hops between Lambda steps dominated at their request volume. Caveat: one team, one tightly-coupled high-throughput workload; it is not a blanket "microservices are bad" result.

```bars
title: Prime Video infra cost after consolidating to a monolith
unit: % of original
Distributed microservices | 100
Single-process monolith | 10
```
- A widely-cited 2025 CNCF survey figure (via secondary sources) reports that ~42% of organisations that adopted microservices have consolidated services back into larger deployable units.
- Google's Service Weaver and Spring Modulith are real frameworks built specifically to support the modular-monolith shape.

**Working rule of thumb for 2026:** default to a modular monolith. Reach for microservices only when a *specific, already-felt* pain forces it — independent team scaling (Conway's Law), genuinely independent deploy cadences, or a real per-service scaling bottleneck. Splitting a monolith into network-connected pieces that still share a database and still deploy together is not microservices; it is "a monolith with extra HTTP calls," and strictly worse.

**Interview framing:** if asked "microservices or monolith," don't pick one. Name the actual forcing function — team count, deploy cadence, blast radius — and reason from there.

```recall
Q: What is the default architecture for 2026, and when do you deviate from it?
A: Default to a modular monolith; reach for microservices only when a specific already-felt pain forces it, such as independent team scaling, independent deploy cadences, or a real per-service scaling bottleneck.
Q: Why is "a monolith with extra HTTP calls" strictly worse than the monolith it came from?
A: It pays the distributed-systems tax (partial failure, latency, retries, idempotency) while still sharing a database and deploying together, so it gains none of the independence that would justify the cost.
Q: Does the Prime Video result prove microservices are bad?
A: No; it is one high-throughput, tightly-coupled workload where per-step orchestration and S3 hops dominated, so it argues against over-decomposition, not against the style in general.
Q: What is the right order: boundaries then extraction, or extraction then boundaries?
A: Boundaries first; enforce module boundaries in-process, let them harden, then extract only the module with a proven bottleneck. Extraction does not create boundaries.
```
lessons.deeper:
**The mechanism people skip: the distributed-systems tax.** The moment a call crosses the network you inherit partial failure (the callee may have done the work but the response was lost), latency variance, the need for retries + idempotency, and the CAP trade-off. A modular monolith keeps those calls in-process, so an invocation is a function call: no serialization, no timeout tuning, one transaction, one stack trace. Microservices trade that simplicity for *independent deployability* and *independent scaling* — and if you're not cashing in on at least one of those, you paid the tax for nothing.

**Concrete scenario.** A payments team runs a modular monolith with three modules: `ledger`, `payouts`, `reconciliation`. Reconciliation runs a nightly batch that pegs 8 CPU cores for two hours; the rest of the app is a steady 5% CPU. That's a *real* independent-scaling forcing function — you'd rather not provision the whole box for a nightly spike. So you extract `reconciliation` (and only that) into its own service with its own autoscaling group. `ledger` and `payouts` stay in-process because they share transactions and always deploy together. This is the correct shape: extract on a felt bottleneck, not on a diagram.

**The failure mode people get wrong: the distributed monolith.** Teams split by noun (`user-service`, `order-service`, `product-service`), then discover every request fans out to all three and they still share one database. Now they have network hops, distributed transactions, *and* coupled deploys — every downside of microservices with none of the independence. The tell: you can't deploy one service without deploying the others, or a schema change touches three repos.

```flow
dir: LR
req: Request | actor
usr: user-service | step
ord: order-service | step
prd: product-service | step
db: Shared database | store
req -> usr : fans out
usr -> ord : network hop
ord -> prd : network hop
usr -> db : all share
ord -> db : one schema
prd -> db : coupled deploys
```

**Common follow-ups**

- *"When is the network hop actually worth it?"* — When a service scales, deploys, or fails on a genuinely different curve from its neighbours (the reconciliation batch above), or when a distinct team needs to own its release cadence.
- *"How do you split a monolith safely?"* — Enforce module boundaries in-process first (Spring Modulith / Service Weaver), let them harden, then extract the module that has a proven bottleneck. Boundaries earn extraction; extraction doesn't create boundaries.
- *"What breaks first when you go distributed too early?"* — Data consistency. A shared database across services means no service truly owns its data, so you get lock contention and hidden coupling. Each service must own its store first.
- *"Isn't the Prime Video result proof microservices are bad?"* — No — it's one high-throughput, tightly-coupled workload where per-step orchestration and S3 hops dominated. It argues against *over*-decomposition, not against the style.

lessons.title: CQRS
lessons.body:
Command Query Responsibility Segregation: use a different model to *update* data than the model you use to *read* it. Separate write and read paths, sometimes separate datastores entirely.

Fowler's own bliki is the load-bearing quote: "you can use a different model to update information than the model you use to read information. For some situations this separation can be valuable, but beware that for most systems CQRS adds risky complexity."

**When it wins:** read and write workloads have genuinely different shapes — writes are normalised and transactional, while reads need heavily denormalised, pre-joined views for dashboards — or read and write scale independently by orders of magnitude.

```bars
title: Read vs write load that justifies CQRS (illustrative)
unit: ops/sec
Writes | 200
Reads | 50000
```

**When it hurts:** most systems should not use it. It is a targeted tool for a specific asymmetry, not a default architecture. It introduces eventual consistency between the write model and the read model that every caller and every UI now has to account for. If you can't name the read/write asymmetry that forces it, you don't need it.

```recall
Q: What specific asymmetry justifies CQRS?
A: Read and write workloads with genuinely different shapes or scale, such as normalised transactional writes versus heavily denormalised dashboard reads, or reads outscaling writes by orders of magnitude.
Q: Where does the eventual-consistency lag in CQRS come from?
A: The write side emits a change that a projector consumes asynchronously to update the read model, so there is a propagation window during which the read view is stale.
Q: What read-after-write bug do teams ship when they ignore that lag?
A: A user edits data, the command returns, the UI re-queries the read model and shows the old value because the projector has not caught up; fixes include returning the new value directly or reading the write model for that screen.
Q: Is CQRS the same as event sourcing?
A: No; CQRS is separate read and write models, event sourcing is storing state as an event log. They pair well because events can feed projections, but each stands alone.
```
lessons.deeper:
**The mechanism: two models, and how the read side stays fresh.** The write model is normalised and validation-heavy — it accepts commands (`PlaceOrder`, `CancelOrder`), enforces invariants, and persists the change. The read model is one or more denormalised *projections* shaped exactly for a query ("orders per customer with totals", "today's revenue by region"), often in a different store (Postgres for writes, Elasticsearch/Redis for reads). The link between them is a *propagation* step: the write side emits a change (a domain event or a CDC stream), a projector consumes it and updates the read views. That propagation is asynchronous, which is precisely where the eventual-consistency lag lives.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as UI
    participant W as Write model
    participant P as Projector
    participant R as Read model
    U->>W: command (PlaceOrder)
    W-->>U: 202 accepted
    W->>P: OrderPlaced event
    P->>R: update projection
    Note over R: read view now fresh
    U->>R: query "my orders"
```

**Concrete scenario.** An e-commerce catalog takes ~200 writes/sec (price and stock edits) but serves ~50,000 reads/sec on product pages, many with complex filters. Writes go to a normalised Postgres schema; a projector consumes change events and maintains a flattened Elasticsearch index with pre-computed facets. Reads never touch Postgres. Read and write scale on completely independent hardware — the exact asymmetry that justifies CQRS.

**The failure mode people get wrong: assuming read-after-write consistency.** A user edits their profile, the command returns 202, the UI immediately re-queries the read model — and shows the *old* value because the projector hasn't caught up (typically tens to hundreds of ms). Teams that don't design for this ship confusing "my change didn't save" bugs. Fixes: return the new value from the command directly, read from the write model for that one screen, or show an optimistic UI. You cannot pretend the lag is zero.

**Common follow-ups**

- *"CQRS vs event sourcing — same thing?"* — No. CQRS is separate read/write models; event sourcing is storing state as an event log. They pair well (events feed projections) but each stands alone.
- *"Do you need two databases?"* — No. CQRS can be two models against one store. Separate stores is an optimisation for the scaling/shape asymmetry, not a requirement.
- *"How do you handle the eventual-consistency window?"* — Bound it and make it visible: measure projection lag, and on write-then-read screens either read the write model or echo the command result.
- *"When is CQRS the wrong call?"* — Any CRUD app where reads and writes share the same shape and scale. It adds a projector, a second model, and consistency reasoning for zero payoff.

lessons.title: Event sourcing
lessons.body:
Persist state as an append-only sequence of events rather than current-state rows. Current state is derived by replaying the log (or replaying from a periodic snapshot).

```flow
dir: LR
cmd: Command | actor
log: Event log | store
snap: Snapshot | store
fold: Fold apply | step
state: Current state | step
cmd -> log : append
snap -> fold : start from
log -> fold : replay after
fold -> state : derive
```

Two independent sources say the same thing. Fowler: "Event Sourcing ensures that all changes to application state are stored as a sequence of events... we can also use the event log to reconstruct past states." Azure's Architecture Center: "Adopt event sourcing when its benefits, like auditability and historical reconstruction, justify the pattern's complexity. For most systems and most parts of a system, traditional data management is sufficient."

**When it wins:** you need a true audit trail, temporal queries ("what did this look like on date X"), or you are already doing CQRS and want the write-side events to double as the mechanism that feeds the read-side projections.

**When it hurts:** most systems don't need it, and the long-term cost people underestimate is **schema versioning** — replaying events written years ago, in an old shape, forever. Once an event is in the log it is history; you can't migrate it the way you'd ALTER a table.

```recall
Q: Why is schema versioning the cost people underestimate with event sourcing?
A: Events are immutable history, so you cannot ALTER old ones; the fold logic and consumers must handle every past event shape forever, typically via upcasters that transform old versions on read.
Q: When is event sourcing worth its complexity?
A: When you need a true audit trail, temporal queries like "what did this look like on date X", or you already do CQRS and want the write-side events to feed read-side projections.
Q: How do snapshots keep replay cheap without becoming a source of truth?
A: They cache the folded state at a version so load starts there and replays only later events; they are rebuildable from the raw log, so they are a cache you can always delete and regenerate.
Q: How do you correct an event written by mistake?
A: Append a compensating event; you never delete, because both the mistake and its correction are part of the true history.
```
lessons.deeper:
**The mechanism: rebuild state by folding the log.** Current state isn't stored — it's *computed*. You load every event for an entity in order and apply each to an initially-empty aggregate: `state = events.reduce(apply, empty)`. `AccountOpened` → balance 0; `Deposited 100` → 100; `Withdrew 30` → 70. The event store is append-only, so writing is a single insert with an optimistic-concurrency check (expected version N, reject if the stream moved). The obvious problem — an account with 4 million events would take forever to replay — is solved with **snapshots**: periodically persist the folded state at version N, then on load start from the latest snapshot and replay only the events after it. A snapshot is a cache, not a source of truth; you can always delete every snapshot and rebuild from the raw log.

**Concrete scenario.** A bank ledger uses event sourcing because the audit requirement is absolute: every balance must be explainable by a sequence of legal transactions, and regulators can ask "what was this balance on 2024-03-15?". That's a native temporal query — replay the stream up to that timestamp. Snapshots are taken every 500 events; a typical account loads one snapshot + a handful of recent events. The log *is* the audit trail, for free.

**The failure mode people get wrong: event schema evolution.** You emitted `{ amount: 100 }` for three years, then the business needs currency, so you want `{ amount: 100, currency: "USD" }`. You cannot ALTER the old events — they're immutable history. So every consumer and the fold logic must handle *both* shapes forever, usually via an **upcaster** that transforms old event versions into the current shape on read (defaulting `currency` to USD for legacy events). Teams that treat events like mutable rows corrupt their history or break replay. Rule: events are facts that happened; you version and upcast, you never rewrite.

**Common follow-ups**

- *"How do you query 'all accounts with balance > X'?"* — You don't, against the log — that's a cross-entity read. You build a projection (a read model / CQRS view) that the events feed. Event sourcing answers "how did *this* entity get here," not ad-hoc aggregate queries.
- *"What are snapshots and when do you take them?"* — A cached fold of state at a version, taken every N events or on a timer, to bound replay cost. Rebuildable from the log, so never authoritative.
- *"How do you handle a bad event that was written by mistake?"* — Append a corrective/compensating event; you don't delete. The mistake and its correction are both part of the true history.
- *"When is event sourcing overkill?"* — When you don't need audit, temporal queries, or event-driven projections. For most CRUD, current-state rows are simpler and sufficient — Azure's own guidance says so.

lessons.title: Saga: distributed transactions without 2PC
lessons.body:
A business transaction that spans multiple services can't use a distributed two-phase commit in practice. A **saga** models it as a sequence of local transactions, each with a **compensating transaction** that undoes it if a later step fails.

The failure path is the whole point — a later step fails, and you walk *backwards*, compensating each completed step:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant O as Orchestrator
    participant Pay as Payment
    participant Inv as Inventory
    participant Ship as Shipping
    O->>Pay: charge card
    Pay-->>O: ok
    O->>Inv: reserve stock
    Inv-->>O: ok
    O->>Ship: create shipment
    Ship-->>O: FAILED
    Note over O: run compensations in reverse
    O->>Inv: release stock
    O->>Pay: refund charge
```

Two implementation styles:
- **Orchestration** — a central coordinator tells each service what to do next and triggers compensations on failure. Easier to reason about and debug (one place holds the state machine), but the coordinator becomes a critical dependency.
- **Choreography** — each service publishes events and reacts to others' events, with no central coordinator. More decoupled, but the flow is implicit: to understand it end-to-end you have to read every service's event handlers.

**The hard part:** compensations are not free rollbacks. "Refund the payment" is a different operation from "the charge never happened," with its own edge cases (what if the money was already spent downstream?). Choreographed sagas are notoriously hard to debug without strong distributed tracing.

```recall
Q: Why can a cross-service business transaction not use two-phase commit in practice?
A: 2PC needs a blocking coordinator holding locks across every service for the whole transaction; it does not scale and stalls everything if the coordinator dies mid-commit, so sagas trade isolation for availability.
Q: What property do sagas give up that a single ACID transaction provides, and why does it bite?
A: Isolation; other transactions can observe intermediate states (money charged before the order is confirmed, stock held mid-flight), which is where subtle saga bugs live.
Q: When do you choose orchestration over choreography?
A: For complex flows with four or more steps or conditional branches, because a central coordinator holds the state machine in one readable place; choreography fits two or three loosely-coupled steps.
Q: What must be true of every saga step and compensator for retries to be safe?
A: They must be idempotent, keyed on the saga ID, so a retried charge or a retried refund recognises it already ran and does not double-apply the effect.
```
lessons.deeper:
**The mechanism, spelled out.** A saga is a state machine over local ACID transactions. Each forward step `Tᵢ` has a compensator `Cᵢ` that semantically undoes it. On failure at step `k`, you run `C₍ₖ₋₁₎ … C₁` in reverse. The non-obvious requirements: every step must be **idempotent** (the coordinator may retry after a lost response, so `chargeCard` must not double-charge — key it on the saga ID), and every compensator must be **commutative-safe** and able to run even if the forward step's result was ambiguous. Sagas give you *atomicity* (all-or-nothing eventually) but explicitly **not isolation** — other transactions can observe the intermediate states, which is where the subtle bugs live.

**Orchestration vs choreography, concretely.** In *orchestration*, an `OrderSaga` object holds the state (`AWAITING_PAYMENT`, `AWAITING_STOCK`, `COMPENSATING`) and issues commands; the compensation flow is one readable method. In *choreography*, `Payment` emits `PaymentCharged`, `Inventory` listens and emits `StockReserved`, `Shipping` listens — and on failure `Shipping` emits `ShipmentFailed`, which `Inventory` and `Payment` must each listen for to trigger their own compensation. No single place holds the flow.

**Concrete scenario.** Order fulfilment: charge €50, reserve one unit of SKU-123, book a courier. The courier API returns 503. The orchestrator runs `releaseStock(SKU-123)` then `refund(€50)`. The isolation gap: between "stock reserved" and "stock released," a second customer saw the item as out of stock — a real, observable intermediate state a 2PC transaction would have hidden.

**The failure mode people get wrong: unreliable compensation and lost isolation.** Teams assume `refund` always succeeds — but the payment provider can be down exactly when you need to compensate, so compensators themselves need retries, a dead-letter queue, and an alert for stuck sagas. And they forget the isolation gap: money is charged before the order is confirmed, stock is held mid-flight. You mitigate with *semantic locks* (mark the record `PENDING` so others treat it carefully) and by ordering steps so the reversible/cheap ones run first.

**Common follow-ups**

- *"Orchestration or choreography — which do you pick?"* — Orchestration for complex flows (4+ steps, conditional branches) because the state machine is explicit and debuggable; choreography for 2–3 loosely-coupled steps where a central coordinator is overkill.
- *"Why not two-phase commit?"* — 2PC needs a blocking coordinator holding locks across services for the whole transaction; it doesn't scale and it stalls everything if the coordinator dies mid-commit. Sagas trade isolation for availability.
- *"What if a compensation itself fails?"* — Retry with backoff, then dead-letter and alert a human. Compensators must be idempotent so retries are safe; a permanently stuck saga is an operational, not silent, failure.
- *"How do you make steps idempotent?"* — Key every operation on the saga/transaction ID so a retried `charge` or `reserve` recognises it already ran and returns the prior result instead of repeating the effect.

chapters.title: DDD & boundaries
chapters.summary: How to decide where a service or module boundary actually goes — the DDD vocabulary plus Conway’s Law.

lessons.title: Bounded contexts
lessons.body:
A bounded context is an explicit boundary within which a domain model — its objects, rules, and vocabulary — is internally consistent. Outside that boundary, the same word can mean something genuinely different.

Fowler's example: at a utility company, "meter" meant subtly different things in different parts of the org — the grid-to-location connection, the grid-to-customer connection, or the physical device. These are **polysemes**: the same word, genuinely different concepts. DDD's answer is *not* to force one canonical definition; it is to give each context its own precise model and map explicitly between them.

**Why it matters practically:** this is the DDD concept that maps most directly onto "where do I put the service/module boundary." A bounded context is a *candidate* boundary — not automatically one, but the strongest signal you have.

**How to spot one:** look for where the *language changes*. If the "Customer" the sales team means (a lead, a deal stage) is a fundamentally different concept from the "Customer" support means (a ticket history, an entitlement), you have found a context boundary — even if today's code has one `Customer` class serving both.

```flow
dir: LR
word: Word Customer | step
sales: Sales context | store
support: Support context | store
lead: Lead, deal stage | step
ticket: Tickets, entitlement | step
word -> sales : means
word -> support : means
sales -> lead : models as
support -> ticket : models as
```

```recall
Q: Why does DDD refuse to force one canonical definition of a polyseme like "meter"?
A: Because the term genuinely means different concepts in different parts of the org; a single canonical model would be wrong somewhere, so each context gets its own precise model with explicit mappings between them.
Q: What is the practical signal that you have found a bounded-context boundary?
A: The language changes: the same word names a fundamentally different concept, with different attributes and rules, in two parts of the system.
Q: Why is a bounded context only a candidate service boundary, not automatically one?
A: It is the strongest signal for where a boundary could go, but team structure, data ownership, and change cadence still decide whether splitting there is worth the cost.
```

lessons.title: Aggregates and the sizing mistake
lessons.body:
An aggregate is a cluster of domain objects treated as a single consistency unit for changes. One member is the **aggregate root** — the only object external code may reference directly; everything else inside is reached through it. The aggregate's job is to enforce its own **invariants** (business rules that must always hold) within a single transaction boundary.

**The common mistake is aggregates that are too large.** Modelling an entire `Order` — all its line items, shipments, and payment history — as one aggregate that must be loaded and locked together for any change creates contention (two people can't edit different line items at once) and makes the transaction boundary far bigger than the invariant that actually needs protecting.

**The corrective heuristic:** make aggregates as small as possible while still fully enforcing their invariant. If two pieces of data don't need to be transactionally consistent with each other *right now*, they probably don't belong in the same aggregate — reference the other aggregate by ID and accept eventual consistency between them.

```flow
dir: LR
order: Order root | step
line: LineItem | step
ship: Shipment | store
pay: Payment | store
order -> line : one tx
order --> ship : by id, eventual
order --> pay : by id, eventual
```

This is the same instinct as boundary-drawing one level down: keep together only what must change together atomically.

```recall
Q: Why is an aggregate that is too large a problem?
A: It forces unrelated data to be loaded and locked together for any change, creating contention (two edits cannot proceed at once) and a transaction boundary far wider than the invariant actually needs.
Q: What is the rule for deciding whether two entities belong in the same aggregate?
A: Keep them together only if they must be transactionally consistent right now; if not, reference the other by ID and accept eventual consistency between the two aggregates.
Q: Why is the aggregate root the only object external code may reference?
A: So the root can enforce its invariants in one transaction boundary; letting outside code mutate inner members directly would bypass those rules and corrupt consistency.
```

lessons.title: Where to draw the boundary
lessons.body:
Synthesising DDD into practical heuristics for "where does this line go":

1. **Business capability alignment** — a boundary should correspond to something the business does as a unit ("pricing," "fulfillment," "identity"), not to a technical layer. There should never be a "database service."
2. **Data ownership** — if two pieces of data are always read and written together and nothing else touches one without the other, they belong together. If a team constantly needs another team's data to do its job, either the boundary is wrong or you need a clean, explicit contract (API/event) across it, not a shared table.
3. **Team size / Conway's Law** — the org that owns a boundary needs to be a real, coherent team, not a line that cuts across half of two teams.
4. **Change cadence** — parts that change for different reasons, on different timelines, owned by different stakeholders, are a signal *for* a boundary. Parts that always change together are a signal *against* splitting them — splitting them just adds cross-service coordination for changes that were always going to ship together anyway.

The mistake to avoid: drawing boundaries around nouns you happen to see in the code, rather than around the things that change independently.

```steps
Capability | Align the boundary with something the business does as a unit, never a technical layer
Data ownership | Keep data that is always read and written together on one side of the line
Team / Conway | Make sure one real coherent team can own the boundary end to end
Change cadence | Split parts that change for different reasons on different timelines; keep together parts that always change at once
```

```recall
Q: Why is "a database service" a boundary anti-pattern?
A: Boundaries should align with business capabilities, not technical layers; a database service splits a horizontal layer, so every capability must cross it to do anything, which couples everyone to it.
Q: Change cadence points both ways. When is it a signal for a boundary and when against?
A: Different reasons, timelines, and stakeholders for change argue for a boundary; parts that always change together argue against splitting, since a split only adds cross-service coordination for changes that would ship together anyway.
Q: What is the core mistake these heuristics are meant to prevent?
A: Drawing boundaries around nouns seen in the code rather than around the things that genuinely change, are owned, and are consistent independently.
```

lessons.title: Conway's Law
lessons.body:
Melvin Conway, 1968: "Any organization that designs a system will produce a design whose structure is a copy of the organization's communication structure." Fowler's gloss: "if a single team writes a compiler, it will be a one-pass compiler; if the team is divided into two, it will be a two-pass compiler."

The mechanism is human, not technical: software coupling is enabled by human communication. If you can talk easily to the author of some code, it is easier to build shared understanding, which makes your code more coupled to theirs — through shared assumptions, not just function calls. Fowler adds: "if an architecture is designed at odds with the development organization's structure, then tensions appear in the software structure."

**Inverse Conway Maneuver:** deliberately reorganise teams into the shape you want the *architecture* to end up in, rather than designing an architecture and hoping the org follows. If you want a modular architecture, structure teams around those modules first; the architecture follows the communication paths. The modern operational lens on this is *Team Topologies* (stream-aligned, platform, enabling, and complicated-subsystem teams).

```flow
dir: LR
org: Team structure | actor
comm: Communication paths | step
arch: System structure | store
org -> comm : shapes
comm -> arch : copies into
arch --> org : tension if mismatched
```

**Interview framing:** Conway's Law is one of the highest-leverage things to raise unprompted when discussing boundaries. It reframes "how should I split this system" as inseparable from "how is my organisation structured, and can I change it." Reasoning about boundaries purely technically — data, traffic — while ignoring the org dimension is exactly the half senior interviewers listen for.

```recall
Q: What is the mechanism behind Conway's Law, and why is it human rather than technical?
A: Easy communication between authors builds shared understanding and shared assumptions, which couples their code; so coupling tracks the org's communication structure, not just its function calls.
Q: What is the Inverse Conway Maneuver and when would you use it?
A: Reshape teams into the architecture you want so the design follows the communication paths; use it when you want a target architecture rather than designing one and hoping the org conforms.
Q: Why is reasoning about boundaries only technically a weak answer in an interview?
A: Because architecture copies the org's communication structure, so ignoring team structure means your boundaries will fight the org and tension will show up in the code regardless of the technical split.
```

chapters.title: Cross-cutting concerns
chapters.summary: Resilience, observability, API evolution, and release patterns — the concerns that cut across every service regardless of style.

lessons.title: Circuit breaker
lessons.body:
Wrap calls to a dependency in a state machine: **closed** (calls pass through), **open** (after enough failures, fail fast without calling the dependency), **half-open** (after a cooldown, let one trial request through to test recovery).

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Caller
    participant B as Breaker
    participant D as Dependency
    C->>B: request
    B->>D: forward (closed)
    D-->>B: errors pile up
    Note over B: threshold hit -> OPEN
    C->>B: request
    B-->>C: fail fast (no call to D)
    Note over B: cooldown -> HALF-OPEN
    C->>B: request
    B->>D: trial call
    D-->>B: success -> CLOSED again
```

**When it wins:** it stops a caller from wasting threads and connections hammering a dependency that is already down, and it prevents **cascading failure** — one slow dependency taking down every service that calls it by exhausting their resources waiting.

**Pitfall:** tuned too aggressively, it trips on transient blips and makes a healthy system look down; too loosely, it doesn't protect you in time. It must be paired with a sane fallback (cached data, degraded response) — "fail fast" alone just moves the outage to the caller.

**One recency note:** Netflix's Hystrix popularised this pattern but has been in maintenance mode since 2018 and was dropped from Spring Cloud. The current reference implementation is resilience4j (JVM), Polly (.NET), or opossum (Node). Citing Hystrix as your *current* tool in 2026 is a stale-knowledge signal.

```recall
Q: What does the open state do, and why is that the point of the breaker?
A: It fails fast without calling the dependency after failures cross a threshold, so the caller stops wasting threads and connections on a dependency that is already down and cannot cascade its failure upward.
Q: Why must a circuit breaker be paired with a fallback?
A: "Fail fast" alone just relocates the outage to the caller as instant errors; the value comes from what the open state serves instead, such as cached data, a degraded response, or a queued async path.
Q: What does the half-open state prevent?
A: Flapping straight back into a still-broken dependency; after cooldown it admits only a few trial calls and reopens on any failure, so full traffic resumes only once the dependency is actually healthy.
Q: Why should slow calls, not just errors, count toward tripping the breaker?
A: A dependency at very high latency is not returning errors but is still exhausting your thread pool just as effectively, so counting slow calls catches the resource exhaustion a status-code check would miss.
```
lessons.deeper:
**The state machine, with the thresholds that actually matter.** Three states, and the transitions are threshold-driven, not vibes:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Caller
    participant B as Breaker
    Note over B: CLOSED — count failures in a rolling window
    C->>B: call fails past threshold
    Note over B: failure rate >= 50% over >= 20 calls -> OPEN
    C->>B: call while OPEN
    B-->>C: fail fast instantly
    Note over B: cooldown 30s elapses -> HALF-OPEN
    C->>B: limited trial calls
    Note over B: trials succeed -> CLOSED; any fail -> OPEN
```

- **Closed:** calls pass through; the breaker counts failures over a *rolling window* — the key config is a **failure-rate threshold over a minimum call volume** (e.g. resilience4j default: open when ≥50% of the last ≥20 calls fail — the volume floor stops one bad call in a quiet period from tripping it).
- **Open:** every call fails fast (no downstream call) for a fixed **cooldown** (e.g. 30s), giving the dependency room to recover.
- **Half-open:** after cooldown, admit a small number of *trial* calls; if they succeed, close; if any fail, re-open and restart the cooldown. This is what prevents flapping straight back into a still-broken dependency.

Also count **slow calls** as failures (resilience4j does): a dependency at p99 = 10s isn't erroring, but it's exhausting your thread pool just as effectively as one returning 500s.

**Concrete scenario.** A checkout service calls a fraud-scoring API with a 200ms budget. The fraud API degrades to 8s latency. Without a breaker, checkout threads block on those 8s calls, the thread pool saturates, and checkout — a healthy service — goes down because of a *dependency's* slowness. With a breaker configured on slow-call rate, it opens after the fraud API's slow-call rate crosses 50%, and checkout instantly falls back to "approve with async review," staying up.

**The failure mode people get wrong: a breaker with no fallback.** "Fail fast" without a fallback just relocates the outage — the caller now errors instantly instead of slowly. The breaker's value is realised by what happens in the open state: serve cached/stale data, a degraded response, or a queued async path. Second common mistake: tuning too tight (trips on transient blips, false outages) or too loose (never protects in time). Tune against real traffic, not guesses.

**Common follow-ups**

- *"Circuit breaker vs retry — when each?"* — Retry handles *transient* single-call failures; the breaker handles *sustained* dependency failure. Pair them, but never retry while open (that defeats the point). Retries feed the breaker's failure count.
- *"What thresholds do you set?"* — A failure-rate % over a minimum call volume, a cooldown before half-open, and a slow-call duration threshold. Numbers come from the dependency's SLO and your latency budget, not defaults.
- *"How does it prevent cascading failure?"* — By capping resources spent on a down dependency, so one failing service can't exhaust the thread/connection pools of everything calling it.
- *"Why is Hystrix a red flag now?"* — Maintenance mode since 2018, dropped from Spring Cloud. Current tools: resilience4j, Polly, opossum.

lessons.title: Retry with backoff and jitter
lessons.body:
On a transient failure, retry after a delay that grows exponentially (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s), with randomised **jitter** added so many clients retrying at once don't all hit the dependency at the same instant. AWS's own Builders' Library guidance is the primary source here.

Without jitter, synchronised retries turn a brief blip into a **retry storm**: the dependency recovers for a moment, every client retries in the same instant, and it falls over again.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C1 as Client 1
    participant C2 as Client 2
    participant C3 as Client 3
    participant D as Dependency
    Note over C1,C3: no jitter - all retry at t+2s
    C1->>D: retry
    C2->>D: retry
    C3->>D: retry
    D-->>C1: overloaded again
    Note over C1,C3: with jitter - retries spread out
    C1->>D: retry (t+1.7s)
    C2->>D: retry (t+2.3s)
    C3->>D: retry (t+2.9s)
```

**Two hard rules.** First, retrying a *non-idempotent* operation (e.g. "charge the card") without an idempotency key can double-charge — so make the operation idempotent before you retry it. Second, retries must always be bounded (max attempts) and paired with a timeout; an unbounded retry loop against a dead dependency never gives up.

```steps
Attempt | Call the dependency with an explicit timeout
Classify | Retry only transient failures; fail fast on 4xx and permanent errors
Backoff | Wait an exponentially growing delay: 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s
Jitter | Add randomness to the delay so clients do not retry in the same instant
Bound | Stop after max attempts and surface the failure instead of looping forever
```

```recall
Q: What is a retry storm and how does jitter prevent it?
A: Synchronised clients all retry at the same instant and knock a recovering dependency back over; jitter randomises each client's delay so retries spread out instead of landing together.
Q: Why must you make an operation idempotent before retrying it?
A: Because at-least-once retries can re-send a non-idempotent operation like "charge the card," double-applying the effect; an idempotency key lets the server recognise and ignore the duplicate.
Q: Why must retries always be bounded and paired with a timeout?
A: An unbounded retry loop against a dead dependency never gives up, wasting resources and hiding the outage; a max-attempt cap plus per-call timeout forces the failure to surface.
```

lessons.title: Bulkhead and cell-based isolation
lessons.body:
Isolate resources — thread pools, connection pools, or whole deployment units — per dependency or per tenant, so one dependency's failure or one tenant's abusive load can't exhaust resources shared by everything else. Named after ship bulkheads that keep a hull breach from sinking the whole vessel.

**When it wins:** multi-tenant systems, or any system calling several downstream dependencies with very different reliability profiles. Without a bulkhead, one flaky dependency's slow calls can consume the entire thread pool and starve calls to healthy dependencies too.

**Bulkhead at scale — cell-based architecture.** AWS's Well-Architected Framework treats cell-based architecture explicitly as a bulkhead pattern applied to whole deployment units: "a cell-based architecture uses multiple isolated instances of a workload... each cell is independent, does not share state with other cells, and handles a subset of the overall workload requests." A request is routed to exactly one cell (via a partition key cached at login), and a failure inside a cell cannot escape it. InfoQ's 2025 trends panel calls it out as a rising resilience technique, connected to a string of 2025 cloud outages where one shared service or config change triggered cascading failures across everything.

```flow
dir: LR
req: Request | actor
router: Router | gate
c1: Cell 1 | store
c2: Cell 2 | store
c3: Cell 3 | store
req -> router : partition key
router -> c1 : subset A
router -> c2 : subset B
router -> c3 : subset C
```

```recall
Q: What resource exhaustion does a bulkhead prevent that a timeout alone does not?
A: One flaky dependency's slow calls consuming the entire shared thread or connection pool and starving calls to healthy dependencies; isolating a pool per dependency contains that blast radius.
Q: How does cell-based architecture apply the bulkhead idea at deployment scale?
A: Each cell is an independent instance of the whole workload handling a subset of requests with no shared state, so a failure inside one cell cannot escape to the others.
Q: Why is a partition key central to cell-based isolation?
A: It routes each request to exactly one cell deterministically, so a tenant or request stays contained in its cell and a cell failure affects only that subset of traffic.
```

lessons.title: Timeout budgets
lessons.body:
Every call to a dependency needs an explicit timeout. And in a call chain — A calls B calls C — each hop's timeout must be shorter than the *remaining* budget of the hop that called it, so a slow leaf service doesn't make every caller up the chain wait the maximum possible time.

```flow
dir: LR
a: A budget 3s | step
b: B budget 2s | step
c: C budget 1s | step
a -> b : calls, 2s cap
b -> c : calls, 1s cap
```

The concrete failure this prevents: if A gives itself 3s but calls B with no timeout, and B calls a dead C, then A's threads pile up waiting on a call that will never return — exhausting A's pool for *unrelated* requests too. That is the single most common way one dependency's outage becomes everyone's outage.

The rule of thumb: at each hop, spend only a fraction of the budget you were given, and reserve the rest for the caller's own work and for a fallback. Timeouts are the first, cheapest line of defence — the one that circuit breakers and bulkheads build on top of. If a call can block, it needs a timeout, full stop.

```recall
Q: Why must each hop's timeout be shorter than the remaining budget of its caller?
A: So a slow leaf cannot force every caller up the chain to wait its own maximum; the inner timeout fires first and returns control before the outer budget is exhausted.
Q: What concrete failure does a missing timeout on a dependency cause?
A: Threads pile up waiting on a call that may never return, exhausting the caller's thread pool and taking down unrelated requests too, so one dependency's outage becomes everyone's.
Q: Why are timeouts described as the foundation that circuit breakers and bulkheads build on?
A: They bound how long any single call can block; without that bound, breakers and bulkheads have nothing to measure or isolate against, so a blocking call still starves resources.
```

lessons.title: Observability and OpenTelemetry
lessons.body:
The observability triad, and what each is *for*:
- **Logs** — discrete, timestamped event records; best for "what exactly happened at this point."
- **Metrics** — aggregated numeric time series (request rate, error rate, latency percentiles); best for "is the system healthy right now" and for alerting.
- **Traces** — the path of a single request across services, showing where time went at each hop; best for "why was *this* request slow" in a distributed system.

**OpenTelemetry (OTel) is the current standard**, and this is a genuinely recent, datable shift. All three signals — traces, metrics, and logs — reached GA in 2025 (logs lagged the other two for years), and OTel formally graduated as a CNCF project in 2026, described as "the de facto standard for open source observability" with the second-highest project velocity in the cloud-native ecosystem after Kubernetes.

**Why it matters practically:** OTel gives you one vendor-neutral instrumentation API across all three signals, plus a Collector that fans data out to whatever backend you use (Datadog, Grafana, Honeycomb, CloudWatch). Instrument with OTel semantic conventions rather than a vendor-proprietary agent where you have the choice — otherwise switching observability vendors later becomes a full re-instrumentation project.

```flow
dir: LR
app: Instrumented app | step
sdk: OTel SDK/API | step
col: OTel Collector | step
back1: Vendor A | store
back2: Vendor B | store
app -> sdk : logs/metrics/traces
sdk -> col : OTLP export
col -> back1 : fan out
col -> back2 : swap vendor
```

```recall
Q: Why reach for a trace rather than a metric when a single request is slow?
A: Metrics are aggregated time series that tell you the system's overall health, so they cannot explain one request; a trace shows that request's path across services and where time went at each hop.
Q: What does the OTel Collector buy you that a vendor agent does not?
A: One vendor-neutral instrumentation that fans data out to any backend, so switching observability vendors is a Collector config change rather than a full re-instrumentation project.
Q: When would you alert on a metric instead of on logs or traces?
A: For "is the system healthy right now" signals like error rate and latency percentiles; those are aggregate numeric series suited to thresholds, whereas logs and traces are for diagnosing a specific event after an alert fires.
```

lessons.title: API versioning and evolution
lessons.body:
The core principle across nearly every current source: **version only when you make a genuinely breaking change.** Prefer backward-compatible, additive evolution whenever possible, because versioning is itself a maintenance cost.

```flow
dir: LR
change: Proposed change | step
q: Breaking? | gate
add: Ship additively | step
ver: Cut new version | step
dep: Deprecate old | step
change -> q
q -> add : no
q -> ver : yes
ver -> dep : Sunset header
```

Strategies, with a practical split:
- **URI versioning** (`/v1/orders`) — the pragmatic default for public APIs: visible, cache-friendly, trivially routable at a gateway.
- **Header-based versioning** (a custom header or `Accept` media-type) — better for internal services where you control every client, since URIs stay stable. It is the one most poorly implemented in practice: teams forget to enforce that clients send it and silently default to "latest," which quietly breaks old clients.
- **Date-based versioning** — pin a client to a release date, resolve internally; the more granular option, common where an API ships frequent additive changes.

**The trap:** "additive" is not the same as "safe." Adding a new optional field or a new endpoint is generally safe; renaming or removing a field, changing a field's type, or changing existing behaviour is breaking — even if the JSON shape looks unchanged. Adding a *required* field, or a new enum value an old client's switch statement doesn't handle, breaks clients despite looking additive.

**Deprecation:** announce with real dates, use a `Sunset` HTTP header where applicable, and give clients a genuine migration window rather than a silent cutover.

```recall
Q: Why is adding a new required field a breaking change even though it looks additive?
A: Existing clients do not send the field, so requests that worked before now fail validation; "additive" only means safe when old clients keep working unchanged.
Q: When would you choose header or media-type versioning over URI versioning?
A: For internal services where you control every client and want URIs to stay stable; its risk is that teams forget to enforce the header and silently default to latest, breaking old clients.
Q: What does the Sunset header plus a dated deprecation window prevent?
A: A silent cutover; it gives clients explicit notice and time to migrate before the old version stops working.
```

lessons.title: Feature flags
lessons.body:
Feature flags **decouple deploy from release**. You ship code to production dark, then turn it on for a subset of traffic — internal users, a percentage rollout, a specific tenant — independent of the deploy pipeline. This splits "did the deploy work" and "was the feature a good idea" into two separable questions instead of one high-stakes moment.

```flow
dir: LR
deploy: Deploy dark | step
flag: Flag off | gate
intl: Internal users | step
pct: 1 to 100 percent | step
all: Full release | store
deploy -> flag : code in prod
flag -> intl : enable subset
intl -> pct : ramp
pct -> all : if healthy
pct --> flag : kill switch off
```

**Patterns:**
- **Boolean kill-switch** — the fastest rollback path; flip a feature off without a redeploy if something goes wrong.
- **Percentage rollout** — ramp from 1% to 100% while watching metrics.
- **Targeting rules** — by user attribute, tenant, or region.
- **Multi-variate flags** — for A/B experimentation.

**Risks.** The main one is **flag debt**: flags that outlive their purpose and never get cleaned up, leaving dead conditional branches and a combinatorial testing surface. The other is using a flag as a permanent substitute for a real rollback path — a flag is a *temporary* decoupling mechanism, not a substitute for deploy hygiene. Give every flag an owner and an expiry.

```recall
Q: What two questions does decoupling deploy from release let you ask separately?
A: "Did the deploy work" and "was the feature a good idea"; the code ships dark first, so a deploy problem and a feature problem no longer collapse into one high-stakes moment.
Q: Why is a boolean kill-switch the fastest rollback path?
A: It turns a feature off without a redeploy, so you recover in seconds by flipping a flag instead of waiting for a pipeline to ship the previous build.
Q: What is flag debt and how do you prevent it?
A: Flags that outlive their purpose, leaving dead branches and a combinatorial test surface; prevent it by giving every flag an owner and an expiry so stale flags get removed.
```

lessons.title: Blue-green, canary, and rolling
lessons.body:
Three ways to ship a new version without a hard cutover:

- **Rolling deployment** — replace old instances with new ones gradually, a few at a time. Simple, but both versions run at once during the rollout, so your API and data must tolerate both simultaneously.
- **Blue-green** — run two full, identical production environments (blue = current live, green = new), and switch all traffic at the router level at once. Rollback is instant (flip back to blue), but you need double the infrastructure during the switch, and any shared stateful resource (the database) still needs its own compatibility story.
- **Canary** — release the new version to a small slice of real traffic first, watch key metrics (error rate, latency), then progressively widen the slice if healthy or roll back fast if not. Lowest blast radius, at the cost of needing good real-time observability to detect a bad canary before it is fully out.

```flow
dir: LR
traffic: Live traffic | actor
router: Router split | gate
old: Old version | store
canary: Canary new | store
metrics: Watch metrics | gate
traffic -> router
router -> old : most traffic
router -> canary : small slice
canary -> metrics
metrics -> router : healthy, widen
metrics --> old : bad, roll back
```

**The common thread:** none of these are safe without the observability to detect a problem quickly (the OTel section) and the resilience patterns — timeouts, circuit breakers — to contain a problem's blast radius while you roll back. These are not independent topics; they compose into one story about shipping safely.

```recall
Q: What makes blue-green rollback instant, and what does it cost?
A: Both full environments run in parallel, so you flip the router back to blue immediately; the cost is double the infrastructure during the switch plus a compatibility story for any shared stateful resource like the database.
Q: Why does a canary have the lowest blast radius of the three?
A: It exposes only a small slice of real traffic to the new version while you watch metrics, so a bad release harms few users and can be rolled back before it is fully out.
Q: What must be true of your API and data during a rolling deployment?
A: Both versions run at once during the rollout, so the API contract and data schema must tolerate old and new instances simultaneously.
Q: Why are these patterns unsafe without observability and resilience patterns?
A: You need metrics to detect a bad release quickly and timeouts/circuit breakers to contain its blast radius while you roll back; without them a gradual rollout just spreads the failure slowly.
```

chapters.title: Messaging & event flow
chapters.summary: How services talk asynchronously — and what goes wrong when they do.

lessons.title: Message queues vs pub/sub
lessons.body:
Both decouple a sender from a receiver so work happens asynchronously, but they differ in *who gets the message*.

A **message queue** (point-to-point) delivers each message to exactly **one** consumer. Many workers can read from the same queue, but a given message is processed once — this is **work distribution**. Use it to spread a backlog of tasks (send email, resize image) across a worker pool. SQS, RabbitMQ.

```flow
dir: LR
prod: Producer | actor
q: Task queue | store
w1: Worker 1 | step
w2: Worker 2 | step
w3: Worker 3 | step
prod -> q : enqueue tasks
q -> w1 : msg to one
q -> w2 : msg to one
q -> w3 : msg to one
```

**Pub/sub** (publish-subscribe) delivers each message to **every** subscriber. The publisher doesn't know who's listening; N independent consumers each get their own copy. Use it for **event fan-out** — one "order placed" event feeds billing, inventory, and analytics, each reacting independently. Kafka topics, SNS, Google Pub/Sub.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Publisher
    participant T as Topic
    participant Billing
    participant Inventory
    participant Analytics
    P->>T: "order placed"
    T->>Billing: event copy
    T->>Inventory: event copy
    T->>Analytics: event copy
```

The interview distinction: "one consumer does this work" → queue; "many systems need to know this happened" → pub/sub. Kafka blurs the line — it's a durable log where **consumer groups** give you queue semantics (one group = one logical consumer) while multiple groups give you pub/sub.

```recall
Q: What is the one-sentence rule for choosing a queue versus pub/sub?
A: If one consumer should do the work, use a queue (each message to exactly one worker); if many systems need to know the event happened, use pub/sub (each subscriber gets its own copy).
Q: How does Kafka provide both semantics with consumer groups?
A: Within one consumer group the partitions are split so each message is handled once (queue semantics); adding more independent groups makes each group receive its own full copy (pub/sub fan-out).
Q: Why does pub/sub decouple the publisher from scaling consumers?
A: The publisher does not know who is listening, so you can add or remove subscribers without changing the producer, each reacting independently to the same event.
```

lessons.title: Backpressure & dead letter queues
lessons.body:
Async messaging introduces two failure modes you must answer for.

**Backpressure** — what happens when producers outpace consumers? Messages pile up. A little buffering is the *point* of a queue (it absorbs bursts), but unbounded growth means rising latency and eventual memory/disk exhaustion. Handling it: let the queue buffer bursts, **scale consumers** when depth grows (autoscale on queue length), and if the source is synchronous, **shed load** — reject or slow producers rather than fall over. The anti-pattern is pretending the queue is infinite.

```flow
dir: LR
prod: Producers | actor
q: Queue depth | store
check: Depth rising? | gate
scale: Autoscale consumers | step
shed: Shed load | gate
prod -> q : enqueue
q -> check
check -> scale : yes
scale --> shed : still growing
shed --> prod : reject or slow
```

**Dead letter queue (DLQ)** — what happens to a message that keeps failing? A consumer that can't process a message (bad data, downstream is down) shouldn't retry it forever and block the queue, nor drop it silently. After N failed attempts the message is moved to a **dead letter queue** — a side queue for poison messages.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Q as Main queue
    participant W as Worker
    participant DLQ as Dead letter queue
    Q->>W: message (attempt 1)
    W-->>Q: fail, requeue
    Q->>W: message (attempt 2, 3…)
    W-->>DLQ: still failing → move to DLQ
    Note over DLQ: inspect, fix, replay later
```

The DLQ turns "a bad message silently wedges the pipeline" into "a bad message is set aside for a human to inspect and replay" — which is why it's a standard part of any serious queue design. Pair it with idempotent consumers, since at-least-once delivery means the same message can arrive twice.

```recall
Q: Why is "the queue will buffer it" an unsafe answer to backpressure?
A: Buffering absorbs bursts, but unbounded growth raises latency and eventually exhausts memory or disk; you must scale consumers on depth and, for synchronous sources, shed load rather than treat the queue as infinite.
Q: What problem does a dead letter queue solve that endless retries do not?
A: A poison message retried forever blocks the queue and burns capacity; moving it to a DLQ after N attempts sets it aside for inspection and replay without wedging the pipeline or dropping it silently.
Q: Why must DLQ-based designs pair with idempotent consumers?
A: At-least-once delivery and retries mean the same message can be processed more than once, so consumers must produce the same effect on a duplicate as on the first delivery.
```

chapters.summary: Tokens, sampling, attention and the KV cache, embeddings, and how to pick a model: the mechanics that explain cost, latency and quality.

lessons.title: Tokens, context windows, and cost
lessons.body:
A model never sees your text. It sees tokens: integer ids for sub-word pieces produced by a tokenizer. Everything downstream, context limits, latency, and the bill, is counted in tokens, not words or characters. Interviewers probe this because an engineer who thinks in words will mis-size a window, under-budget cost, and be surprised when non-English input costs double.

## How tokenization works

Most frontier models use byte-pair encoding (BPE) or a close variant. BPE starts from raw bytes and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new symbol, learning a fixed vocabulary (tens of thousands of tokens) from a training corpus. Common words become one token; rare words split into pieces; arbitrary bytes always have a fallback, so nothing is unencodable.

A rough rule for English: 1 token is about 4 characters, or about 0.75 words. So 1000 tokens is roughly 750 English words. This ratio is only a heuristic. Code, punctuation, numbers, and non-English scripts break it.

> **Rule of thumb.** For English prose, tokens are about 1.33x the word count. Treat this as an estimate for budgeting, then measure with the real tokenizer before you quote a cost.

## Context window: input plus output share one budget

The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can attend to in a single call, and it is shared by input and output. If the window is 200k tokens and your prompt is 190k, you have at most 10k tokens of output left. Many APIs let you cap output with a `max_tokens` parameter; set it, because an uncapped generation can run until it hits the window and bill you for every token.

```stack
title: What fills a 200k token window (illustrative)
unit: k tokens
System prompt | 2 | fixed, cacheable
Tool schemas | 6 | fixed, cacheable
Retrieved chunks | 24 | per query
Chat history | 40 | grows every turn
User message | 1
Output reserve | 8
```

The chat-history segment is the dangerous one: it grows every turn, so a long conversation silently eats the budget retrieval and output need. This is why agents compact history and why RAG trims to top-k chunks instead of stuffing documents.

```check
Q: The window is 200k tokens and your prompt is 196k. You need a 6k-token report. How much report can you get?
- All 6k tokens, because output has its own separate budget
* At most about 4k tokens, because input and output share the window
- All 6k tokens, because the model drops the oldest prompt tokens
Why: The context window counts input and output together, so 196k of input leaves about 4k for output. Output has no separate budget, and the model does not quietly drop your prompt to make room: depending on the API, the call fails or the output stops at the limit. Shorten the prompt or use a model with a larger window.
```

## Prefill and decode: two different costs

A request runs in two phases.

- Prefill: the model processes the whole input in parallel to build its internal state. This is compute-heavy but one pass.
- Decode: the model generates output one token at a time, each token depending on all previous ones. This is sequential.

```flow
dir: LR
in: Input tokens | actor
pre: Prefill pass | model
dec: Decode loop | model
out: Output tokens | actor
in -> pre : full prompt
pre -> dec : state ready
dec -> dec : one token
dec -> out : stream
```

The split matters for both latency and price. Time to first token is dominated by prefill (how long your input is). Time between tokens is dominated by decode. Providers often price input and output tokens differently, with output more expensive, because decode is the slower, serial phase.

## Why cost and latency scale with tokens

Every token in the window is processed, so doubling the prompt roughly doubles prefill work, and every extra output token is another serial decode step. There is no free context: a longer system prompt is paid on every single call. This is the core reason retrieval beats dumping everything into a huge window, and the reason prompt caching exists.

## Worked cost arithmetic (illustrative)

Do not quote live per-token prices as fact, they move. Reason in ratios. Suppose a provider charges input at 1 unit per 1k tokens and output at 3 units per 1k tokens (illustrative).

| Call | Input tokens | Output tokens | Cost (units) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Short Q and A | 500 | 200 | 0.5 + 0.6 = 1.1 |
| RAG answer | 6000 | 400 | 6.0 + 1.2 = 7.2 |
| Long agent turn | 40000 | 800 | 40.0 + 2.4 = 42.4 |

The agent turn costs almost 40x the short one, and nearly all of it is input. The lesson: input length is usually the cost driver in retrieval and agent systems, which is exactly what prompt caching attacks.

## Non-English and code inflate token counts

A tokenizer trained mostly on English spends more tokens per unit of meaning on other languages, because their characters and words were not merged into efficient single tokens. The same sentence can cost roughly 2x to 3x the tokens in some languages versus English, and far more for scripts far from the training distribution. Code also tokenizes less efficiently than prose because of punctuation, indentation, and identifiers.

```python
# Sketch: always measure, do not guess
enc = tokenizer_for(model)              # the model's own tokenizer
n_in = len(enc.encode(prompt))          # count before sending
budget = window - n_in - output_reserve # tokens left for the model
assert budget > 0, "prompt too large for the window"
```

> **Pitfall.** Estimating a non-English or code-heavy prompt with the English words-times-1.33 rule. You will under-count tokens, overflow the window, or under-budget cost. Count with the model's tokenizer.

```recall
Q: Input and output share one window. Why does an uncapped max_tokens risk a surprise bill?
A: Generation can run until it hits the window, so you pay for every output token up to that cap, and output tokens are usually the pricier kind. Set max_tokens.
Q: Why does a longer system prompt cost more than its one-time size suggests?
A: It is part of the input on every single call, so its token cost is paid per request, not once.
Q: Why does the same text cost more tokens in some non-English languages?
A: The tokenizer learned efficient merges mostly from English, so other scripts split into more, smaller tokens, inflating the count 2x to 3x or more.
Q: In a RAG or agent request, where does most of the cost usually come from?
A: Input tokens (retrieved context, history, tool schemas), which is why prompt caching and retrieval trimming matter more than shortening the answer.
```
lessons.deeper:
### Why BPE, and what the alternatives are

BPE (Sennrich et al., 2016, for NMT; popularised for GPT-2 as a byte-level variant) was chosen because it hits a sweet spot: a fixed vocabulary that keeps common words whole for efficiency, splits rare words into reusable pieces for coverage, and, in its byte-level form, can encode any input at all because every byte is a valid starting symbol. Alternatives include WordPiece (BERT) and Unigram/SentencePiece (used by many multilingual and open models), which pick merges by a probabilistic objective rather than raw frequency. The practical upshot is the same: text to integer ids, with a vocabulary fixed at training time.

### Counting tokens correctly

Use the model's own tokenizer, not a generic one. OpenAI documents its tokenizers (the `tiktoken` library; `o200k_base` for recent GPT-4-class models, `cl100k_base` for older ones). Anthropic exposes a token-counting endpoint so you can measure Claude prompts without a local encoder (as of 2026, re-check). Chat messages also carry a small per-message overhead for role and formatting tokens, so a precise budget adds a few tokens per message on top of the content.

### A sharper cost model

Total cost per call is approximately:

```text
cost = (input_tokens * price_in) + (output_tokens * price_out)
```

Two refinements matter in production. First, with prompt caching the input term splits into a cheap cached-prefix read and a full-price uncached remainder, so ordering the prompt so the stable part comes first can cut the input term substantially (see the prompt-caching lesson). Second, in multi-turn agents the input term grows every turn as history accumulates, so a conversation of N turns can have input cost scaling with N squared if history is never trimmed. Compaction and summarisation exist to break that curve.

### Context window is not free capacity

A larger window raises the ceiling, not the floor on cost. Sending 200k tokens because you can means paying prefill on 200k tokens and, often, worse accuracy as the useful signal gets diluted among distractors (the lost-in-the-middle effect, covered in the RAG-versus-long-context lesson). The window is a limit to respect, not a target to fill.

lessons.title: Sampling and determinism
lessons.body:
At each step the model outputs a score for every token in its vocabulary. How those scores become the next token is sampling, and it is the knob that decides whether the model is a careful extractor or a creative writer. Interviewers ask about this to see whether you know that temperature 0 is not a guarantee of determinism, and that the right setting depends on the task.

## From logits to a token

The raw per-token scores are logits. Softmax turns them into a probability distribution. Sampling then picks a token from that distribution. The decoding parameters reshape the distribution before the pick.

```flow
dir: LR
logits: Raw logits | model
temp: Temperature scale | step
soft: Softmax | step
trunc: top-p / top-k cut | gate
pick: Sample token | step
logits -> temp : scores
temp -> soft : scaled
soft -> trunc : probabilities
trunc -> pick : kept set
```

- Temperature divides the logits before softmax. Low temperature sharpens the distribution toward the top token; high temperature flattens it, giving rarer tokens a chance.
- Top-k keeps only the k highest-probability tokens, then renormalises and samples among them.
- Top-p (nucleus) keeps the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities sum to at least p, then samples among them. It adapts the cut to how peaked the distribution is.

## What temperature actually does to the distribution

```bars
title: Effect of temperature on token probability (illustrative)
unit: percent
Top token at temp 0.2 | 92
Top token at temp 0.7 | 61
Top token at temp 1.2 | 38
```

Lower temperature concentrates mass on the single best token, so output is more repetitive and predictable. Higher temperature spreads mass out, so output is more varied but more likely to drift or err. These numbers are illustrative, the exact shape depends on the model and the context.

## Which setting for which task

| Task | Temperature | top-p | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Extraction, classification, structured output | 0 to 0.2 | 1.0 | Want the single most-likely, repeatable answer |
| Code generation | 0 to 0.3 | 0.9 to 1.0 | Correctness over variety |
| Summarisation, QA | 0.2 to 0.5 | 0.9 | Slight variation, stay grounded |
| Brainstorming, creative drafts | 0.7 to 1.0 | 0.9 to 1.0 | Want diversity across runs |

> **Rule of thumb.** Change one of temperature or top-p, not both at once. They both prune the distribution, so tuning them together makes the effect hard to reason about.

## Temperature 0 is not guaranteed deterministic

Setting temperature to 0 makes the model pick the top token (greedy decoding), which should be deterministic in theory. In practice, hosted APIs are documented as non-deterministic by default. OpenAI states plainly that chat completions are non-deterministic and that even with a fixed `seed` and matching `system_fingerprint`, outputs are only mostly identical, with a small chance of divergence due to the inherent non-determinism of the models (OpenAI API docs and cookbook, as of 2026, re-check).

The causes are structural, not sampling noise: floating-point addition is not associative, so GPU kernels that sum in a different order give slightly different logits; batching and mixture-of-expert routing can change the computation depending on what else is in the batch; and backend configuration can change under you, which the `system_fingerprint` field is meant to signal.

> **Pitfall.** Writing an eval or a cache key that assumes temperature 0 means identical output. The rerun can differ on the same prompt, breaking exact-match caches and flaky-looking tests. Compare semantically or pin to a specific model and accept small variation.

## Seeds and reproducibility

Some providers expose a `seed` parameter to request reproducible sampling, and a `system_fingerprint` to tell you when the backend changed. Use them to reduce variance, but treat exact reproducibility as best-effort, not contractual. For anything that must be stable (regression evals, audit trails), log the full request, the model id, the fingerprint, and the raw output, so you can detect drift rather than assume it away.

```python
# Sketch: extraction wants determinism-as-far-as-possible
resp = client.generate(
    model="a-small-fast-model",
    prompt=prompt,
    temperature=0,      # greedy
    top_p=1.0,
    seed=42,            # best-effort reproducibility
    max_tokens=256,
)
log(resp.system_fingerprint, resp.text)  # record to detect backend drift
```

