After fusion you have a ranked candidate list, but it was produced by cheap methods. A cross-encoder reranker re-scores each query-candidate pair by reading them together in one model pass, which catches relevance the separate bi-encoder embeddings missed. It is accurate but slow, tens of milliseconds per pair, so you run it only on the small fused candidate set (say top twenty to fifty), never the whole corpus.

```bars
title: Where latency goes in a hybrid pipeline (illustrative)
unit: ms
BM25 search | 10
Dense ANN search | 15
RRF fusion | 1
Cross-encoder rerank top-30 | 300
```

The reranker dominates the latency budget, which is the central trade-off: it buys precision at real cost, so you tune the candidate count to balance accuracy against the deadline.

> **Rule of thumb.** Chip Huyen's advice, worth repeating: try keyword retrieval (BM25) before reaching for vector search. The cheap baseline is often strong, and a vector DB adds cost and can obscure exact-keyword matches. Add dense retrieval where it demonstrably helps, not by default.

```recall
Q: Why does fusing BM25 and dense retrieval beat either one alone?
A: Their failure modes are complementary. Dense misses exact identifiers and rare terms, BM25 misses synonyms and paraphrase. Fusing covers both query types with one pipeline.
Q: Why does RRF use ranks instead of the retrievers raw scores?
A: BM25 scores and cosine distances are on incompatible scales, so adding them directly is meaningless. Ranks are comparable across both lists, so fusing on position needs no score calibration.
Q: In the worked example D (ranks 1 and 3) beat E (ranks 2 and 2). What does that reveal about RRF?
A: It rewards strong agreement, being top in one list plus decent in the other narrowly beats being merely good in both. High placement in any list contributes a large term.
Q: Why run the cross-encoder on only the top candidates, not the whole corpus?
A: It reads each query-candidate pair jointly, tens of milliseconds each, far too slow for millions of documents. It only re-scores the small set the cheap retrievers already shortlisted.
Q: Chip Huyen suggests trying BM25 before vector search. Why is that the cheaper-first order?
A: BM25 needs no embedding model, no vector index, and no ANN tuning, yet is often strong on its own. You add dense retrieval only where it measurably helps, avoiding needless cost and complexity.
```
lessons.deeper:
### BM25 in one paragraph

BM25 scores a document for a query by summing, over the query terms it contains, a weight that rises with how often the term appears in the document (with diminishing returns, so a term repeated twenty times is not twenty times as strong) and with how rare the term is across the whole corpus (inverse document frequency, so common words like the contribute almost nothing). It also normalises for document length so a long document does not win just by containing more words. The result is a strong lexical baseline that has been the default in search engines for decades, and it is exactly the signal dense embeddings throw away when they compress text into a smooth semantic space.

### Implementing the fusion from scratch

The algorithm is deliberately small. Take two ranked lists of document ids. Build a dictionary mapping each document id to its accumulated score. For each list, walk it in rank order and add one over sixty plus rank to that document's entry, creating the entry at zero if it is new. After both lists are processed, sort the dictionary by value descending and return the top results. There is no training, no score normalisation, and no tuning beyond the single constant, which is why RRF became the default hybrid merge in OpenSearch, Elasticsearch, Azure AI Search, and others. A from-scratch implementation is a common interview drill precisely because it is short enough to write live and still forces you to explain why rank-based fusion avoids the score-scale problem.

```python
# Sketch: RRF over any number of ranked id lists
def rrf(lists, k=60):
    scores = {}
    for ranked in lists:                 # each is a list of doc ids, best first
        for rank, doc_id in enumerate(ranked, start=1):
            scores[doc_id] = scores.get(doc_id, 0.0) + 1.0 / (k + rank)
    return sorted(scores, key=scores.get, reverse=True)
```

### Weighted fusion and its tension with RRF

Plain RRF treats both retrievers as equally trustworthy. When one is clearly stronger on your workload you can weight its term, multiply the dense contribution by a factor above one, say, so its rankings count for more. The catch is that a weight is one more parameter to tune against an eval set, and tuning it wrong can make hybrid worse than the better single retriever. The honest default is unweighted RRF, which needs no tuning and is hard to beat, and you reach for weights only when a measured gap justifies the extra parameter. This is the same measure-before-tuning discipline that governs chunk size and k.

### Latency budgeting

The reranker is the expensive stage, so the candidate count feeding it is the main latency lever. Reranking thirty candidates at ten milliseconds each is three hundred milliseconds, reranking a hundred is a second, often past an interactive budget. If you must rerank more, run the two retrievals in parallel (they are independent) so their latencies overlap rather than add, and consider a smaller or distilled reranker. The decision rule: pick the candidate count as the largest your deadline allows, because reranker precision generally improves with more candidates up to a point, then set the retrieval k to feed it.

lessons.title: Query rewriting and routing
lessons.body:
The query a user types is rarely the query your retriever wants. It carries pronouns that only make sense in the chat so far, it is phrased as a question when your corpus is written as statements, or it bundles two questions that live in different documents. Query transformation is the layer that rewrites the raw input into one or more retrieval-ready queries before anything hits the index. Interviewers probe it because it is where cheap wins and expensive mistakes both live.

## Condensing chat history into a standalone query

In a conversation, retrieval must run on a self-contained query, but the user wrote what about its pricing. Embed that and you retrieve nothing useful, its has no referent in vector space. The fix is a condensation step: give a small model the recent turns and ask it to rewrite the latest message as a standalone question, what is the pricing of the enterprise plan. This is the single highest-value transform in any multi-turn RAG system and the first one to add.

```flow
dir: LR
hist: Chat history | store
msg: Latest message | actor
rw: Rewrite to standalone | model
ret: Retriever | store
hist -> rw : prior turns
msg -> rw : its pricing?
rw -> ret : enterprise plan pricing
```

## Multi-query, HyDE, and step-back

Three transforms generate better queries rather than just cleaning the current one.

- **Multi-query.** Ask a model to produce several paraphrases of the query, retrieve for each, and fuse the result lists. It covers vocabulary the user did not use, if the corpus says automobile and the user said car, a paraphrase bridges the gap.
- **HyDE** (Hypothetical Document Embeddings; Gao, Ma, Lin, Callan, Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels, 2022). Instead of embedding the question, ask the model to write a hypothetical answer, then embed that and retrieve. The generated passage shares vocabulary and shape with real answer documents, so it often sits closer to them in embedding space than the terse question does. The paper notes the document is fake and may contain false details, that is fine, because you embed it for its shape, never show it to the user.
- **Step-back prompting** (Zheng et al., Google DeepMind, Take a Step Back, 2023). For a narrow question, first ask a broader one, which school of physics governs this, retrieve the general principle, then answer. It helps reasoning-heavy questions where the specific phrasing retrieves trivia but the principle is what is needed.

## Decomposition for multi-hop questions

Some questions cannot be answered by any single chunk because they chain facts. Who succeeded the CEO who launched the Model Y needs the launcher of Model Y, then that person's successor, two retrievals, not one. Decomposition splits the question into sub-questions, retrieves and answers each, and composes the results. Attempting it as one retrieval fails quietly: the top chunks match the surface words and miss the hop.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant D as Decomposer
    participant R as Retriever
    participant A as Answerer
    U->>D: multi-hop question
    D->>R: sub-question 1
    R-->>D: fact 1
    D->>R: sub-question 2
    R-->>A: fact 2
    A-->>U: composed answer
```

## Routing: send the query to the right place

Routing is a classifier, often a small model or a few rules, that picks the destination for a query before retrieval. A query about last quarter's revenue goes to the finance index, a how-do-I question goes to the docs index, a greeting skips retrieval entirely and goes straight to a chat response. Routing keeps each index small and on-topic, which raises precision, and it avoids spending a retrieval round trip on queries that need none.

| Transform | What it fixes | Main cost |
|---|---|---|
| History condensation | Pronouns and context from prior turns | One small model call |
| Multi-query | Vocabulary mismatch, recall | N retrievals plus fusion |
| HyDE | Question and answer phrased differently | One generation per query |
| Step-back | Narrow phrasing retrieves trivia | One extra retrieval |
| Decomposition | Multi-hop, chained facts | Several retrievals, slower |
| Routing | Wrong index, wasted retrieval | One classification |

## When transformation hurts

Every transform adds a model call, so it adds latency and cost and introduces a new failure point, a bad rewrite retrieves worse than the raw query would have. For a short, well-formed, single-hop question against one clean index, the raw query is often best and transformation is pure overhead. Multi-query and decomposition multiply the retrieval load, so they can blow a latency budget on a path that needs an answer in under a second.

> **Interview.** Do not list transforms as a menu. Name the specific failure each one fixes, then say that for a simple single-hop query you would skip them, because the strong signal is knowing when the raw query already wins.

```recall
Q: Why must a multi-turn RAG system rewrite the user message before retrieving?
A: The raw message carries pronouns and context from earlier turns, so embedded alone it has no referent and retrieves poorly. Condensing it into a standalone query restores the meaning the retriever needs.
Q: HyDE embeds a hypothetical answer the model admits may be false. Why does that still improve retrieval?
A: You embed it for its shape and vocabulary, which match real answer documents more closely than the terse question does, so it lands nearer them in embedding space. It is never shown to the user, so its falseness is harmless.
Q: When does query decomposition beat a single retrieval, and why does the single retrieval fail?
A: On multi-hop questions that chain facts across documents. A single retrieval matches surface words and misses the intermediate fact, so no one chunk can answer it, decomposition retrieves each hop separately.
Q: What does routing buy you beyond picking an index?
A: It keeps each index small and on-topic, raising precision, and lets some queries skip retrieval entirely (greetings, chit-chat), saving a round trip and tokens.
Q: Give a case where adding a query transform makes the system worse.
A: A short, well-formed, single-hop query against one clean index. The transform adds latency, cost, and a chance of a bad rewrite that retrieves worse than the original query would have.
```
lessons.deeper:
### Multi-query fusion, concretely

Multi-query only helps if you fuse the lists sensibly. The usual method is Reciprocal Rank Fusion: for each document, sum one over sixty plus its rank across every list it appears in, then sort by that sum (Cormack, Clarke, Buttcher, SIGIR 2009; sixty is their fixed constant). A document retrieved near the top by several paraphrases accumulates a high fused score, while one that appears for a single paraphrase only ranks lower. The point is that fusion rewards agreement across rewrites, which is exactly the signal that a document is robustly relevant and not an artefact of one phrasing. This is the same fusion math used to merge keyword and dense results in hybrid search.

### Why HyDE works, and when it does not

Dense retrieval compares a query vector to document vectors, but questions and documents are different kinds of text, a question is short and interrogative, a document is longer and declarative, so even a perfectly relevant document can sit far from the question in embedding space. HyDE sidesteps the mismatch by turning the question into something document-shaped before embedding. The failure mode is a domain the model knows nothing about, there, the hypothetical answer is confidently wrong in content and in vocabulary, so it steers retrieval toward the wrong neighbourhood. HyDE helps most on open-domain questions a general model can plausibly answer and least on private jargon-heavy corpora, which is often exactly where RAG is deployed, so measure it rather than assuming it helps.

### Routing as the control point

A router is a small classifier, which means it can be wrong, and a misroute sends the query to an index that cannot answer it, a silent failure that looks like bad retrieval. Two defences: give the router a fallback that searches all indexes when confidence is low, and log routing decisions so you can measure misroute rate as its own metric. In agent systems the same idea reappears as tool selection, the model routes a request to one of several tools or retrievers, and the design questions, keep the choices few and well described, measure how often the right one is picked, are identical.

### Latency budgeting across transforms

Each transform is a serial dependency before retrieval even starts, so they stack on the critical path. A condensation call plus a HyDE generation plus retrieval plus a reranker plus the final answer is five sequential model or index round trips. If your target is a sub-second response, you cannot afford all of them, you pick the one or two that your eval shows actually move recall and drop the rest. Where transforms are independent, several paraphrase retrievals in multi-query, run them in parallel so they cost one round trip of latency rather than N, even though they still cost N retrievals of work.

lessons.title: RAG versus long context
lessons.body:
With million-token context windows available, a natural question is why retrieve at all, why not stuff the whole corpus into the prompt. This is one of the most actively contested, fastest-moving debates in the field, so treat every specific number here as fast-moving and re-verify before quoting it. The strong interview answer is never RAG is dead or RAG always wins, it is a clear statement of the cost, accuracy, and freshness trade-offs and what you would benchmark before deciding.

## The decision table

| Factor | Favours RAG | Favours long context |
|---|---|---|
| Corpus size | Large, millions of docs | Bounded, fits in a window |
| Update frequency | Changes often | Mostly static |
| Citations | Needed, per-document | Not required |
| Access control | Per-document permissions | Uniform access |
| Reasoning | Within retrieved chunks | Across the whole corpus |
| Cost per query | Low, send only top-k | High, send everything |

The metaphor that sticks: RAG is the filing cabinet you pull the right folder from, long context is the bigger whiteboard you lay everything on. Many systems do both, retrieve a broad candidate set, then reason over a larger-than-chunk window of it.

## The cost math

The reason you cannot just always use long context is that cost scales with every input token on every call. Retrieval sends a few thousand tokens of top-k chunks, long context sends the whole corpus each time.

```bars
title: Input tokens sent per query (illustrative)
unit: k tokens
RAG top-k chunks | 4
Long context small corpus | 100
Long context large corpus | 900
```

One 2026 benchmark reported long context scoring higher on correctness at roughly twenty-six times the per-query token cost of RAG (secondary source, plausible given per-token pricing, not independently confirmed, re-verify). Prompt caching changes this math: if the long context is a stable prefix reused across calls, the cached read is far cheaper than a fresh send, which undercuts the older long context is always too expensive framing, but only when the context actually repeats.

## Accuracy is not monotonic in context length

Bigger context does not mean better answers. A January 2025 arXiv study found long-context prompting often outperforms RAG on QA benchmarks, especially encyclopedic questions, while RAG kept an edge on dialogue and general queries. But raw window size has a known failure: models recall information at the start and end of a long input better than information in the middle, the lost-in-the-middle effect (Liu et al., Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts, Stanford, 2023).

> **Pitfall.** Reading a passing needle-in-a-haystack test as proof the model reasons well over long context. Finding one planted fact is far easier than synthesising across many scattered facts, so a green needle test can coexist with poor real-world long-context reasoning.

## Needle tests versus real reasoning

A needle-in-a-haystack test hides one fact in a long document and checks retrieval of it. Passing it shows the model can locate a planted string, not that it can combine twenty facts spread across the input into one answer. Real multi-document reasoning is the harder bar, and it degrades with length and with distractor volume well before the window fills. So a model can advertise a million-token window, pass needle tests, and still answer a genuine cross-document reasoning question worse than a focused RAG prompt would.

```recall
Q: Why can a million-token window not simply replace retrieval?
A: Cost and latency scale with every token sent on every call, accuracy drops on long inputs via lost-in-the-middle, and permissions and freshness still need a retrieval layer. Capacity is not free quality.
Q: What does prompt caching change about the RAG versus long context cost comparison?
A: If the long context is a stable prefix reused across calls, the cached read is far cheaper than resending it, weakening the long-context-is-too-expensive argument, but only when the context genuinely repeats.
Q: Why is passing a needle-in-a-haystack test weak evidence of long-context reasoning?
A: It tests locating one planted fact, which is far easier than synthesising many scattered facts. A model can pass it and still reason poorly across a long, distractor-heavy input.
Q: Name two reasons unrelated to accuracy that force RAG over long context.
A: Per-document access control (long context gives uniform access) and freshness or citations (RAG keeps knowledge external, updatable, and attributable per document).
Q: What is the strong interview answer to RAG versus long context?
A: Not that one wins. Name the cost, accuracy, and freshness trade-offs, note the debate is unsettled and fast-moving, and say what you would benchmark on your own eval set before choosing.
```
lessons.deeper:
### Why the debate is genuinely unsettled

Both camps have real evidence, which is why a confident one-liner is the wrong answer. Long-context studies show it winning on some QA benchmarks, especially fact-dense encyclopedic questions where the relevant passage, once in the window, is easy to use. RAG studies show it winning on freshness, cost, and tasks needing precise retrieval or citations. The results depend heavily on corpus, question type, model, and how retrieval was tuned, so a benchmark that favours one can be flipped by changing those. The honest position states what is settled, cost scales with tokens, accuracy is not monotonic in length, permissions and freshness need external data, and what is not, which approach wins on a given QA mix, and treats the rest as something to measure.

### The retrieve-then-stuff hybrid

The practical architecture is rarely pure. Retrieve a broad candidate set, more than you would feed a chunk-level prompt, then place that larger set into a long-context window and let the model reason over it. This captures the strengths of both: retrieval filters millions of documents down to a relevant, affordable subset (preserving cost control, freshness, and access filtering), while the long window lets the model reason across that subset rather than being confined to five chunks. It is also where prompt caching helps most, if the retrieved set is stable across a short session, the window becomes a cacheable prefix.

### Cost arithmetic you can defend

Do not quote live prices. Reason in ratios. If RAG sends roughly four thousand input tokens per query and long context sends two hundred thousand, long context sends about fifty times the input tokens, so at equal per-token price it costs about fifty times as much on input, before any output. Prompt caching can cut the repeated-prefix portion substantially, often to a small fraction of a fresh read, but only the stable prefix benefits, the per-query variable part (the new question) is never cached. So the defensible claim is directional: long context costs an order of magnitude or more per query unless caching recovers most of it, and whether that is worth the accuracy it buys depends on your query mix and is a benchmark question, not a principle.

### Freshness and permissions, the deciding factors

Two needs settle the choice regardless of accuracy. Freshness: if the corpus changes between calls, long context must re-send the current state every time and you must assemble it, whereas RAG retrieves the current index automatically. Permissions: if different users may see different documents, RAG filters by access tag at retrieval time, while a static long-context prompt bakes one view for everyone, forcing a separate prompt per permission set. In enterprise systems these two often decide the architecture before accuracy or cost enters the conversation, which is why they belong at the front of a strong answer.

chapters.title: Agents and context
chapters.summary: Workflows vs agents, the loop, memory, multi-agent trade-offs, human checkpoints, MCP, and context engineering.

lessons.title: Agents versus workflows
lessons.body:
The split between workflows and agents is the first distinction an interviewer draws, because it decides how much control you hand the model and therefore your cost, latency, and failure profile. Anthropic's "Building effective agents" (Dec 2024) set the vocabulary the field still uses. Get the definition exact, give a concrete example of each, and know the one question that decides between them.

## The definition split

Both are agentic systems. The difference is who owns the control flow.

- A workflow orchestrates LLMs and tools through predefined code paths. You write the control flow; the model fills in steps you laid out.
- An agent lets the model dynamically direct its own process and tool use, deciding the next step from what it observes. By late 2025 Anthropic's working shorthand compressed to an LLM autonomously using tools in a loop.

```flow
dir: TB
task: Task | actor
q: Who picks next step? | gate
wf: Workflow | step
ag: Agent | model
code: You wrote the path | step
loop: Model decides, loops on tools | step
task -> q : incoming
q -> wf : code decides
q -> ag : model decides
wf -> code : predictable
ag -> loop : flexible
```

The test is a single question: is the sequence of steps fixed and knowable at build time, or must it be decided at runtime from what the model sees? Fixed means workflow. Decided at runtime means agent.

## A concrete example of each

A workflow: triage an incoming support email. Classify it, retrieve the relevant policy, draft a reply, run a safety check, and send if the check passes. Every input takes the same five steps in the same order. You wrote that path. The model makes each step smart, but it never chooses what to do next, so the system is predictable and cheap and you can test each stage in isolation.

An agent: fix a failing test in a codebase. The model must run the tests, read the traceback, decide which file to open, edit it, re-run, and repeat, and the number and order of those steps depend on what each observation reveals. You cannot hardcode the path because you do not know how many files it will touch or what the error will be. The loop earns its cost here precisely because the control flow is unknowable in advance.

## When the loop earns its cost

Agents trade latency, cost, and error compounding for flexibility. The trade is worth it only under specific conditions.

| Signal | Favors workflow | Favors agent |
|---|---|---|
| Step sequence | Fixed, knowable upfront | Must be decided at runtime |
| Step count | Bounded, small | Open-ended |
| Latency budget | Tight | Tolerant |
| Cost sensitivity | High | Can absorb more tokens |
| Error tolerance | Low, needs predictability | Can recover mid-task |

```bars
title: Relative token cost by system shape (illustrative)
unit: x
Single augmented call | 1
Workflow with few steps | 2
Autonomous agent | 4
```

> **Interview.** The strong answer resists reaching for an agent. Start with the simplest thing that works, often one call with retrieval, then a workflow, and only make it an agent when the task is open-ended, the steps cannot be hardcoded, and the latency and cost are acceptable. Naming the trade-offs is what separates a senior answer from "agents are more powerful."

## The simplest-solution rule

Anthropic's explicit guidance is to find the simplest solution first and increase complexity only when needed. For many applications a single optimised call with retrieval and in-context examples is enough. The cost of an agent is not just tokens: autonomy multiplies per-step error, makes behaviour harder to test, and makes failures harder to reproduce. Reach for it when the flexibility is the point, not because it sounds advanced.

```recall
Q: What single question decides workflow versus agent?
A: Is the sequence of steps fixed and knowable at build time (workflow, you write the control flow), or must it be decided at runtime from what the model observes (agent, the model directs its own process)?
Q: Why not default to an agent since it is more flexible?
A: Agents trade latency, cost, and error compounding for flexibility, are harder to test and reproduce, and multiply per-step error. Most tasks are solved more cheaply and reliably by a single call or a workflow.
Q: Give a task that must be an agent and say why.
A: Fixing a failing test: the number and order of steps depend on each observation (the traceback, which file, whether the fix works), so the control flow cannot be hardcoded.
Q: What is Anthropic's late-2025 shorthand for an agent?
A: An LLM autonomously using tools in a loop, deciding each next step from what it observes.
```
lessons.deeper:
### Agentic systems is the umbrella, not a third category

A common slip is to treat "agentic" as a synonym for "agent." Anthropic uses agentic systems as the umbrella covering both workflows and agents, with the control-flow owner as the dividing line inside it. This matters in interviews because candidates who call every LLM-plus-tool system an agent lose the distinction that the whole discussion rests on. A fixed five-step pipeline that calls tools is an agentic system and a workflow; it is not an agent, because the model never chose the sequence.

### The augmented LLM sits under both

Underneath either shape is the same unit: an LLM augmented with retrieval, tools, and memory. A workflow wires several augmented calls together along a path you define. An agent puts one augmented call in a loop and lets it decide when to call a tool and when to stop. Seeing both as compositions of the same building block is why you can start with one call and grow into a workflow and then an agent without rearchitecting, and why the decision is incremental rather than a fork at the start.

### Error compounding is the hidden cost of autonomy

The reason "just make it an agent" is dangerous is multiplicative error. If each step in an autonomous loop is 95% reliable and nothing checks intermediate results, a ten-step task is roughly 0.95^10, about 60% end to end. A workflow fights this with gates between fixed steps; an agent has fewer natural places to insert a gate because the steps are not known in advance. This is the concrete mechanism behind the advice to prefer workflows when you can, and it is the number to cite when asked why more autonomy is not free.

### Source and currency

The workflow-versus-agent definition, the agentic-systems umbrella, the augmented-LLM building block, and the simplest-solution-first guidance are from Anthropic, "Building effective agents" (Dec 2024). The compressed "LLM autonomously using tools in a loop" phrasing reflects Anthropic's later framing. The relative token figures (an agent around 4x a chat) come from Anthropic's multi-agent research write-up and are illustrative orders of magnitude, not a quote to pin to any one task (2026, re-check).

lessons.title: The five workflow patterns
lessons.body:
A workflow orchestrates LLM calls through code paths you write, not through a model that decides its own next step. Anthropic's "Building effective agents" (Dec 2024) names five patterns that cover almost every production workflow, and interviewers use them as a shared vocabulary. Knowing when each one applies, and the one cheaper option that often beats all of them, is the point.

## The augmented LLM is the building block

Every pattern composes the same unit: a single LLM call augmented with retrieval, tools, and memory. Before reaching for any pattern, ask whether one augmented call with good retrieval and a few in-context examples already solves the task. Anthropic's own guidance is to find the simplest solution first and add structure only when a concrete failure forces it. The patterns below are what you add, in rough order of cost, when one call is not enough.

## Prompt chaining

Decompose the task into a fixed sequence of steps, each call consuming the previous output. Add a programmatic gate between steps to catch a bad intermediate result before it propagates.

```flow
dir: LR
in: Input | actor
s1: Step 1 call | model
gate: Check output | gate
s2: Step 2 call | model
out: Result | step
in -> s1 : task
s1 -> gate : draft
gate -> s2 : passed
gate --> in : failed, retry
s2 -> out : final
```

Use it when the task decomposes cleanly into fixed subtasks and you want to trade latency for accuracy by making each call easier. Example: write a document outline, check it meets criteria, then write the document from the outline.

## Routing

Classify the input, then dispatch to a specialised prompt or model. A cheap model handles easy inputs, a capable model handles hard ones, and each downstream prompt stays focused instead of trying to cover every case at once.

```flow
dir: LR
in: Query | actor
cls: Classify | model
easy: Cheap model | model
hard: Capable model | model
out: Answer | step
in -> cls : input
cls -> easy : simple
cls -> hard : complex
easy -> out : response
hard -> out : response
```

Use it when inputs fall into distinct categories that are better handled separately and classification is reliable. Example: route general questions, refund requests, and technical support into different pipelines.

## Parallelization

Run several LLM calls at once and aggregate their outputs. It has two variations. Sectioning splits a task into independent subtasks run in parallel. Voting runs the same task several times and combines the results for confidence.

```flow
dir: TB
in: Task | actor
split: Fan out | step
a: Call A | model
b: Call B | model
c: Call C | model
agg: Aggregate | step
out: Result | step
in -> split : task
split -> a : section or vote
split -> b : section or vote
split -> c : section or vote
a -> agg : output
b -> agg : output
c -> agg : output
agg -> out : combined
```

Use sectioning for speed on independent parts, and voting when multiple attempts raise confidence. Example of sectioning: one model answers the user while a second screens the query for policy violations, which works better than asking one call to do both.

## Orchestrator-workers

A central LLM breaks the task into subtasks at runtime and delegates each to a worker call, then synthesises the results. The difference from parallelization is that the subtasks are not predefined, the orchestrator decides them from the input.

```flow
dir: TB
in: Task | actor
orch: Orchestrator | model
w1: Worker | model
w2: Worker | model
syn: Synthesize | model
out: Result | step
in -> orch : task
orch -> w1 : subtask decided at runtime
orch -> w2 : subtask decided at runtime
w1 -> syn : partial
w2 -> syn : partial
syn -> out : final
```

Use it when you cannot predict the subtasks in advance. A coding change does not know how many files it will touch until it reads them, so the orchestrator spawns a worker per file it discovers.

## Evaluator-optimizer

One LLM call generates a candidate, a second evaluates it against explicit criteria, and the generator revises using that feedback, in a loop until the evaluator passes it or a cap is hit.

```flow
dir: LR
gen: Generator | model
ev: Evaluator | gate
out: Result | step
gen -> ev : candidate
ev --> gen : feedback, revise
ev -> out : accepted
```

Use it when you have clear evaluation criteria and iteration measurably improves the output, for example literary translation or complex search where a first draft rarely lands.

> **Rule of thumb.** Add exactly one pattern when a specific failure demands it. A fixed pipeline with a quality problem wants evaluator-optimizer; unpredictable decomposition wants orchestrator-workers; distinct input types want routing.

## Trade-offs

| Pattern | Adds | Costs | Reach for when |
|---|---|---|---|
| Prompt chaining | Accuracy per step, gates | Serial latency | Fixed, decomposable task |
| Routing | Specialised handling, cheaper mix | A classifier to maintain | Distinct input categories |
| Parallelization | Speed or confidence | Parallel token spend | Independent parts or voting |
| Orchestrator-workers | Runtime decomposition | Unpredictable cost | Subtasks unknown in advance |
| Evaluator-optimizer | Iterative quality | Multiple round trips | Clear criteria, iteration helps |

The line to agents: all five are workflows, you own the control flow. The moment the model must decide the control flow itself, you have crossed into an agent loop, which costs and latency rise again.

```recall
Q: Why try a single augmented call before any pattern?
A: Many tasks are solved by one call with retrieval and in-context examples. Patterns add latency, cost, and failure surface, so you add one only when a concrete failure forces it.
Q: What distinguishes orchestrator-workers from parallelization?
A: Parallelization runs predefined subtasks; the orchestrator decides the subtasks at runtime from the input, so the number and nature of workers are not known in advance.
Q: When does evaluator-optimizer pay off, and when is it waste?
A: It pays off when there are clear evaluation criteria and iteration measurably improves output. It is waste when the first draft is already good enough or criteria are vague, because you pay for extra round trips with no gain.
Q: What separates every workflow pattern from an agent?
A: In a workflow you write the control flow in code; in an agent the model decides the next step dynamically. Crossing that line raises cost, latency, and error compounding.
```
lessons.deeper:
### Sectioning versus voting, concretely

Both are parallelization, but they aggregate differently and solve different problems. Sectioning assigns each parallel call a different slice of the work and concatenates the outputs: call A drafts section one, call B drafts section two, and you stitch them. The win is latency and focused attention, since each call reasons about less. Voting assigns every call the same task and reduces the outputs to one answer, by majority, by any-flag, or by a vote threshold you tune. The win is confidence and controllable precision or recall: screening content for a policy violation with three prompts and flagging if any one trips raises recall at the cost of false positives; requiring two of three raises precision. Choosing the threshold is a direct false-positive versus false-negative trade, the same lever you tune in a classifier.

### Why gates matter in a chain

A prompt chain multiplies per-step error. If each of four steps is 90% reliable and errors pass downstream unchecked, the chain is roughly 0.9^4, about 66% end to end. A gate between steps that rejects a bad intermediate and retries, or routes to a fallback, breaks that multiplication by catching the error before it compounds. This is why Anthropic draws the gate explicitly in the chaining diagram: the gate, not the extra model call, is what makes a longer chain reliable rather than more fragile.

### Patterns compose

These are not mutually exclusive. A real system routes first, then runs a prompt chain inside the branch for complex inputs, with an evaluator-optimizer loop on the final generation step and parallel voting on a safety screen. The skill is composing the minimum set, each justified by a failure you actually observed, rather than assembling an elaborate graph up front. Anthropic's framing is explicit: start simple, measure where it breaks, and add the one pattern that addresses the break.

### Source

The five patterns, the sectioning and voting split, the augmented-LLM building block, and the simplest-solution-first guidance are from Anthropic, "Building effective agents" (Dec 2024). The orchestrator-workers point that subtasks are decided at runtime, not predefined, is the paper's stated distinction from parallelization. These patterns are stable vocabulary as of 2026, though framework names around them keep changing, so re-check tooling claims.

lessons.title: The agent loop and its interface
lessons.body:
An agent is an LLM running tools in a loop until the task is done or it must check in. The loop itself is simple; what makes one agent ship and another thrash is the interface you give it to the world and the limits you impose from outside. Interviewers probe stop conditions and tool design because those, not the model, decide whether an autonomous loop converges.

## The loop anatomy

The classic cycle is plan, act, observe, adjust, repeat. The model proposes a step, your code runs the tool, the result returns as a new observation appended to the context, and the model re-plans on the whole growing transcript.

```flow
dir: LR
plan: Plan next step | model
cap: Under budget? | gate
act: Run tool | tool
obs: Observe result | step
done: Answer | step
plan -> cap : propose
cap -> act : within caps
act -> obs : result
obs -> plan : append, re-plan
cap -> done : task complete or cap hit
```

The back edge from observe to plan is the loop: every observation feeds the next plan. There is no magic, it is a state machine over the context window that keeps re-invoking the model on a transcript that grows by one reasoning step, one tool call, and one result each iteration.

## Stop conditions

Autonomous loops do not reliably self-terminate. A confused agent will retry the same broken action forever or declare victory early. You must impose limits from outside the model.

- A maximum iteration count, so the loop cannot run unbounded.
- A cost or token budget, checked before each step, so spend is capped even if iterations are not the binding limit.
- A checkpoint that hands control to a human before any high-blast-radius action (the human-in-the-loop lesson covers this).

Never trust the model to stop itself. The caps are infrastructure you build around the loop, enforced in your code, not an instruction in the prompt.

## Step and cost budgets

The two budgets answer different questions. The iteration cap bounds how many times the model may act; the cost cap bounds how much it may spend. A task can blow the cost budget in few iterations if each step stuffs the window, so check both. A clean design surfaces how much budget remains to the model as an observation, so it can prioritise, and forces a graceful stop or a checkpoint when a cap is reached rather than a hard crash.

```python
# Sketch: the agent loop with external caps
msgs = [system, user]
spent = 0
for step in range(MAX_STEPS):          # iteration cap
    resp = client.generate(msgs, tools=TOOLS)
    spent += resp.cost
    if spent > COST_CAP:               # cost cap
        return checkpoint(msgs, "budget hit")
    if not resp.tool_calls:
        return resp.text               # model answered, stop
    for call in resp.tool_calls:
        out = run_tool(call.name, call.args)
        msgs.append(tool_result(call.id, out))
```

## Tool set design: the agent-computer interface

The model routes entirely on tool names, descriptions, and schemas, so the tool set is the agent's interface to the world, the ACI. Anthropic's three principles: simplicity, transparency (surface the plan explicitly), and treating tool definitions with the same care as a human-facing API, minimal overlap and unambiguous descriptions, with error prevention baked in. A documented real failure: relative file paths broke once the agent changed directories, and switching every tool to absolute paths fixed it.

Designing a tool set for a coding agent makes the principles concrete. Keep the set small and orthogonal: read, search, apply-patch, run-command, run-tests. Make returns something the model can act on, a run-tests tool that returns the failing assertion and line lets the model fix it directly, while one that returns only pass or fail forces guesswork. Gate the destructive tools (apply-patch, push) behind approval or a sandbox; let the read tools run freely.

> **Pitfall.** Overlapping or vaguely described tools. If two tools could both plausibly apply, the model picks wrong, and this is the single biggest driver of bad tool calls. Fewer, sharper tools beat a large catalogue.

> **Rule of thumb.** Design each tool as the interface a careful but literal collaborator will use, because that is exactly what the model is. If a human would need to guess what a tool does from its name and description, so will the model.

## Interview angle

If pressed for academic vocabulary, this is a ReAct-style loop, interleaving reasoning and acting; Anthropic describes the same mechanism in plainer terms. The questions that matter are how you stop a runaway loop (external caps plus a human checkpoint), why tool descriptions carry so much weight (the model selects purely on the schema), and why more steps is not free (error compounds per step).

```recall
Q: Why must stop conditions come from outside the model?
A: Autonomous loops do not reliably self-terminate; a confused agent retries forever or stops early. Max-iteration and cost caps are enforced in your code around the loop, not trusted to the prompt.
Q: What is the agent-computer interface and why does it dominate tool-selection accuracy?
A: It is the tool names, descriptions, and schemas the model routes on. The model has nothing else to choose by, so overlapping or ambiguous tools cause wrong calls regardless of model quality.
Q: Why check a cost budget separately from an iteration cap?
A: A task can exhaust the cost budget in few iterations if each step stuffs the context. The caps bound different things, how often it acts versus how much it spends, so both must be checked.
Q: Why should a run-tests tool return the failing assertion rather than pass or fail?
A: The richer return lets the model act directly on the error; a bare pass or fail forces it to guess the cause, wasting iterations and inviting wrong edits.
```
lessons.deeper:
### The loop is a state machine over the context window

Each iteration appends three things: the model's reasoning, the tool call it chose, and the tool result. Then the whole transcript is re-sent. This has a direct consequence that the plan-act-observe picture hides: context grows every step, so a twenty-step loop can multiply the token count several fold. Uncurated, the loop walks straight into context rot, recall degrading within the advertised window, and the agent begins ignoring its earliest instructions. This is why the agent loop and context engineering are the same problem viewed twice: the loop produces the growth that context engineering must manage with compaction and note-taking.

### Error compounding, quantified

Autonomy multiplies per-step error. If each step is 95% reliable and nothing checks intermediate state, a ten-step chain is roughly 0.95^10, about 60% end to end; at twenty steps it is near 36%. More steps is not free, and this is the number to cite when asked why you bound the loop aggressively. The mitigation is twofold: fewer, more reliable steps (better tools and clearer returns raise per-step reliability), and gates or checkpoints that catch a bad state before it propagates.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant M as Model
    participant G as Guard
    participant T as Tool
    M->>G: propose step N
    G-->>M: under caps, proceed
    M->>T: call tool
    T-->>M: result appended
    Note over M: re-plan on full transcript
    G->>M: cap hit, force stop
```

### Worked example

A coding agent told to fix the failing test: plan, run tests (act), read the traceback (observe), open the offending file, edit, re-run tests, observe green, stop. The ACI decides whether this is three clean iterations or ten flailing ones. Absolute paths in every tool argument prevent the classic failure where the working directory changed and a relative path broke. A test tool that returns the assertion and line collapses the guess-and-check loop into a direct fix.

### Source and currency

The plan-act-observe loop, the three ACI principles, the absolute-paths anecdote, and the self-termination warning are from Anthropic, "Building effective agents" (Dec 2024). As of 2026 provider SDKs increasingly offer server-side tool loops and computer-use, so check current SDK capabilities before hand-rolling the loop (fast-moving, re-check).

lessons.title: Agent memory
lessons.body:
A model has no memory between calls; the only thing it knows is what sits in the context window right now. Agent memory is the set of strategies that let a task outlive one window, by deciding what to carry in-context, what to persist outside it, and when to read each back. Interviewers probe it because a multi-day agent that remembers nothing repeats work and contradicts itself, while one that remembers everything drowns in its own history.

## Working context versus long-term store

Two tiers, with different costs and lifetimes.

- Working context is what is in the window this turn: the system prompt, tools, recent messages, the current file or plan. Fast to use, but finite and degrading, every token competes for the attention budget.
- A long-term store lives outside the window: files, a database, a vector index. Unbounded and durable, but every fact in it costs a retrieval step and a context slot to bring back in.

```flow
dir: LR
agent: Agent | model
win: Working context | step
store: Long-term store | store
agent -> win : reads every turn
win --> store : write durable facts
store --> win : retrieve on demand
agent -> store : query
```

The whole discipline is the traffic between these two: promote a fact to the store before the window evicts it, and pull it back only when the current step needs it.

## Scratchpad and notes

The cheapest memory is a note the agent writes to itself outside the window and reads back later. A scratchpad holds within-task state, the plan, open bugs, decisions made, and survives a context reset because it is a file, not a message. The pattern: before compacting or resetting, the agent writes the load-bearing state to a notes file; after the reset it reloads that small, high-signal summary instead of the forty stale observations that produced it.

```steps
Observe | The agent accumulates reasoning and tool results in the window as it works
Note | Before the window fills, write decisions, open bugs, and the goal to a notes file
Compact | Summarize or reset the conversation, dropping stale intermediate output
Reload | Read the notes back so the agent resumes with high-signal state, not raw history
```

## Summarisation and compaction

When the window nears its limit, summarise the conversation and restart from the summary plus the recently touched state. The hard part is not summarising, it is choosing what to keep. Keep decisions, the current goal, unresolved bugs, and file or line anchors; drop stale tool output, superseded plans, and verbose intermediate reasoning. A compaction that keeps the wrong things loses the thread; one that keeps the right 300 tokens lets the agent run arbitrarily long. Anthropic frames this as a core long-horizon technique in its context-engineering work.

## Retrieval-based memory

For facts too numerous to hold in-context, write them to a store and retrieve on demand, the same machinery as RAG but pointed at the agent's own history. Each memory is embedded and indexed; when a step needs prior context, the agent queries for the few relevant memories rather than carrying all of them. This is how an assistant recalls a preference you stated last week without replaying the whole conversation: the preference is a retrievable record, not a resident message.

## Episodic versus semantic memory

A useful split borrowed from cognitive science.

| Kind | Holds | Example | Retrieval |
|---|---|---|---|
| Episodic | Specific events, in time order | "On Tuesday the user rejected plan A" | By recency or similarity to the event |
| Semantic | Distilled facts, time-independent | "The user prefers metric units" | By relevance to the current need |

Episodic memory answers what happened; semantic memory answers what is true. A good design distils episodes into semantic facts over time, so the store does not grow without bound and the useful signal is not buried in a transcript.

## Write policies and staleness

A memory store is only as good as its hygiene. Three policies decide its quality.

- What to write: durable, reusable facts and decisions, not session narrative or transient state. Writing everything turns the store into noise.
- When to write: at real checkpoints (a decision made, a preference learned), not on a timer that captures half-formed state.
- Staleness: facts expire or get superseded. "The user prefers plan A" is wrong the moment they switch to B. Without an update or expiry policy, retrieval surfaces confidently stale facts, which is worse than no memory.

> **Pitfall.** Treating memory as append-only. A store that never updates or expires facts will confidently return a preference the user already reversed. Stale memory is more dangerous than absent memory because the agent trusts it.

> **Rule of thumb.** Memory is a cache you curate, not a log you append. If a fact is not durable, reusable, and current, it does not belong in the long-term store.

Designing a memory strategy for a multi-day agent task combines all of this: a scratchpad for within-session state, compaction at the window limit, a semantic store of distilled facts with expiry, and just-in-time retrieval so the window stays small.

```recall
Q: Why is a bigger context window not a substitute for a memory strategy?
A: The window is finite and degrades (context rot), and it resets between sessions. A long task exceeds any window and spans resets, so durable state must live in an external store and be retrieved on demand.
Q: What is the hard part of compaction?
A: Choosing what to keep. Keep decisions, the goal, open bugs, and anchors; drop stale tool output and superseded plans. Keeping the wrong things loses the thread.
Q: How do episodic and semantic memory differ, and why distil one into the other?
A: Episodic holds specific time-ordered events; semantic holds distilled time-independent facts. Distilling episodes into semantic facts keeps the store bounded and the signal retrievable instead of buried in a transcript.
Q: Why is stale memory worse than no memory?
A: The agent trusts a retrieved fact. A superseded preference returned confidently causes wrong actions, whereas absent memory at least prompts the agent to ask or re-derive.
```
lessons.deeper:
### Memory is context engineering with persistence added

Everything here is the context-engineering discipline, finding the smallest set of high-signal tokens, extended across time and sessions. The working context is the window you curate each turn; the store is where you park what will not fit but will be needed again. The two new problems persistence adds are write policy (what earns a durable slot) and staleness (how a durable fact stops being true). Both are absent in a single-turn setting, which is why memory is its own topic rather than a footnote to context engineering.

### A concrete multi-day loop

Consider an agent migrating a service over three days. Day one it decides the target API, migrates two modules, and leaves two tests failing. If it holds this only in-context, day two starts from a reset and the knowledge is gone. The memory design: write to a notes file "target API is vN; auth and billing modules migrated; tests X and Y failing; do not touch config.ts" as a semantic record, and keep an episodic log of what was tried and rejected so day two does not re-walk a dead end. Day two reloads the semantic record (small, current) and queries the episodic log only when it hits a decision it might have faced before. The window stays small; the task survives the reset.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Agent
    participant W as Window
    participant S as Store
    A->>W: work until near limit
    W->>S: write decisions and open bugs
    Note over W: reset
    S-->>W: reload semantic record
    A->>S: query episodic log on demand
```

### Staleness mechanics

The cleanest staleness policy attaches a scope and a version to each fact. A preference is current until a newer contradicting write supersedes it; a derived fact is valid until the thing it was derived from changes. Retrieval then prefers the latest write for a given key and can drop facts past an expiry. Without this, two contradictory memories coexist and retrieval returns whichever scores higher on similarity, which has nothing to do with which is true. This is the memory analogue of cache invalidation, and it is hard for the same reason.

### Source and currency

The window-as-finite-degrading-resource framing, and compaction, note-taking, and sub-agents as long-horizon techniques, are from Anthropic, "Effective context engineering for AI agents" (Sep 2025). The episodic-versus-semantic split is standard cognitive-science vocabulary applied to agents. Provider platforms are adding native memory primitives (memory tools, context editing) as of 2026, so re-check what the platform gives you before building a store from scratch (fast-moving).

lessons.title: Single versus multi-agent
lessons.body:
Multi-agent systems sound like the obvious next step up from one agent, and they are the easiest place to over-engineer. The decision rests on one measured trade: Anthropic's own research system beat a single agent by a large margin on breadth-first work, but at many times the token cost. Interviewers want to hear when that trade pays and, more tellingly, when quoting the headline number is the wrong move.

## The headline trade

Anthropic's Research feature uses a lead agent that spawns parallel subagents, each with an isolated context window returning only a condensed summary. On an internal eval this multi-agent setup beat a single agent by 90.2%, at roughly 15x the token cost of a normal chat (a single agent runs around 4x). Anthropic attributes most of the gain to one thing: token usage alone explained about 80% of the performance variance on the BrowseComp benchmark, with tool-call count and model choice as the other factors.

That framing is the whole lesson. The multi-agent win comes largely from spending more compute in parallel, not from emergent coordination. So the system wins when the task is breadth-first and parallelisable, and loses when it is narrow, latency-sensitive, cost-constrained, or has tightly interdependent subtasks.

```flow
dir: TB
lead: Lead agent | model
a: Subagent A | model
b: Subagent B | model
c: Subagent C | model
syn: Synthesize | model
out: Answer | step
lead -> a : bounded subtask, own context
lead -> b : bounded subtask, own context
lead -> c : bounded subtask, own context
a -> syn : 1-2k token summary
b -> syn : 1-2k token summary
c -> syn : 1-2k token summary
syn -> out : combined
```

The subagent transcripts never enter the lead's context; only the summaries do. That isolation is the real mechanism, more on it below.

## When multiple agents help

Two concrete benefits justify the cost.

- Parallel breadth. Independent sub-questions (research six competitors, check twelve files) run concurrently, so wall-clock time drops even as token cost rises.
- Context isolation. Each subagent explores in a clean window and hands back only a small digest. The lead never sees the messy intermediate work, so its own window stays high-signal and does not rot.

```bars
title: Token cost by shape (illustrative, from Anthropic figures)
unit: x chat
Single agent | 4
Multi-agent research | 15
```

## When they just multiply cost and bugs

The failure mode is interdependent subtasks. If subagent B needs subagent A's output, you have serialised them and still paid the coordination tax, which is worse than one agent. Multi-agent also multiplies the ways things go wrong: a subagent misreads its brief, two subagents duplicate work, the lead mis-synthesises partial results. For a narrow, latency-sensitive, or tightly coupled task, a single agent is both cheaper and more reliable.

> **Pitfall.** Quoting "90.2% better" to justify multi-agent on the wrong task. That number is for breadth-first, parallelisable work only. On a narrow or interdependent task you pay 15x for worse coordination, and the number does not apply.

## Coordination patterns

A 2026 Anthropic write-up names five patterns and when each fits.

| Pattern | Fits |
|---|---|
| Generator-verifier | Quality-critical output with explicit criteria |
| Orchestrator-subagent | Clear decomposition into bounded subtasks |
| Agent teams | Parallel, independent, long-running subtasks |
| Message bus | Event-driven pipelines, growing ecosystems |
| Shared-state | Collaborative work building on each other's findings |

The recommendation: start with the simplest pattern and evolve based on where it struggles, never pick one because it sounds sophisticated.

## Interview angle

The strong answer defaults to a single agent and names the specific condition that would change your mind: parallelisable breadth plus tolerance for cost and latency. If asked to judge the hype, Anthropic's own line is that true multi-agent systems are still in their infancy, which is a direct quote and a safer stance than endorsing any pattern as settled.

```recall
Q: What actually produces the multi-agent performance gain?
A: Mostly spending more tokens in parallel. Anthropic found token usage alone explained about 80% of the BrowseComp variance; it is compute scaled by parallelism, not emergent coordination.
Q: When is a single agent the right default?
A: Narrow scope, latency- or cost-sensitive tasks, or interdependent subtasks. Start here and move to multi-agent only for parallelisable breadth you can afford.
Q: Why is quoting 90.2% often a mistake?
A: It applies only to breadth-first parallelisable work. On a narrow or tightly coupled task the trade reverses: you pay around 15x for worse coordination, and the number does not transfer.
Q: What is the real benefit of context isolation across subagents?
A: Each subagent works in a clean window and returns only a small summary, so the lead's context stays high-signal and avoids rot, rather than one window bloating with every thread's raw work.
```
lessons.deeper:
### Why the 15x is structural, not overhead

The cost is not inefficiency you can tune away. A lead plus N subagents means N separate context windows, each re-reading its slice of the task and doing its own tool calls, plus the lead's synthesis pass, plus the context that gets passed around and re-billed at each handoff. Anthropic measured the multi-agent research system at roughly 15x a chat and a single agent at about 4x; production bills often land higher than a per-agent spreadsheet predicts precisely because the between-agent costs (context transfer, retries, verification, orchestration) compound across every handoff. Budgeting multi-agent as "N times single-agent" systematically underestimates.

### Context isolation is the win, parallelism is the speedup

These are two different benefits and interviews reward separating them. Parallelism cuts wall-clock time: six subagents research six competitors at once. Context isolation protects quality: each subagent's messy transcript stays out of the lead's window, so the lead synthesises six clean 1 to 2k token digests instead of degrading under one bloated history. A task can want one without the other. If the sub-questions are independent but small, you may want isolation (clean synthesis) without needing much parallelism; if they are large but must share state, parallelism helps but isolation breaks down because they need each other's intermediate work.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant L as Lead
    participant A as Subagent A
    participant B as Subagent B
    L->>A: bounded subtask, own context
    L->>B: bounded subtask, own context
    A-->>L: 1-2k token summary
    B-->>L: 1-2k token summary
    Note over L: synthesize, transcripts never enter lead
```

### Worked example

"Compare our pricing against six competitors." A single agent does six web trips crammed into one window that bloats and degrades by competitor four. The multi-agent shape: the lead spawns six subagents, each researches one competitor in isolation and returns a 1.5k-token digest, and the lead synthesises six clean digests. This is exactly the breadth-first, independent-subtask shape the 90.2% figure was measured on. Change the task to "trace how a single bug propagates through our six services," where each step depends on the previous, and the same shape serialises and loses to one agent.

### Source and currency

The 90.2% gain, roughly 15x versus 4x token cost, the lead-plus-isolated-subagents architecture, and the "token usage explains about 80% of BrowseComp variance" finding are from Anthropic's multi-agent research system write-up (2025). The five coordination patterns and the "in its infancy" quote are from Anthropic's later agent-engineering writing. Patterns and tooling here are churning as of 2026, so present none as settled (fast-moving, re-check).

lessons.title: Human in the loop checkpoints
lessons.body:
An agent is supposed to act on its own, but autonomy and safety are not opposites. The design question is not whether a human reviews the agent, it is which actions need review and how to insert the checkpoint without destroying the agent's usefulness. Interviewers probe this because the wrong policy either lets an agent delete production data or buries the user under approval prompts until they rubber-stamp everything.

## The lever is irreversibility and blast radius

Gate on consequences, not on action type. The question for any action is: if this goes wrong, how hard is it to undo and how far does the damage reach? Read-only and easily reversible actions run freely. Destructive, externally visible, or expensive actions require explicit approval.

```flow
dir: LR
agent: Agent | model
gate: Risk check | gate
run: Run freely | tool
human: Request approval | gate
act: Execute | tool
agent -> gate : proposed action
gate -> run : read-only or reversible
gate -> human : destructive or external
human -> act : approved
human --> agent : rejected, re-plan
```

Concretely: searching, reading files, and running a sandboxed query run without asking. Sending an email, deleting data, spending money, or pushing code require a human to approve first. And regardless of action, a max-iteration and cost cap is always on, so a confused loop cannot run away even inside the allowed-freely tier.

## Risk tiers

Sort every tool into a tier up front, so the policy is a property of the tool, not a judgment the model makes each time.

| Tier | Examples | Policy |
|---|---|---|
| Read-only | Search, read file, fetch | Run freely |
| Reversible write | Draft, write to scratch, local edit | Run freely, keep an undo |
| Irreversible or external | Send email, delete, charge, deploy | Require approval |
| High blast radius | Bulk delete, production change | Approval plus a second check |

## Interrupt and resume with durable state

A checkpoint is only useful if the agent can pause and later continue without losing its place. That requires durable state: when the agent hits a gated action, it serialises its context (the plan, what it has done, the pending action) to a store, surfaces the approval request, and halts. When the human approves or rejects, the agent rehydrates that state and resumes from the exact point, applying the decision. Without durable state, an approval that arrives minutes later finds the agent's context gone and the task has to restart.

```steps
Reach gate | Agent proposes a destructive or external action
Persist | Serialize plan, history, and the pending action to durable state
Request | Surface the approval to the human with enough context to decide
Resume | On a decision, rehydrate state and continue from the exact point
```

## Approval fatigue

The failure that undoes a good policy. If the agent asks for approval too often, the human stops reading and approves reflexively, which is the same as having no checkpoint. The fix is to gate on real risk only, batch related approvals into one decision where possible, give the human enough context to decide quickly, and let trusted low-risk actions run freely. A policy that interrupts on everything is not safer, it trains the reviewer to ignore interrupts.

> **Pitfall.** Gating on action type instead of consequence, so a harmless read behind a confirmation and a destructive delete behind the same confirmation train the user to click through both. Gate on blast radius, not category.

> **Rule of thumb.** If a human will approve an action without reading it, that checkpoint is doing nothing. Reserve interrupts for decisions a human would actually stop and think about.

## This is design, not a library

The model does not provide checkpoints; you build them. The approval gate, the risk tiers, the durable state, and the caps are infrastructure in your application around the loop. The model proposes an action; your code decides whether it needs a human before it runs.

```recall
Q: Why gate on irreversibility and blast radius rather than action type?
A: Consequence is what matters. A read and a delete sorted into the same confirmation train the user to click through both; gating on how hard it is to undo and how far damage spreads targets the interrupts where they count.
Q: What does interrupt-and-resume require, and what breaks without it?
A: Durable state: the agent serializes its context and pending action, halts, and rehydrates on a decision. Without it, a delayed approval finds the context gone and the task must restart.
Q: What is approval fatigue and how do you prevent it?
A: Asking so often that the human approves reflexively, which nullifies the checkpoint. Prevent it by gating on real risk only, batching approvals, and giving enough context to decide fast.
Q: Why keep caps on even for freely-run actions?
A: A confused loop can run away within the allowed tier (endless cheap reads, runaway spend). Max-iteration and cost caps bound the loop regardless of per-action approval.
```
lessons.deeper:
### Why consequence beats category

Action type is a poor proxy because the same category spans wildly different blast radii. "Write to a database" is reversible against a scratch table and catastrophic against the production users table; "run a command" is harmless as a read and destructive as a recursive delete. Sorting by category forces you to gate the whole category at its worst case, which over-gates the safe uses and breeds fatigue, or at its average, which under-gates the dangerous ones. Sorting by consequence, computed from the specific target and reversibility, lets the harmless uses run and reserves the interrupt for the genuinely risky call. In practice this means the gate inspects the arguments, not just the tool name: delete with a narrow, scoped target may be reversible; delete with a wildcard is high blast radius.

### Durable state and the confused-deputy risk

Interrupt-and-resume introduces a subtle security concern. The serialised state and the approval request can themselves carry injected instructions if any of the agent's context came from untrusted content. A human who approves "send the summary email" without seeing that the agent also queued an exfiltration call has been turned into a confused deputy. So the approval surface must show the human the exact action and its arguments, resolved, not a model-written paraphrase of what it intends. The checkpoint protects you only if the thing approved is the thing that runs.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Agent
    participant P as Policy
    participant H as Human
    A->>P: proposed action + args
    P-->>A: low risk, run
    P->>H: high risk, show exact action
    H-->>A: approve or reject
    Note over A: caps always on
```

### Calibrating the tiers

The tiers are not fixed, they are a risk budget you tune from observed behaviour. If the agent is reliably correct on reversible writes, widen the freely-run tier; if a class of action keeps causing incidents, pull it up a tier and add a second check. The goal is the minimum interruption that still catches the actions a human would want to stop, measured against real outcomes rather than guessed in advance. This mirrors the guardrails discipline: start conservative, watch false positives (needless interrupts) and false negatives (missed risky actions), and move the line.

### Source and currency

The irreversibility-and-blast-radius framing, the read-freely versus approve-destructive split, and the always-on caps are drawn from Anthropic's agent-building guidance. The confused-deputy concern connects to the prompt-injection and guardrails lessons. Platform support for durable interrupt-and-resume is maturing as of 2026, so check what your framework provides before building the state machine yourself (fast-moving, re-check).

lessons.title: Model Context Protocol
lessons.body:
MCP is an open standard, introduced by Anthropic in Nov 2024, for connecting AI applications to external tools, data, and workflows through one client-server protocol, often described as a USB-C port for AI applications. The distinction interviewers test is that tool calling is the mechanism, while MCP standardises the transport and discovery layer around it, so one integration serves every compatible client. Verify specifics against modelcontextprotocol.io, which is the primary source for the architecture below.

## Host, client, server

MCP follows a client-server architecture with three named participants.

- The host is the AI application that coordinates one or more clients, for example an IDE or a desktop assistant.
- A client is a component inside the host that maintains one connection to one server and fetches context from it.
- A server is a program that exposes context to clients. It can run locally or remotely; "server" names the role, not the location.

The host creates one client per server. Connect an IDE to a monitoring server and a filesystem server and it instantiates two clients, one per connection.

```flow
dir: LR
host: Host app | actor
c1: Client 1 | step
c2: Client 2 | step
s1: Tool server A | tool
s2: Tool server B | tool
host -> c1 : one per server
host -> c2 : one per server
c1 -> s1 : JSON-RPC
c2 -> s2 : JSON-RPC
s1 --> c1 : tools, resources, prompts
s2 --> c2 : tools, resources, prompts
```

## Tools, resources, prompts

A server exposes three primitives, and knowing the split is a common question.

- Tools are actions the model can invoke (run a query, send a message), the model-controlled primitive.
- Resources are context data the client can read (a file, a record), application-controlled.
- Prompts are reusable interaction templates a user or app can select.

The data layer is JSON-RPC 2.0: clients and servers exchange requests and responses, with notifications when no response is needed (for example, a server telling the client its tool list changed).

## stdio versus streamable HTTP

MCP defines two transports, and the choice follows where the server runs.

| Transport | Mechanism | Fits |
|---|---|---|
| stdio | Standard input/output between local processes | Local servers, one client, no network overhead |
| Streamable HTTP | HTTP POST with optional Server-Sent Events | Remote servers, many clients |

Streamable HTTP supports standard HTTP authentication (bearer tokens, API keys, custom headers), and MCP recommends OAuth to obtain tokens. stdio has no network surface because it is process-to-process on one machine.

## Why the protocol pays for itself

The payoff is combinatorial. Without MCP you write a bespoke integration per tool per application, an N-clients times M-tools problem. With MCP a server exposes its capability once, and any compatible host connects, so the work grows with N plus M, not N times M.

```steps
Expose once | A server defines its tools, resources, and prompts a single time
Discover | Any MCP host connects and queries the server for its capabilities
Reuse | Every other compatible host reuses the same server with no new wiring
Scale | New clients and new servers compose without per-pair integration work
```

For a true one-to-one integration, one agent and one internal API you own, the protocol overhead may not pay off yet; the counter-argument is optionality for future clients and a uniform auth and discovery story.

## Security risks

Connecting a host to third-party servers widens the attack surface. An untrusted server can return tool descriptions or resource content that act as injected instructions (indirect prompt injection), a malicious server can impersonate a trusted one, and over-broad tool scopes let a compromised server reach more than it should. Defences are least-privilege tool scoping, authenticating and pinning server identity, isolating untrusted content, and human approval before destructive tool calls. Treat a tool server's output as untrusted data, not as instructions.

> **Interview.** Tool calling is the mechanism; MCP is the standard for discovery and transport around it. The value is combinatorial reuse across clients and servers, and the main risk is that connecting untrusted servers imports a prompt-injection and permission surface you must contain.

```recall
Q: What is the difference between tool calling and MCP?
A: Tool calling is the mechanism, the model emits a call and the app runs it. MCP standardises the transport and discovery layer so a server exposes its tools, resources, and prompts once and any compatible host connects, without the mechanism changing.
Q: Name the three MCP participants and the one-client-per-server rule.
A: Host (the app coordinating clients), client (one connection to one server, inside the host), server (exposes context). The host creates one client per server it connects to.
Q: When does stdio beat streamable HTTP?
A: stdio fits a local server serving one client with no network overhead; streamable HTTP fits remote servers serving many clients and carries HTTP auth. The transport follows where the server runs.
Q: Why can connecting a third-party MCP server be dangerous?
A: Its tool descriptions and returned content are untrusted and can carry injected instructions, it may impersonate a trusted server, and over-broad scopes let a compromised server overreach. Scope least privilege, pin identity, isolate content, and gate destructive calls.
```
lessons.deeper:
### The two layers

MCP is a data layer over a transport layer, and keeping them separate explains why the same tools work over stdio and HTTP. The data layer is the JSON-RPC 2.0 protocol: capability and version discovery, the primitives (tools, resources, prompts), and notifications. The transport layer handles connection, message framing, and authentication, and comes in the two mechanisms above. Because the transport is the outer layer and the data layer is inner, the same JSON-RPC messages ride either transport unchanged, which is why a server written once is reachable both locally and remotely. The primitives are where most developer interest sits, because they define exactly what context a server can share.

### Discovery is what makes it a protocol, not an SDK

The feature that separates MCP from "just call the API" is runtime discovery. A client queries a server for its supported protocol versions, capabilities, and identity, then lists its tools, and can subscribe to notifications when that list changes. This is why a host can connect to a server it was not built against and still use it: the capabilities are discovered, not compiled in. The same mechanism is the security hinge, discovered tool descriptions are attacker-controllable if the server is untrusted, so discovery is both the value and the risk.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant H as Host
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    H->>C: connect to server
    C->>S: discover capabilities
    S-->>C: tools, resources, prompts
    C->>S: call tool with args
    S-->>C: result
    Note over C: notify on list change
```

### Governance moved to a neutral foundation

On Dec 9, 2025 Anthropic donated MCP to the Agentic AI Foundation, a directed fund under the Linux Foundation, co-founded by Anthropic, Block, and OpenAI, with other companies joining as members. MCP became a founding project alongside Block's goose and OpenAI's AGENTS.md, and changes now go through a community Specification Enhancement Proposal process rather than a single vendor. The governance transfer is well corroborated across the Linux Foundation, Anthropic, and the MCP project itself. Adoption counts (one announcement cited more than 10,000 published servers as of Dec 2025) vary by source and methodology, so cite the governance fact as settled and treat raw adoption percentages as directional, not exact (2026, re-check against modelcontextprotocol.io and the Linux Foundation announcement).

lessons.title: Context engineering
lessons.body:
Context engineering is the 2025 reframing that interviewers now expect you to know by name.
