Anthropic's definition (Sep 29, 2025): the set of strategies for curating and maintaining the optimal set of tokens during inference, everything that lands in the window, not just the prompt. The reason it matters is that the context window is a finite, degrading resource, and "just add more information" stops helping and starts hurting past a point.

## Prompt engineering versus context engineering

Prompt engineering is about writing one instruction well. Context engineering treats the entire window, system prompt, tool definitions, MCP-supplied data, retrieved documents, and message history, as a finite resource you curate iteratively, at every turn of an agent loop. The shift is from authoring a static string to managing a budget that changes each turn as observations accumulate.

```flow
dir: TB
turn: Each agent turn | step
sys: System prompt | step
tools: Tool schemas | step
rag: Retrieved docs | store
hist: Message history | step
scratch: Working state | step
win: Context window | gate
turn -> win : assemble
sys -> win : stable, cacheable
tools -> win : stable, cacheable
rag -> win : capped, reranked
hist -> win : compacted
scratch -> win : protected
win --> turn : curate again next turn
```

The back edge is the point: curation is not a one-time setup, it repeats every turn because the window's contents change every turn.

## Why it matters: context rot

As token count grows, recall accuracy degrades even well within the advertised context limit. Transformer attention is O(n^2) in pairwise token relationships and training skews toward shorter sequences, so a model has an effective attention budget that depletes, a gradient, not a hard cliff. The guiding principle, verbatim from Anthropic: finding the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens that maximise the likelihood of some desired outcome.

```bars
title: Recall as context grows (illustrative shape, not a benchmark)
unit: relative recall
Window 20% full | 10
Window 60% full | 9
Window near limit | 6
```

The numbers above are an illustrative shape, not measured results; the point is the decline begins before the advertised limit, so capacity is not the fix.

## Techniques for long-horizon tasks

Four strategies keep a long task inside a healthy window.

```steps
Compaction | Near the limit, summarize the conversation and restart from the summary plus recently touched state
Note-taking | The agent writes persistent notes outside the window and reads them back after a reset
Sub-agents | Offload deep exploration to a clean context window that returns a condensed summary
Just-in-time retrieval | Hand the agent references (paths, queries) and let it load data on demand, like using an index
```

The hard part of compaction is the choice of what to keep (decisions, open bugs, the goal) versus discard (stale tool output, superseded plans). Note-taking externalises state so it survives a reset. Sub-agents isolate context so the lead window stays small. Just-in-time retrieval avoids pre-loading everything by passing lightweight references the agent resolves when needed.

## The window as a budget

Treat the window as a fixed budget you allocate deliberately, not a bucket you fill.

| Segment | Share | Discipline |
|---|---|---|
| System prompt and tools | Small, stable | Keep first, cacheable; watch bloated schemas |
| Retrieved context | The biggest swing | Cap to a few reranked chunks, not fifty |
| Message history | Grows every turn | First thing to compact |
| Working state | Protect | The current file, plan, open bugs |
| Output headroom | Reserve | A full window with no room to answer fails |

> **Pitfall.** "Just add more context", dumping the whole codebase, all history, and every retrieved doc into one window. Past the effective attention budget accuracy drops, and the model buries your actual instruction under low-signal filler. More tokens can make it worse.

> **Key idea.** Curation beats capacity. A bigger window does not fix context rot because recall degrades within the advertised limit; the smallest high-signal set wins.

```recall
Q: How does context engineering differ from prompt engineering?
A: Prompt engineering writes one instruction well. Context engineering curates the entire window, system prompt, tools, retrieved data, history, iteratively every turn, because the contents change each turn as observations accumulate.
Q: What is context rot and why does a bigger window not solve it?
A: Recall degrades as the window fills, even within the advertised limit, because attention is O(n^2) and training skews short, giving an effective attention budget that depletes. More capacity does not stop the decline, so curation is the fix.
Q: Name the four long-horizon techniques and what each solves.
A: Compaction (summarize and restart when near the limit), note-taking (external state surviving a reset), sub-agents (isolated windows returning digests), just-in-time retrieval (load data on demand via references).
Q: What makes compaction hard?
A: Choosing what to keep. Keep decisions, the goal, and open bugs; drop stale output and superseded plans. Keeping the wrong tokens loses the thread while still spending budget.
```
lessons.deeper:
### The window budget, concretely

A rough allocation for a working agent turn (illustrative, tune to your model): system prompt and tool definitions stable and cacheable at roughly 5 to 15% of the budget, with bloated tool schemas the quiet eater of this slice; retrieved documents the biggest swing, which you cap to three to eight reranked chunks rather than fifty; message history growing every turn and the first thing to compact; scratch and working state (the current file, the plan, open bugs) protected; and reserved headroom for the response, because a full window with no room to answer simply fails. The reason to budget rather than fill is context rot: recall degrades within the advertised limit because attention is O(n^2) over token pairs and training skews to shorter sequences, an effective attention budget that depletes gradually.

### What to keep versus drop when compacting

Keep decisions made, unresolved bugs, the current goal, and file or line anchors. Drop stale tool output, superseded plans, and verbose intermediate reasoning. The whole skill of compaction is that choice: a summary that keeps the right 300 tokens lets an agent run for hundreds of steps, while one that keeps the wrong tokens strands it. This is also where context engineering and agent memory meet, compaction decides what gets promoted to a durable note and what is discarded.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Agent
    participant W as Context window
    participant N as Notes (external)
    A->>W: near limit, summarize
    W-->>N: persist decisions and open bugs
    N-->>A: reload after reset, small and high-signal
    Note over A: just-in-time retrieval for the rest
```

### Worked example

A coding agent forty tool-calls into a refactor nears the limit. Compaction: summarise "migrated auth module to the new API; tests X and Y still failing; do not touch config.ts" into about 300 tokens, write it to a notes file, and restart from that summary plus the two files currently open. The agent keeps momentum without re-reading forty stale observations. Contrast the naive path, carrying all forty observations forward, where by step sixty the earliest instruction ("do not touch config.ts") is buried and the agent violates it.

### Source and currency

The definition, the smallest-high-signal-set principle, context rot, and the four techniques (compaction, note-taking, sub-agents, just-in-time retrieval) are from Anthropic, "Effective context engineering for AI agents" (Sep 29, 2025). The term was popularised more broadly in 2025 and platforms have since added primitives such as context editing and memory tools. Window sizes and prompt-caching economics keep shifting, but the curation discipline holds even as the specific numbers move (2026, re-check).

chapters.title: Production
chapters.summary: Evals, observability, safety, prompt injection, cost and latency, fine-tuning, and serving: what separates a demo from a system people trust.

lessons.title: Why evals come first
lessons.body:
An eval is a repeatable test that scores your system's output against known-good behaviour. Every primary source names evaluation as the hard part of AI engineering, and the reason is structural: an LLM feature has no compiler and no deterministic unit test to tell you it still works after you change a prompt or swap a model. The eval suite is that signal. Interviewers probe this because an engineer who ships prompt changes without an eval gate is flying blind, and they can usually tell within one question whether you have actually run one.

## Why evals come first, not last

With ordinary code you write the function, then test it. With an LLM feature the output space is open and the failure modes are unknown until you look, so you build the eval set first and let it define what good means. Chip Huyen puts it directly: there is no single simple solution to evaluation, a combination of methods is required, and the highest ratio of value still comes from manual inspection of real outputs. Build the dataset, look at failures by hand, and only then automate the scoring. The eval is not a formality you add before launch, it is the instrument you steer with from the first prompt.

> **Key idea.** You cannot improve what you cannot measure, and with LLMs you cannot measure without first building the set of cases that define correct.

## Unit-style vs end-to-end

Two granularities, and strong answers name both.

- **Unit-style** evals test one component in isolation with a tight assertion: does the extractor return valid JSON, does the router pick the right branch, does retrieval return the gold chunk in the top k. Fast, cheap, and they localise the failure.
- **End-to-end** evals run the whole pipeline on a realistic input and score the final answer. They catch interaction bugs a component test misses, but when they fail they do not tell you which stage broke.

Run both. Unit evals keep each stage honest, end-to-end evals catch the seams between stages.

## Offline vs online

```steps
Offline | Run before deploy against a fixed set of golden, adversarial, and regression cases
Online | Measure live traffic with user signals, sampled human review, and production metrics
Harvest | Turn every real production failure into a new permanent offline case
```

Offline eval is cheap and repeatable and gates every change, but it is only as good as its coverage and it goes stale as real inputs drift. Online eval sees the true input distribution but is slower and noisier to attribute. Neither replaces the other, and neither replaces looking at real outputs by hand.

## Regression gating in CI

The payoff of an offline set is that it becomes a gate. Wire it into CI the way you wire unit tests: a prompt or model change runs the suite, and a drop past a threshold blocks the merge. The subtlety is that LLM scores are noisy, so gate on an aggregate over a set large enough that normal variance does not trip it, not on a single case flipping.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev
    participant CI as Eval suite in CI
    participant Prod as Production
    Dev->>CI: new prompt or model
    CI-->>Dev: score drop, block merge
    Dev->>Prod: ship behind A/B
    Prod-->>Dev: online signal
    Note over Dev: harvest failures into set
```

## Trade-offs

| Choice | Cheap and fast | Catches real failures | Localises the bug |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unit-style offline | yes | partly | yes |
| End-to-end offline | medium | yes | no |
| Online metrics | no, needs traffic | yes, true distribution | no |
| Manual inspection | no, does not scale | yes, highest value | yes |

The decision rule: lead with offline unit and end-to-end as the pre-merge gate, confirm with an online metric on rollout, and never stop sampling real outputs by hand.

## Failure modes

The classic mistake is a single blended is the answer good score. When it dips you cannot tell whether retrieval missed the document or the model reasoned badly over a good one, and those have opposite fixes. Decompose instead: for a RAG system, score retrieval and generation separately. The second trap is trusting offline numbers alone, they cannot anticipate the live input distribution, which is why the online signal is the real rollout gate.

```recall
Q: Why build the eval set before writing the final prompt, not after?
A: An LLM feature has no deterministic test, so the eval set is the only signal that a change helped. It also defines what good means for an open output space, which you cannot know until you look at real cases.
Q: An end-to-end eval score drops. Why is that not enough to act on?
A: It tells you the pipeline got worse but not which stage, since retrieval, generation, and tool use all feed the final answer. You need unit-style evals per stage to localise the fix.
Q: Why gate a merge on an aggregate over many cases instead of any single case regressing?
A: LLM scores are noisy, so a single case can flip from run to run without a real regression. Gating on an aggregate over a large enough set keeps normal variance from blocking good changes.
Q: Offline eval said plus five percent but the online A/B is flat. What happened?
A: The offline set does not match the production input distribution, so the gain did not generalise. The live metric is the real gate because it sees the true traffic.
Q: What does harvesting regressions buy you over time?
A: Every fixed production bug becomes a permanent test, so the suite grows toward real failure coverage and the same bug cannot silently return.
```
lessons.deeper:
### What a case looks like

A good offline case is a triple: input, expected behaviour, and a scorer. The expected behaviour is rarely an exact string, so the scorer is the design decision. For extraction, assert on a parsed field and compare structurally, so wording does not matter. For classification, compare the label and compute precision, recall, and F1 over the set. For retrieval, record the gold chunk id and check whether it appears in the top k. For open-ended generation, you usually need an LLM judge, validated against human labels before you trust it, covered in its own lesson. The rule is to make the scorer as deterministic as the task allows and reach for a judge only when nothing cheaper captures correct.

### Metrics by task type

| Task | Metrics |
|---|---|
| Classification | precision, recall, F1 |
| Retrieval | recall@k, MRR, nDCG |
| Extraction | field exact match, schema validity rate |
| Open generation | faithfulness, answer relevance, judge score |

Naming the right metric for the task is a fast way to show you have actually measured one. A follow-up often asks why not accuracy for everything, and the answer is that accuracy hides class imbalance and ignores ranking, so a retriever with 0.95 accuracy on a mostly-irrelevant corpus can still bury the one relevant chunk below k.

### Dataset construction, the part people skip

Seed with golden examples of known-good input and output. Add adversarial cases: edge inputs, empty inputs, prompt-injection attempts, inputs in the wrong language. Then continuously harvest regressions from production so every real failure becomes a case. Aim for coverage of the real usage distribution, not raw volume, a few hundred well-chosen cases that span your actual traffic beat ten thousand near-duplicates. This is the manual work Huyen calls the highest value per unit effort, and it is also the part an interviewer uses to separate people who have run an eval from people who have read about one.

### Worked example

A RAG support bot. Build 200 triples of question, expected answer, and expected source document. Retrieval eval: does the expected source appear in the top k, giving recall@5 = 0.86. Generation eval, run only on the cases where retrieval succeeded so you isolate the generator: is the answer faithful to the retrieved chunk, scored by an LLM judge plus 50 human-labelled spot checks. Splitting them surfaces a result like generation looks 92 percent faithful but recall@5 is only 0.71, which tells you the fix is chunking or reranking, not the prompt. A single blended score would have hidden exactly that.

### A fast-moving caveat

Eval and tracing tooling churns, names like RAGAS, DeepEval, LangSmith, Braintrust, and Phoenix come and go in capability (as of 2026, re-check). Pick by whether the tool fits the taxonomy above, offline and online, per-component and end-to-end, not by a blog ranking. The taxonomy is stable, the tools are not.

lessons.title: Building eval datasets
lessons.body:
An eval is only as good as the dataset behind it, and the dataset is where most teams underinvest. A model change that scores plus three points on a stale, unrepresentative set tells you nothing about production. Building the set is the manual work Chip Huyen calls the highest ratio of value in all of evaluation. Interviewers ask about it because sourcing, sizing, and slicing a dataset is where the real judgement lives, scoring is comparatively mechanical.

## Where cases come from

Three sources, each with a different bias, and a strong set blends all three.

- **Production logs** are the ground truth for your real input distribution. They are the only source that reflects what users actually send, including the inputs you never imagined. The cost is labelling, and the risk is privacy.
- **Synthetic cases** are generated by a model from a schema or seed. Cheap and fast, good for covering a space systematically and for stress-testing before you have traffic. The risk is that they drift from real phrasing and over-sample the easy middle.
- **Expert-written cases** are hand-authored by someone who knows the domain. The most expensive and the most valuable for hard, rare, or high-stakes cases a log sample would miss.

```steps
Seed | Hand-write a small golden set that encodes known-good behaviour
Grow | Sample production logs to match the real input distribution
Augment | Add synthetic cases to cover gaps and edge inputs the logs miss
Harvest | Fold every real production failure back in as a permanent case
```

## How many, and how sure

Dataset size is a confidence question, not a round-number question. A pass rate measured on n cases carries sampling error, and the width of that error bar is roughly proportional to one over the square root of n. The practical consequence is sharp: moving from 100 to 400 cases roughly halves the error bar, but moving from 400 to 1600 only halves it again, so returns diminish fast.

> **Numbers.** A pass rate near 0.9 on 100 cases has a 95 percent interval of roughly plus or minus 6 points (illustrative, from the standard binomial error). To call a plus 2 point change real, you need a set large enough that 2 points sits outside the noise, which usually means several hundred cases per slice, not per suite.

A few hundred well-chosen cases that span your real traffic beat ten thousand near-duplicates. Volume without coverage buys false confidence.

## Slicing

A single aggregate score hides the failures that get you fired. Slice the set by the dimensions that matter: input language, query type, document source, user segment, short vs long input. A system can post 0.9 overall while sitting at 0.6 on the one slice that is your highest-value customer.

```bars
title: Aggregate hides a broken slice (illustrative)
unit: pass rate
Overall | 0.90
English queries | 0.94
Non-English queries | 0.61
Multi-hop queries | 0.58
```

The decision rule: gate on the worst important slice, not only the mean. The mean can rise while a slice you care about collapses.

## Contamination and leakage

Two distinct failures that both inflate your numbers.

- **Train/test leakage** happens when a case, or something near-identical, appears in both your few-shot prompt examples and your eval set. The model has effectively seen the answer, so the score is a memory test, not a generalisation test. Keep prompt examples and eval cases strictly disjoint.
- **Benchmark contamination** happens when a public benchmark leaked into the model's pretraining corpus. A frontier model can score high on a famous benchmark because it memorised it, not because it reasons. This is why a private, held-out set built from your own data is worth more than any public leaderboard number.

| Trap | Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Prompt-example leakage | eval score far above production quality | disjoint example and eval pools |
| Benchmark contamination | strong on public set, weak on yours | hold out a private set from your own data |
| Over-easy synthetic | high score, real users still fail | mix in production logs and adversarial cases |

## Maintaining a golden set

The golden set is the stable, curated core you trust most: known-good cases, reviewed, versioned like code, and changed deliberately. Treat edits to it as commits with review, because silently editing the golden set is how a team fools itself into thinking quality improved. Grow it by harvesting production failures, retire cases that no longer reflect real usage, and re-balance slices as traffic shifts. A living golden set is a product asset, not a one-time deliverable.

```recall
Q: Why is a private held-out set worth more than a public benchmark score?
A: Public benchmarks can leak into a model's pretraining data, so a high score may be memorisation rather than reasoning. A private set built from your own data cannot have been seen and reflects your real distribution.
Q: Your eval set is 50 cases and a change scores plus two points. Why not ship on that?
A: With 50 cases the sampling error is far wider than two points, so the change is inside the noise. You need several hundred cases per slice before a two-point move is distinguishable from chance.
Q: What breaks if your few-shot prompt examples also appear in the eval set?
A: The model has effectively seen the answers, so the eval becomes a memory test and the score overstates real quality. Keep example and eval pools strictly disjoint.
Q: Why slice the dataset instead of reporting one aggregate pass rate?
A: An aggregate can stay high while a specific important slice, like non-English or multi-hop queries, collapses. Slicing surfaces the failure the mean hides so you can gate on the worst important slice.
Q: What is the role of synthetic cases if production logs are the ground truth?
A: Synthetic cases cover gaps and edge inputs systematically and let you build a set before you have traffic. They complement logs rather than replace them, because they can drift from real phrasing.
```
lessons.deeper:
### The confidence arithmetic

Treat a pass rate as a proportion p measured on n independent cases. The standard error is sqrt(p times (1 minus p) divided by n), and the 95 percent interval is roughly p plus or minus 1.96 times that. At p = 0.9 and n = 100 the standard error is sqrt(0.09 / 100) = 0.03, so the interval is about plus or minus 0.06. At n = 400 it falls to about plus or minus 0.03, at n = 1600 to about plus or minus 0.015. Two lessons fall out. First, to detect a small improvement you need the interval narrower than the improvement, which sets your minimum n. Second, because the error scales with one over sqrt(n), each halving of the error bar costs four times the cases, so there is a natural ceiling past which more data is not worth the labelling. These are illustrative applications of the standard binomial error, not a benchmark result.

### Sourcing without poisoning privacy

Production logs are the best source and the most dangerous. Before a real user input enters an eval set, strip or redact PII, and prefer to store a reference and a derived label rather than raw sensitive text. For regulated domains, keep the eval set inside the same trust boundary as the production data and do not ship it to a third-party eval service without checking the data agreement. The engineering point for an interview: the eval dataset inherits the data-handling obligations of the data it was sampled from, it is not a lower-sensitivity artifact just because it is called test data.

### Synthetic generation that does not collapse

Naive synthetic generation asks a model for more examples like these and gets a cluster of near-duplicates around the easy centre of the distribution. Better: generate against an explicit schema of dimensions you want covered, for example query type crossed with document source crossed with difficulty, and sample the cells deliberately so the hard and rare cells are represented. Then have a human or a second model filter for realism, discarding cases no real user would send. The goal is coverage of the space, especially its corners, not fluency.

### Versioning and drift

Version the dataset the way you version a schema. Each eval run records which dataset version it ran against, so a score is only comparable to another score on the same version. When you add or retire cases, bump the version and re-baseline, because comparing a new model on v3 of the set to an old model on v2 is meaningless. Track input drift separately: periodically compare the distribution of recent production inputs against the dataset, and when they diverge, that is the signal to resample. A dataset that never changes is quietly going stale against a moving world (as of 2026, re-check your tooling for drift detection).

lessons.title: Evaluating a RAG system
lessons.body:
A RAG system fails in two completely different ways: retrieval can miss the document, or generation can mangle a document it was given. These need opposite fixes, so a single end-to-end score is almost useless for debugging. The core skill, and the thing interviewers test, is evaluating retrieval and generation separately with the right metric for each, and knowing the arithmetic well enough to compute recall@k, MRR, and nDCG by hand.

## Split the pipeline, then measure each half

```flow
dir: LR
q: Query | actor
ret: Retriever | model
chunks: Top-k chunks | store
gen: Generator | model
ans: Answer | step
q -> ret : question
ret -> chunks : ranked list
chunks -> gen : context
q -> gen : question
gen -> ans : grounded answer
ret --> chunks : retrieval metrics
gen --> ans : generation metrics
```

Measure retrieval first. If the answer text never entered the context, no prompt or model change on the generation side can produce a correct answer, so retrieval is the first suspect and generation is tuned only once retrieval is good enough. Most teams get this backwards and spend weeks on the prompt against a retrieval defect.

## Retrieval metrics, with the arithmetic

You need a labelled set: each query paired with the ids of the chunks that actually contain the answer (the relevant set). Three metrics, in rising sophistication.

**Recall@k** is the fraction of relevant chunks that appear in the top k. For a query with one relevant chunk, recall@k is simply 1 if that chunk is in the top k and 0 otherwise, averaged over the query set. It answers: did we even fetch the answer.

**MRR**, mean reciprocal rank, rewards putting the first relevant hit high. For each query take the reciprocal of the rank of the first relevant result (1/rank), then average over queries. It cares only about the first hit.

**nDCG@k**, normalised discounted cumulative gain, is the ranking metric for graded relevance: a highly relevant chunk ranked first is worth more than the same chunk ranked tenth, and partially relevant chunks earn partial credit. It discounts gain by position and normalises against the ideal ordering so the score lands in 0 to 1.

### Worked example

Five queries. For each, the rank at which the first relevant chunk appears in the retrieved list:

| Query | First relevant at rank | In top 5 | Reciprocal rank |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 | 1 | yes | 1.000 |
| Q2 | 3 | yes | 0.333 |
| Q3 | not in top 10 | no | 0.000 |
| Q4 | 2 | yes | 0.500 |
| Q5 | 6 | no | 0.167 |

Recall@5 = relevant-found-in-top-5 over queries = 3 / 5 = 0.60. MRR = (1.000 + 0.333 + 0.000 + 0.500 + 0.167) / 5 = 2.000 / 5 = 0.40. Note how they disagree: Q5 counts for MRR (rank 6 gives 0.167) but not for recall@5. That disagreement is the point, recall@k asks did we fetch it within k, MRR asks how high was the first hit.

### nDCG in one worked step

Take one query, k = 3, with graded relevances of the retrieved items being 3, 2, 0 (on a 0 to 3 scale). DCG uses gain over log of position: 3/log2(2) + 2/log2(3) + 0/log2(4) = 3/1 + 2/1.585 + 0 = 3 + 1.262 = 4.262. The ideal ordering of those same relevances is 3, 2, 0 already, so IDCG = 4.262 and nDCG = DCG / IDCG = 1.0. Had the retriever returned them as 0, 2, 3 instead, DCG = 0 + 2/1.585 + 3/2 = 1.262 + 1.5 = 2.762, giving nDCG = 2.762 / 4.262 = 0.65. Same chunks, worse order, lower score, which is exactly what MRR and recall@k cannot see.

## Generation metrics

Once the right chunks are in context, score the answer. The four metrics popularised by RAGAS (Es et al., EACL 2024) split cleanly by layer:

| Metric | Question it answers | Layer |
|---|---|---|
| Context precision | Are the retrieved chunks relevant, and ranked well | retrieval |
| Context recall | Did retrieval fetch everything needed to answer | retrieval |
| Faithfulness | Is every claim in the answer supported by the context | generation |
| Answer relevance | Does the answer actually address the question | generation |

Faithfulness is the hallucination guard: a claim fluent and confident but unsupported by any retrieved chunk is the classic RAG hallucination. Answer relevance catches the opposite, a faithful but evasive answer that never addresses the question.

> **Pitfall.** A high faithfulness score with low context recall. The generator is answering coherently from partial context, so it looks grounded while silently omitting half the answer. Faithfulness alone cannot catch a retrieval gap, which is why you measure context recall beside it.

## Component vs end-to-end

Component metrics localise the bug, end-to-end tells you whether the user got a good answer. Run both. A worked split: context recall 0.62, faithfulness 0.91, end-to-end answer-correctness 0.70. Reading it, the generator is faithful but the retriever is dropping needed chunks on multi-hop questions, so the fix is retrieval, not the prompt, even though faithfulness looked healthy.

```recall
Q: Why measure retrieval before generation when debugging a wrong RAG answer?
A: If the answer chunk never entered the context, no generation change can produce a correct answer. Retrieval is the gating stage, so you confirm it is good before tuning the prompt.
Q: Recall@5 is 0.60 but MRR is 0.40 on the same set. How can both be true?
A: Recall@5 counts only hits within the top five, while MRR credits the first relevant hit at any rank by its reciprocal. A query whose first hit is at rank six adds to MRR but not to recall@5.
Q: What does nDCG capture that recall@k and MRR miss?
A: Order and graded relevance across the whole top k. nDCG rewards putting more-relevant chunks higher and gives partial credit, so it drops when the same chunks are returned in a worse order.
Q: Faithfulness is 0.91 but users still get incomplete answers. Which metric exposes it?
A: Context recall. A high faithfulness score only means the answer is grounded in what was retrieved, not that retrieval fetched everything, so a low context recall reveals the gap.
Q: Why run both component and end-to-end evals instead of one?
A: Component metrics localise which stage failed; end-to-end confirms the user actually got a good answer. One without the other either hides the bug or hides whether it mattered.
```
lessons.deeper:
### DCG, IDCG, and why the log discount

Discounted cumulative gain sums the relevance of each result divided by a position discount, and the standard discount is log base 2 of (position + 1), so position 1 divides by log2(2) = 1, position 2 by log2(3) = 1.585, position 3 by log2(4) = 2, and so on. The log makes the penalty for being one rank lower shrink as you go down the list, which matches how users read: the gap between rank 1 and rank 2 matters far more than the gap between rank 20 and rank 21. IDCG is the DCG of the ideal ordering, the same relevances sorted best-first, and nDCG = DCG / IDCG normalises every query to 0 to 1 so queries with different numbers of relevant items are comparable. Without normalisation a query with five relevant chunks would dominate the average over a query with one, purely by having more gain to accumulate.

### Choosing among the three retrieval metrics

Use recall@k when any correct chunk anywhere in the top k is enough, which is the common RAG case because the generator reads all k. Use MRR when the first hit is what matters, for example a single-answer lookup where the user stops at the first good result. Use nDCG when relevance is graded, not binary, and ranking order inside the top k affects quality, for example when the generator weights earlier chunks more or when you truncate aggressively. For most RAG tuning, recall@k is the primary dial because it directly answers whether the generator will even see the answer, and nDCG is the secondary dial once recall is adequate and you want to tighten ordering for lost-in-the-middle effects.

### Judge-scored generation metrics need their own eval

Faithfulness, answer relevance, and context precision as computed by RAGAS are themselves LLM-judge scores, which means they inherit the biases of LLM-as-judge: position, verbosity, self-preference, and run-to-run variance. Before trusting them as a gate, validate the judge against human labels on a sample and measure its agreement, the same discipline the LLM-as-judge lesson sets out. A faithfulness number is a measurement from an instrument that itself needs calibrating, not ground truth. The RAGAS framework (Es, James, and collaborators, presented at EACL 2024) formalised these four metrics; re-check the current library and its metric definitions, this space moves fast (as of 2026, re-check).

### Where end-to-end answer-correctness fits

End-to-end answer-correctness compares the final answer to a reference answer, usually with a judge or a semantic-similarity score plus an exact-fact check. It is the number closest to user value, but it is the worst at localisation, so treat it as the headline metric you report and the component metrics as the diagnostics you act on. A rise in end-to-end with a drop in context recall, for instance, is a warning that the generator is compensating for a weak retriever by leaning on its parametric memory, which will fail silently on anything outside its training data.

lessons.title: Using an LLM as judge
lessons.body:
Using an LLM to score another LLM's output is now standard, because human review of every output does not scale and open-ended generation has no deterministic scorer. But 2024 and 2025 research documents specific, reproducible biases, so the correct mental model is a measurement instrument that needs calibrating, not an oracle. An interviewer who hears you treat a judge score as ground truth has their answer; one who hears you talk about validating it against humans knows you have shipped one.

## Pointwise vs pairwise

The first design choice is what you ask the judge to do.

- **Pointwise** scoring hands the judge one output and asks for an absolute score, say 1 to 5 or pass/fail against a rubric. Simple and it scales to a single candidate, but absolute scores are unstable: the same output can draw a 3 one run and a 4 the next, and the scale drifts between batches.
- **Pairwise** comparison hands the judge two outputs and asks which is better. Humans and models are both far more reliable at relative judgements than absolute ones, so pairwise is the more trustworthy signal when you are comparing two systems or two prompts.

The decision rule: use pairwise when you are choosing between candidates, which is most A/B and regression work, and reserve pointwise for when you genuinely need a standalone score and have calibrated the rubric.

## The documented biases

Every one of these is paper-backed, and naming them is the fastest way to show you know the failure modes.

| Bias | What the judge does | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Position | favours the first (or last) option in a pairwise prompt | randomise order, score both orders and average |
| Verbosity | rates longer answers higher regardless of quality | control for length, penalise padding in the rubric |
| Self-preference | favours outputs in its own style or from its own family | use a different model family as judge where possible |
| Provenance | rates the same content differently by claimed source | blind the source before judging |
| Fragility | flips verdict on repeated runs of the same case | measure variance, average over runs |

```flow
dir: LR
cand: Candidate pair | step
blind: Blind and shuffle | gate
judge: LLM judge | model
agg: Average both orders | step
human: Human sample | actor
check: Agreement check | gate
cand -> blind : two outputs
blind -> judge : order randomized
judge -> agg : two verdicts
agg -> check : judge score
human -> check : labels
check -> judge : trust only if agreement holds
```

## Calibration against human labels

A judge is trustworthy only to the degree it agrees with humans on cases you have labelled. The standard measure is Cohen's kappa, which corrects raw agreement for the agreement you would get by chance. Its formula is (observed agreement minus expected agreement) divided by (1 minus expected agreement), so a kappa of 1 is perfect, 0 is chance-level, and negative means systematically worse than chance.

> **Numbers.** The Landis and Koch (1977) bands, widely used for inter-rater agreement: 0.0 to 0.2 slight, 0.2 to 0.4 fair, 0.4 to 0.6 moderate, 0.6 to 0.8 substantial, 0.8 to 1.0 almost perfect. Many teams treat substantial, kappa above about 0.6 to 0.7, as the bar before a judge gates releases, but the threshold is a convention, not a law, pick it for the stakes.

Why kappa and not raw percent agreement: if 95 percent of your cases are pass, a judge that blindly says pass agrees 95 percent of the time while measuring nothing. Kappa strips out that chance agreement, so it exposes a judge that looks accurate only because the labels are imbalanced.

## Rubric design

The rubric is the judge's spec, and a vague rubric is the single biggest source of judge noise. A good rubric is concrete and decomposed: instead of rate the answer 1 to 5, define each level with an observable criterion, or better, ask a sequence of yes/no questions (is every claim supported, does it answer the question, is it free of PII) and compose the score from those. Binary sub-questions are far more stable across runs than a holistic number, and they localise why an output failed.

## Trade-offs

| Choice | Scales | Stable across runs | Localises failure |
|---|---|---|---|
| Human review | no | yes | yes |
| Pointwise judge | yes | weakly | partly |
| Pairwise judge | yes | better | partly |
| Binary rubric questions | yes | best | yes |

```recall
Q: Why prefer pairwise comparison over pointwise scoring for A/B work?
A: Models and humans are more reliable at relative than absolute judgements, so pairwise gives a more stable signal when choosing between two candidates. Pointwise scores drift and are noisy run to run.
Q: Why report Cohen's kappa instead of raw percent agreement for judge-vs-human?
A: Raw agreement is inflated by chance when labels are imbalanced, so a judge that always says pass can look accurate while measuring nothing. Kappa subtracts chance agreement and exposes that.
Q: Name two biases that follow from the prompt structure and their fixes.
A: Position bias is fixed by randomising or averaging over both orderings; verbosity bias is fixed by controlling for length and penalising padding in the rubric.
Q: Why decompose a rubric into binary yes/no questions instead of a 1 to 5 score?
A: Binary sub-questions are far more stable across runs than a holistic number and they localise which criterion failed, so the judge is both more reliable and more diagnostic.
Q: You validated a judge last quarter. Why re-validate after swapping the judge model?
A: Biases and agreement are specific to the model and prompt, so a new judge model can introduce self-preference or shift calibration. Agreement must be re-measured before the new judge gates releases.
```
lessons.deeper:
### Why self-preference is the quiet one

Position and verbosity bias are easy to see and easy to control. Self-preference is more insidious: a judge from the same model family as one of the candidates systematically rates that candidate higher because its outputs match the judge's own stylistic priors, not because they are better. In a bake-off where you are deciding whether to switch from model A to model B, using model A as the judge quietly tilts the result toward A. The mitigation is to judge with a different model family from either candidate where you can, and at minimum to disclose the judge's identity when reporting a comparison, because a comparison judged by one of the contestants is not a clean result.

### Measuring the judge's own variance

Before a judge gates anything, run it two or three times on the same identical inputs and measure how often it changes its verdict. A judge that flips 15 percent of its pass/fail calls on re-run cannot gate a merge on a 2 point change, because the gate noise swamps the signal. Two fixes: lower the judge's temperature toward 0 to cut sampling variance, and average over several runs for high-stakes decisions. Report the judge's self-consistency alongside its human agreement, both are properties of your instrument and both bound what you can conclude from its scores.

### Validating and the sampling cost

Calibration is not free: you need human labels on a sample large enough that the kappa estimate is itself stable, which pulls in the same binomial-confidence reasoning as dataset sizing. A kappa computed on 20 cases is almost meaningless; a few hundred labelled cases gives a kappa you can act on. The practical loop: label a validation sample by hand, compute the judge's kappa against those labels, and if it clears your bar, let the judge score the much larger unlabelled set, re-validating on a fresh human sample periodically because both the model and your inputs drift. The judge extends human judgement to scale, it does not replace the human labels that anchor it (as of 2026, re-check tooling for automated agreement tracking).

### A debugging note

When a judge pipeline misbehaves, the usual root cause is not the model but the rubric or the harness: an ambiguous rubric level, a prompt that leaks the expected answer, order that is never shuffled, or provenance that is never blinded. Audit those before blaming the judge model, because a sharper rubric and a blinded, order-randomised harness fix most judge pathologies without touching the model at all.

lessons.title: Observability and tracing for LLM apps
lessons.body:
An LLM app needs trace-level visibility that traditional application monitoring does not give you. Latency and error rate alone cannot tell you why an agent gave a wrong answer, because the answer is the product of a prompt, retrieved context, several tool calls, and a model's reasoning, and any of them can be the fault. Observability for LLM systems means capturing that whole chain per request so you can decompose a vague bug report into a specific stage. Interviewers probe this because an engineer who cannot trace a bad answer back to its stage cannot debug a production LLM system at all.

## Traces and spans

The data model is borrowed from distributed tracing and it fits LLM apps well.

- A **trace** is one end-to-end request: the user's question through to the final answer.
- A **span** is one step inside that trace: an LLM call, a retrieval, a tool call, a guardrail check. Spans nest, so an agent loop is a trace with a span per step and sub-spans for each tool call inside a step.

```flow
dir: TB
trace: Trace, one request | step
embed: Span, embed query | model
ret: Span, retrieve | store
llm: Span, LLM call | model
tool: Span, tool call | tool
out: Span, output guard | gate
trace -> embed : start
embed -> ret : vector
ret -> llm : chunks
llm -> tool : tool request
tool -> llm : result
llm -> out : draft answer
out -> trace : final answer
```

Each span records its inputs, its outputs, its latency, and its token and cost figures, so the trace is a complete, replayable account of what happened.

## What to log

Log enough to reconstruct and replay a request without guessing.

```steps
Prompt | The full prompt and system message actually sent, after templating
Context | The retrieved chunks with their ids and scores
Tool calls | Each tool name, its arguments, and the result returned
Output | The raw model output before and after any post-processing
Usage | Input and output tokens, cost, latency per span and per trace
Metadata | Model and prompt version, user or session id, feedback signal
```

The non-obvious ones are the versions and the retrieved chunks. Without the prompt and model version on every trace you cannot tell whether a quality dip followed a deploy. Without the retrieved chunks you cannot tell a retrieval failure from a generation failure, which is the single most common RAG debugging question.

## Decomposing a wrong answer

This is the payoff and the interview framing. When a user reports the agent gave a wrong answer, the trace sorts it into one of three buckets with different owners and different fixes.

| Category | What the trace shows | Fix lives in |
|---|---|---|
| Retrieval | the right chunk is absent from the context span | chunking, hybrid search, reranking, k |
| Generation | the right chunk is present but the answer ignores or distorts it | prompt, model, citation requirement |
| Tool use | a tool span returned bad data or was called with wrong arguments | tool schema, description, validation |

> **Interview.** The user says it is wrong. You do not say the model hallucinated. You say pull the trace, check whether the answer chunk is in the retrieval span, and that tells you whether this is a retrieval bug or a generation bug, which have opposite fixes.

## Cost and latency dashboards

The same spans that debug correctness also drive cost and latency control. Aggregate token and cost per span to find the expensive step, and per-stage latency to find the slow one. A trace that shows retrieval at 40 milliseconds and the LLM call at 3 seconds tells you where to spend optimisation effort. Watch cost per request and per user as a first-class metric, because a prompt change that quietly doubles context length doubles cost silently unless the dashboard surfaces it.

## PII and privacy

Full-prompt logging collides with privacy. Traces contain exactly the sensitive data users send, so treat the trace store as production-sensitive: redact or hash PII before it lands, set retention limits, and gate access. The tension is real, because the richest trace is also the one that most endangers user data, so log what you need to debug and no more, and prefer references over raw sensitive text where a reference suffices.

## Feedback into evals

Observability closes the loop with evaluation. User signals captured on a trace, a thumbs-down, an edit, a re-ask, mark that trace as a probable failure, and those traces are the richest source of new regression cases. The pipeline is: trace captures the failure, a human confirms it, the case joins the offline eval set, and the next change is gated against it. This is how a production system's own failures become its permanent test suite.

```recall
Q: Why is latency-and-error-rate monitoring not enough for an LLM app?
A: A wrong answer is produced by prompt, context, tool calls, and reasoning together, and none of those shows up as an error or a latency spike. You need the full per-request trace to tell which stage was at fault.
Q: What two logged fields most often decide a RAG debugging question, and why?
A: The retrieved chunks and the prompt and model version. The chunks separate a retrieval failure from a generation failure, and the version tells you whether a quality dip followed a specific deploy.
Q: A user reports a wrong answer. What is the first thing the trace tells you?
A: Whether the answer chunk is present in the retrieval span. If it is absent the bug is retrieval; if it is present but ignored the bug is generation. These have opposite fixes.
Q: Why is the richest trace also a privacy liability?
A: It captures the full prompt and context, which contains exactly the sensitive data the user sent. So the trace store must be treated as production-sensitive with redaction, retention limits, and access control.
Q: How does observability feed back into evals?
A: Traces flagged by user signals like thumbs-down or edits are confirmed by a human and harvested into the offline eval set, turning production failures into permanent regression cases.
```
lessons.deeper:
### Spans as the unit of attribution

The reason the span model is worth adopting rather than ad-hoc logging is attribution. A flat log line per request cannot answer which of three LLM calls in an agent loop was slow or expensive, because the costs are summed and lost. Spans keep each call's cost, latency, and tokens separate and nested under the trace, so you can roll up by span type, retrieval total vs LLM total vs tool total, and attribute a regression to one of them. For an agent that loops, this is the difference between the agent got slow and the second tool call started timing out on turn four, which is actionable. OpenTelemetry-style semantic conventions for LLM spans exist and are converging (as of 2026, re-check), so instrumenting with them keeps you portable across backends.

### The tooling category

This category is genuinely new relative to classic application performance monitoring, and it moves fast, so treat any who is best ranking as opinion. Independent comparisons repeatedly cite LangSmith (coupled to LangChain and LangGraph), Arize Phoenix (framework-agnostic, open-source), Langfuse and Comet Opik (open-source, self-hostable), Braintrust (evaluation-first), and Datadog (if you want LLM traces correlated with existing infrastructure metrics). The selection logic that survives the churn: do you need it self-hostable for data residency, is it tied to your framework or neutral, and does it unify tracing with evaluation so the feedback-into-evals loop is one system rather than two. Pick on those axes, not on a leaderboard (as of 2026, re-check the specific tools).

### Sampling at scale

Logging every full prompt and context for every request is expensive in both storage and privacy exposure once traffic is large. The usual compromise is to log all metadata, token, cost, latency, versions, for every request cheaply, and to retain full prompt-and-context payloads only for a sample plus every request a user flagged or that failed a guardrail. That keeps the aggregate dashboards complete while bounding the sensitive, bulky payload storage to the traces you are most likely to actually inspect. Set the sample rate from your debugging needs and your privacy budget, and always force-capture the failures, because a failure you did not record in full is a regression case you cannot build.

### Replay as the goal

The test of good instrumentation is whether you can replay a request from its trace: re-run the exact prompt against the recorded context and reproduce the output. If the trace captures the templated prompt, the retrieved chunks, the model and parameters, and the tool results, you can. Replayability is what turns a vague user complaint into a deterministic debugging session and what lets you verify a fix against the exact input that broke, so design logging backward from the question can I replay this.

lessons.title: Shipping prompt changes safely
lessons.body:
A prompt is production code: it determines system behaviour, it breaks things when changed, and it needs the same discipline as any other deploy. Teams that edit a prompt in a text box and push it live are shipping an untested behaviour change to every user at once. The safe pattern treats a prompt as a versioned artifact and gates its release behind evals and a staged rollout. Interviewers ask this to separate people who think of prompts as config from people who have been burned by a one-word prompt edit that quietly tanked a metric.

## Prompts as artifacts

The first move is to pull the prompt out of the code and the text box and into a versioned store, so that every prompt has an id and a version, every production response records which prompt version produced it, and a change is a reviewable diff, not an invisible edit. This is what makes everything else possible: you cannot roll back, A/B test, or attribute a regression to a prompt you did not version.

> **Key idea.** If you cannot name the exact prompt version that produced a given production answer, you cannot debug, roll back, or evaluate prompt changes. Versioning is the precondition for everything else in this lesson.

## The two-gate rollout

Shipping a prompt change combines the two eval modes into a pipeline.

```steps
Offline gate | Run the new prompt against golden and regression sets to catch obvious breakage cheaply
Shadow | Run the new prompt on live traffic in parallel, serving the old one, and compare
Canary | Serve the new prompt to a small traffic slice and watch the live metric
A/B | Split traffic and decide on a metric that reflects real value, not a proxy
Promote | Roll out fully, keeping the old version pinned for instant rollback
```

The offline set is a cheap pre-filter: it catches regressions before you spend any live traffic. But offline sets cannot capture the full production input distribution, so the real rollout decision is gated on a live metric. This echoes Huyen's point that there is no single solution to evaluation, the offline set is necessary but not sufficient, and the online signal is where you make the call.

## Shadow, canary, A/B

These are three distinct staging techniques, and naming the difference is a quick credibility signal.

| Technique | Who sees the new prompt | What it measures | Risk to users |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shadow | nobody, runs in parallel | output diff vs old, offline-scored | none |
| Canary | a small percentage | live metric on a slice | bounded to the slice |
| A/B | a controlled split | metric difference with significance | bounded, measured |

Shadow mode is the safest because users never see the new output, you only compare it. Canary bounds the blast radius to a small slice so a bad prompt harms few users and is caught fast. A/B is the statistical decision: enough traffic on each arm to tell a real metric difference from noise.

## Choosing the gate metric

The rollout stands or falls on the metric you gate it on. Pick one that reflects real value, task success rate, edit rate, thumbs-down rate, resolution without escalation, not a convenient proxy like response length or a raw judge score. The classic failure is gating on a proxy that improves while the real outcome gets worse: a prompt that makes answers longer can raise a looks-thorough proxy while lowering actual task success.

```flow
dir: LR
dev: Prompt change | actor
off: Offline eval | gate
shadow: Shadow run | gate
canary: Canary slice | gate
ab: A/B metric | gate
prod: Full rollout | step
dev -> off : new version
off -> shadow : passes
shadow -> canary : no diff regression
canary -> ab : slice healthy
ab -> prod : metric wins
ab --> dev : metric loses, roll back
```

## Rollback and attribution

Because every response records its prompt version, rollback is pinning the previous version, instant and total, and attribution is a group-by on version. When a metric moves, you can line it up against the prompt-version timeline and see whether the move followed a change. Without versioning, a regression that appeared three deploys ago is nearly impossible to localise.

```recall
Q: Why can you not safely ship a prompt change on an offline eval pass alone?
A: Offline sets cannot capture the full production input distribution, so a change that passes offline can still regress a live metric. The real rollout decision is gated on an online metric.
Q: What is the difference between shadow mode and a canary?
A: Shadow runs the new prompt in parallel without serving its output, so users never see it and you only compare. A canary serves the new prompt to a small traffic slice, bounding real user exposure.
Q: Why gate on task success rate rather than response length or a raw judge score?
A: Proxies can improve while the real outcome worsens, for example longer answers that lower actual task success. The gate must reflect real value or it rewards the wrong behaviour.
Q: What does recording the prompt version on every response make possible?
A: Instant rollback by pinning the prior version, and attribution of a metric change to a specific prompt by grouping responses on version. Both are impossible without it.
Q: Why treat a prompt edit as a reviewable diff instead of a text-box change?
A: A prompt is behaviour-defining code, so an invisible edit is an untested change pushed to all users. A diff gets review, a version, and a rollback path, the same safety any code deploy has.
```
lessons.deeper:
### Why a one-word edit is dangerous

Prompt behaviour is not continuous in the prompt text. Adding a single instruction, reordering two sentences, or changing be concise to be brief can shift outputs in ways that are invisible on a handful of examples but material across the real distribution. This is why the eyeball test, try it on three inputs, looks fine, ship, fails: three inputs cannot reveal a change that regresses two percent of a long-tail slice. The discipline that catches it is the same offline-then-online pipeline used for model changes, because a prompt change is a behaviour change of the same kind, just cheaper to make, which is exactly what makes it tempting to ship carelessly.

### Decoupling prompt releases from code releases

A mature setup lets prompts ship on their own cadence, pulled at runtime from the versioned store rather than baked into the application binary. This is powerful and risky. The upside is fast iteration and instant rollback without a code deploy. The downside is that a prompt is now an external input your running system trusts, so the store needs the same access control, review, and audit as code, and the runtime needs a safe default if the fetch fails. Treat the prompt store as part of your deploy surface, not as config, and version-pin what production reads so a change is deliberate, never a surprise fetch.

### A/B significance, briefly

Deciding an A/B needs enough traffic that the metric difference is distinguishable from noise, the same binomial-confidence reasoning as eval dataset sizing. A one-point lift in task success on a few hundred requests per arm is inside the error bar and not a result. Run the test until the interval around the difference excludes zero, or accept you cannot distinguish the arms and keep the simpler prompt. Peeking at the metric and stopping the moment it looks good inflates false positives, so fix the sample size or use a sequential test designed for repeated looks, do not eyeball the running number and call it when it is ahead.

### What to version alongside the prompt

The prompt text alone is not the whole behaviour. Version the model and parameters (temperature, max tokens), the tool schemas, and the retrieval configuration together, because the same prompt against a different model or a different retriever is a different system. The cleanest unit is a named configuration bundle, prompt plus model plus parameters plus tool and retrieval settings, versioned as one artifact and pinned per deploy. That way a response's recorded version identifies the entire behaviour that produced it, not just the words, which is what makes attribution and rollback actually reliable (as of 2026, re-check your prompt-management tooling for bundle-level versioning).

lessons.title: Guardrails and safety layers
lessons.body:
A guardrail is a check that sits outside the model and constrains what goes in, what comes out, or what the system is allowed to do. The interview-relevant insight is architectural, not a product list: guardrails are layers at the system edges, and the strongest ones never trust the generating model to police itself. An engineer who answers add a safety prompt has missed the point; one who talks about input, output, and action layers with a separate screening call has it.

## Three layers

Guardrails sit at three points, and a serious system has all three.

- **Input guardrails** screen what reaches the model: prompt-injection and jailbreak detection, PII redaction before logging, topic and policy filters, length and format limits.
- **Output guardrails** screen what the model produced before it reaches the user: toxicity and policy checks, PII leak detection, schema and groundedness validation, refusal of disallowed content.
- **Action guardrails** screen what the system is allowed to do with the output: approval gates on high-stakes actions, command allow and deny lists, permission and least-privilege checks on tools.

```flow
dir: LR
user: User input | actor
ig: Input guard | gate
llm: LLM | model
og: Output guard | gate
ag: Action guard | gate
tool: Tool or effect | tool
out: Response | step
user -> ig : raw input
ig -> llm : cleaned input
llm -> og : draft output
og -> ag : proposed action
ag -> tool : approved action
og -> out : safe response
```

## Rule vs classifier vs LLM check

Each layer can be enforced three ways, trading latency, cost, and flexibility.

| Mechanism | Latency | Catches | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rule or regex | lowest | known exact patterns, formats, allow and deny lists | brittle, misses paraphrase |
| Classifier | low | learned categories like toxicity or jailbreak | needs training data, fixed classes |
| LLM check | high | nuanced, context-dependent policy | slow, costly, itself fallible |

The decision rule: use the cheapest mechanism that catches the risk. A deny list for rm -rf is a rule, not a model. Toxicity is a classifier. Is this medical advice that needs a disclaimer is an LLM check. Reaching for an LLM check where a rule suffices adds latency and a new failure mode for nothing.

## The separate-call principle

The one primary-sourced architectural recommendation worth stating precisely: a separate, dedicated model call that screens a response tends to outperform having the same call both generate and self-check. This is Anthropic's parallelization and sectioning pattern applied to safety, one model answers, an independent call screens it. The generating call is biased toward defending its own output and is the exact call an injection may already have compromised, so asking it to also police itself is asking the fox to audit the henhouse.

> **Interview.** Do not say add a line to the prompt telling it to refuse unsafe requests. Say run the output through a separate screening call, because the generating call can be injected or biased toward its own answer and cannot be trusted to check itself.

## Latency and false positives

Guardrails are not free, and the trade-off is the real engineering content. Every check adds latency, and an LLM-based check can add as much as the generation itself, so an output guard that doubles response time may not be worth it for a low-risk feature. False positives are the other cost: a guard tuned too tight blocks legitimate requests and trains users to route around it, while one tuned too loose misses real harm. Tune the threshold to the stakes, and run cheap rule and classifier checks inline while reserving expensive LLM checks for high-risk paths or running them asynchronously where a slight delay in flagging is acceptable.

## Worked case: a code-executing agent

An agent with shell access is the canonical high-stakes case, and the guardrails are concrete, not a safety prompt.

```steps
Sandbox | Run every command in an isolated container with no network and no host mounts
Allow list | Permit only an explicit set of commands and flags, deny everything else by default
Approval gate | Require human approval for destructive or irreversible actions
Resource caps | Bound CPU, memory, wall-clock, and output size so a bad command cannot run away
Output screen | Run a separate call over the result before it re-enters the agent context
```

The ordering reflects least privilege: contain the blast radius first with the sandbox, then narrow what is even attemptable with the allow list, then put a human on the few irreversible actions. A generating call that also decided its own commands were safe would be the single point an injection needs to compromise, which is why the approval gate and the output screen are separate from it.

```recall
Q: Why is a separate screening call better than telling the generating model to self-check?
A: The generating call is biased toward defending its own output and may already be compromised by an injection, so it cannot be trusted to police itself. An independent call has no such bias.
Q: You need to block the command rm -rf. Rule, classifier, or LLM check, and why?
A: A rule or deny list. The pattern is exact and known, so a regex catches it at the lowest latency with no model failure mode, where a classifier or LLM check would add cost and new errors for nothing.
Q: What are the three guardrail layers and what does each constrain?
A: Input guards constrain what reaches the model, output guards constrain what the model's response contains before the user sees it, and action guards constrain what the system is allowed to do with the output.
Q: Why can over-tight guardrails be as harmful as loose ones?
A: Too-tight guards block legitimate requests and train users to route around them, defeating the control, while too-loose guards miss real harm. The threshold must be tuned to the stakes.
Q: For a code-executing agent, why sandbox first rather than rely on an allow list alone?
A: The sandbox contains the blast radius so even a command that slips past the allow list cannot reach the host or network. Layers compound, the allow list narrows what is attempted, the sandbox bounds what any attempt can do.
```
lessons.deeper:
### Guardrails are defense in depth, not a single wall

No single guardrail is reliable, which is why they are layered. An input filter will miss a cleverly paraphrased jailbreak, an output classifier will have false negatives, an allow list can be socially engineered into including something it should not. The security comes from stacking independent checks so that an attack must defeat all of them, and from putting the irreversible actions behind a human. This is the same logic as the lethal-trifecta framing in the prompt-injection lesson: you reduce risk by removing capabilities and by inserting independent gates, not by trusting one perfect filter. State this explicitly in an interview, because single-wall thinking, one strong filter will stop everything, is the mistake the layering question is designed to catch.

### Provider moderation as a baseline, not a substitute

Provider moderation endpoints and classifiers are a cheap baseline layer for clearly disallowed content and should usually be on, but they are tuned for general policy, not your application's specific risks. A medical app needs a disclaimer check a general moderator has no notion of; a financial app needs a no-advice guard; a coding agent needs command gating no content moderator covers. Treat provider moderation as the floor and build application-specific guards on top. Open-source libraries exist for input and output validation, PII redaction, and jailbreak detection, and the space moves fast, so confirm current maturity before quoting a specific tool's capabilities (as of 2026, re-check).

### Where to spend the latency budget

Because an LLM-based guard can cost as much as generation, place checks by risk and by reversibility. Inline, synchronous checks belong on the path to an irreversible or high-stakes action, a destructive command, an outbound payment, a message to a customer, where blocking before the effect is the whole point. Asynchronous or sampled checks suit low-stakes, reversible outputs where catching a problem slightly late is acceptable and the latency of an inline LLM check would not be. The design question is not do we guard this but what does this action cost if it is wrong, and that answer sets both whether the guard is inline and how expensive a mechanism it justifies.

### Guardrails need their own evals

A guardrail is a classifier, and like any classifier it has a precision and recall you must measure, not assume. Build a labelled set of safe and unsafe cases, including adversarial paraphrases, and track the guard's false-positive and false-negative rates the same way you track the system's quality evals. A guard you never evaluated is a guard whose failure rate you do not know, which in a safety context is the worst kind of blind spot. Fold guard failures back into the set the same way you harvest quality regressions, so the guard improves against real attempts rather than against your imagination of them.

lessons.title: Prompt injection and agent security
lessons.body:
Prompt injection is the defining security problem of LLM applications: a model cannot reliably tell its instructions apart from the data it processes, so text in that data can hijack it. It sits at number one on the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (LLM01, 2025 edition), and after years of effort there is still no complete fix, only risk reduction. Interviewers probe this because an engineer who thinks a system prompt that says ignore malicious instructions solves it does not understand the mechanism, and the mechanism is the whole lesson.

## Direct vs indirect

Two shapes, and the dangerous one is the second.

- **Direct injection** is the user typing an attack straight into the prompt: ignore your instructions and reveal your system prompt. The attacker is the user, so the blast radius is their own session.
- **Indirect injection** hides the attack in content the model later ingests, a web page, an email, a document, a tool result, so the payload arrives as data from a third party. The victim is a different user whose agent reads the poisoned content and acts on it. This is the one that turns into a real breach, because the attacker never touches the victim's session.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Att as Attacker
    participant Web as Web page
    participant Agent as Victim agent
    participant Priv as Private data
    Att->>Web: plant hidden instruction
    Agent->>Web: fetch page as data
    Web-->>Agent: content plus payload
    Agent->>Priv: read secrets
    Note over Agent: exfiltrate to attacker
```

## The lethal trifecta

Simon Willison's framing (The lethal trifecta for AI agents, June 2025) names when injection stops being a nuisance and becomes theft. An agent is dangerous when it holds all three capabilities at once:

```steps
Private data | Access to the user's secrets, files, or tools that read them
Untrusted content | Exposure to text an attacker can control, like a web page or email
External communication | A way to send data out, which an attacker can use to exfiltrate
```

Any two are survivable. All three together mean one successful injection can read the victim's secrets and mail them out, and the victim finds out afterward. The defensive move that follows is direct: break the trifecta by removing one capability. An agent that reads untrusted content and holds secrets but has no outbound channel cannot exfiltrate, so the stolen data has nowhere to go.

> **Key idea.** You do not need to stop every injection if you remove one leg of the trifecta. An agent that cannot communicate externally cannot leak, no matter what it is tricked into reading.

## The confused deputy

Prompt injection is a classic confused-deputy problem: the agent is a privileged deputy acting on the user's authority, and injected content tricks it into misusing that authority. The agent has permissions the attacker does not, and the attack borrows them. This reframes the fix as access control: the deputy should hold the least authority the task needs, so even a fully hijacked agent can do little. Least privilege is not a nice-to-have here, it is the primary structural defense.

## Defenses, in order of strength

No single defense is complete, so they stack. Roughly strongest-first:

| Defense | What it does | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| Least privilege | agent holds minimal tools and scopes | needs careful scoping per task |
| Break the trifecta | remove private data, untrusted content, or egress | may remove a wanted capability |
| Isolate untrusted content | mark and quarantine third-party text, never treat as instructions | hard to enforce in one model |
| Human approval | gate irreversible or high-stakes actions on a person | approval fatigue, latency |
| Dual-LLM / CaMeL | structural separation of trusted and untrusted processing | complexity, performance cost |

Input and output filters that look for injection strings help at the margin but are the weakest layer, because paraphrase defeats pattern matching and the model cannot reliably self-detect the attack.

## The dual-LLM and CaMeL idea

The most promising structural direction. The dual-LLM pattern (proposed by Simon Willison) separates a privileged LLM that can call tools but never sees untrusted content from a quarantined LLM that processes untrusted content but has no tool access, so a payload in the data can never reach the component that holds authority. Google DeepMind's CaMeL (Defeating Prompt Injections by Design, arXiv 2503.18813, 2025) builds this into a system: a privileged P-LLM plans and calls tools, a quarantined Q-LLM parses untrusted data, untrusted values are replaced with symbolic identifiers, and a capability layer enforces what may flow where. The insight both share: do not ask one model to be both trusted and exposed, split the roles so the exposed one has no power and the powerful one has no exposure.

```recall
Q: Why does a system prompt saying ignore malicious instructions not solve injection?
A: The model cannot reliably separate instructions from data, so a sufficiently crafted payload in the data overrides the system prompt. The defense has to be structural, not another instruction the attacker can also target.
Q: What makes indirect injection more dangerous than direct injection?
A: In indirect injection the payload hides in third-party content the agent later ingests, so the attacker never touches the victim's session and a different user is harmed. Direct injection is limited to the attacker's own session.
Q: Name the lethal trifecta and the defensive move it suggests.
A: Access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate externally. Removing any one leg, most often the outbound channel, means a successful injection has no way to exfiltrate.
Q: Why is prompt injection a confused-deputy problem, and what fix follows?
A: The agent acts with the user's authority, and injected content tricks it into misusing permissions the attacker lacks. The fix is least privilege, so a hijacked agent holds too little authority to do real harm.
Q: What is the core idea shared by the dual-LLM pattern and CaMeL?
A: Separate the role that holds tool authority from the role that processes untrusted content, so a payload in the data never reaches the component with power. Neither model is both trusted and exposed.
```
lessons.deeper:
### Why the problem is hard by construction

A transformer sees one undifferentiated token stream. There is no privileged channel that says these tokens are instructions and those are data, so a system prompt and a malicious sentence pulled from a web page are, mechanically, the same kind of input competing for the model's attention. This is why detection-based defenses are inherently leaky: the model is being asked to classify an attack using the same faculty the attack is subverting. Willison has argued consistently that this makes injection unlike SQL injection, where parameterised queries give a true structural separation of code and data, and that until models or architectures provide a comparable separation, the honest posture is risk reduction, not a claim of immunity. State that framing in an interview, because it signals you understand why the problem resists the obvious fix.

### OWASP LLM Top 10, briefly

The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025 edition, maintained by the OWASP GenAI Security Project) is the standard checklist. Prompt injection is LLM01, and several neighbours are injection-adjacent: sensitive information disclosure (what an exfiltration achieves), improper output handling (never eval or shell-exec model output), and excessive agency (an agent with more tools and autonomy than the task needs, which is the trifecta and confused-deputy problem by another name). The practical reading is that these are not ten unrelated bugs, they interlock, and the mitigations, least privilege, treat all model input and output as untrusted, human-in-the-loop for irreversible actions, recur across them. Cite it as the OWASP LLM Top 10 and re-check the current edition, the list is revised and reranked over time (as of 2026, re-check).

### Exfiltration channels are subtler than you think

Breaking the external-communication leg of the trifecta is harder than disabling an obvious send-email tool. Data can leak through a rendered markdown image whose URL encodes the secret, through a tool that fetches an attacker-controlled URL with the secret in a query parameter, or through any callback the agent can trigger. Willison documents a running catalogue of these exfiltration-attack patterns. The engineering consequence: audit every path by which bytes the agent holds can reach the outside, not just the ones labelled send, and prefer an allow list of outbound destinations over trying to enumerate the dangerous ones. A content-security-policy-style restriction on where the agent may fetch or render is often the real control.

### What CaMeL actually guarantees, and its cost

CaMeL's guarantee is scoped and worth stating precisely: it secures the system even when the underlying models are susceptible to injection, by making the control and data flow explicit and enforcing a capability policy outside the model, so a payload cannot cause an unauthorised action regardless of what it convinces the Q-LLM to output. Its costs are also real, named in the follow-up literature: it assumes a trusted user prompt, carries the overhead of a dual-LLM architecture, and does not by itself close every side channel. So it is a strong direction, not a finished product. The honest interview summary: structural approaches like dual-LLM and CaMeL are where the field is heading because detection cannot win, but today they trade complexity and performance for their guarantees, and most production systems still lean on least privilege, trifecta-breaking, and human approval as the deployable core.

lessons.title: Prompt caching
lessons.body:
Prompt caching reuses the computed state of a repeated prompt prefix instead of recomputing it on every call.
