lessons.title: Evidence, Confidence, and Unknowns in Binary Analysis
lessons.body:
> A finding about a compiled program is a record with a hash, a confidence, an authority, and a list of what it cannot show.

**Type:** Build
**Languages:** Python, C
**Prerequisites:** Phase 13 · 32 (ELF from scratch), Phase 13 · 33 (disassembly and control flow), Phase 13 · 34 (lifting to pseudocode)
**Time:** ~105 minutes

## Learning Objectives

- Build an evidence record modelled on rea's `Evidence` with observed, derived, and inferred confidence.
- Compute content-hash ids that stay the same when the file moves to another folder.
- Record what each provider cannot show as limitations that travel with the record.
- Refuse to state a result until an observed run of the function supports it.
- Keep residual unknowns as revisioned records joined by a hash chain.
- Cache provider answers under an exact key and refuse a stale replay.

## The Problem

You ask an agent what `grade` in `ledger-x86_64-O1.o` returns for a score of 55. The agent calls rea, reads the Ghidra pseudocode, and answers 0. A reviewer asks how the agent knows. The agent has a block of text that Ghidra printed. For the default path, that text reads `uVar1 = -(param_1 >> 0x1f) ^ (uint)((ulong)((long)param_1 * 0x66666667) >> 0x3f);`. The bytes at that point say `xor eax, eax`.

The expression and the instruction both produce 0 for every input. The agent did not know that. It trusted the text because a tool produced it. A 2026 study ran three agents on 24 reverse engineering tasks ([NDSS BAR 2026](https://www.ndss-symposium.org/wp-content/uploads/bar2026-58.pdf)). It named four recurring weaknesses: training bias, over-trust in observations, context limits, and plan persistence. Another 2026 study planted text inside binaries and found that models proposed the planted unsafe action in 35 of 40 cases ([arXiv 2607.12507](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12507)).

rea 6.5.0 gives the agent a vocabulary for this. Every successful tool call produces one `Evidence` record with a `confidence` of `observed`, `derived`, or `inferred`, an `authority`, and a list of `limitations`. The packaged skill tells the agent: "Every conclusion must distinguish observations, inferences, and unknowns. Cite Evidence IDs, preserve limitations and incomplete coverage, and never imply that static analysis observed execution.".

Three things rea leaves to you. Its snapshots cache exact query results, not analysis. Its verification passes a claim when a comparison dimension is unchanged, and its own comment says that a pass "does not establish global implementation equivalence.". Its obligation ledger takes candidates only from JavaScript and managed graphs, so a native function never reaches `verified` through it.

This lesson builds the missing piece in plain Python. You write a ledger that stores every fact about the fixture as a record with a content hash. You make predictions about `percent_change` and `grade`, mark them inferred, and check them against runs of a test program you compile yourself. You import two real rea records and the snapshot they came from, and your ledger recomputes every hash rea wrote.

## Three Words for Confidence, Five for Authority

`confidence` is an enum with three values, never a number. `authority` has five values. When a producer says nothing, rea uses `shipped-artifact` with `observed`.

| Value | Meaning on the fixture | Records in this lesson |
|---|---|---|
| `observed` | A fact read from bytes or from a run | the ELF reader's section and symbol reads, the two Ghidra records, 17 host runs |
| `derived` | A fact computed from observed records | the switch table model, the division model, every unknown mutation |
| `inferred` | An expectation that no observation states yet | 18 predictions |
| `shipped-artifact` | The file on disk was the source | every read of `ledger-x86_64-O1.o` |
| `controlled-replay` | A run you controlled produced the fact | the host runs of `harness.c` |
| `analyst-inference` | Your own judgement | predictions and unknown mutations |
| `historical-reference` | An older source tree or document | none here |
| `external-service` | A service outside the file and the host | none here |

Two confusions cost the most time. The first treats pseudocode as an observation of behaviour. It is an observation of what Ghidra printed. The second treats an empty list as proof of absence. rea's design note is strict: "Missing coverage is unknown, not absence.". The ledger in `code/main.py` encodes both rules.

## The Record

A record has exactly sixteen fields, and rea 6.5.0 rejects any other field. `code/main.py` keeps the same names as rea, so a record from either side validates on the other. The sixteenth field, `relationship_coverage`, says how complete a list of callers or callees is. Its value is `complete`, `partial`, or `unknown`, or `null` when the operation reports no call relationships.

| Field | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `evidence_id` | `ev_` and 64 hex digits, a hash of the content |
| `subject` | `name`, `digest.sha256`, `format`, `architecture`, `local_path`, or `null` |
| `provider` | `id`, `name`, `version` or `null` |
| `analysis_profile` | the provider's settings and their digest, or `null`, always present |
| `predicate_type` | a tag, `rea.analysis` by default |
| `operation`, `parameters` | the tool and its input |
| `raw_result`, `normalized_result` | provider output and the canonical result |
| `confidence`, `authority` | the enums above |
| `environment` | `id`, `platform`, `architecture`, `isolation`, or `null` |
| `limitations` | plain sentences |
| `relationship_coverage` | `status` `complete`, `partial`, or `unknown` with diagnostics, or `null` |
| `locations` | `address`, `address-range`, `artifact-path`, `file-offset`, `file-offset-range` |
| `evidence_links` | the `ev_` ids this record rests on |

This is the real record rea wrote for `grade`, cut to the fields that matter here. The full file is `code/fixtures/rea-evidence-grade.json`, 37,573 bytes.
```json
{
  "evidence_id": "ev_67b6d3f992eaf49a2e16de084b6ebfdd9884e8c5c7f75e175b7bb20f4f748ce1",
  "subject": {
    "name": "ledger-x86_64-O1.o",
    "digest": { "sha256": "9a4a8082ba5e285a732552981a6935e0c5255725664f380e37c44ebfb04d803f" },
    "format": "elf",
    "architecture": "x86_64",
    "local_path": "/private/tmp/aiefs-re/phases/13-tools-and-protocols/35-evidence-confidence-and-unknowns/code/fixtures/ledger-x86_64-O1.o"
  },
  "provider": { "id": "ghidra", "name": "Ghidra", "version": "12.1.4" },
  "analysis_profile": {
    "provider": { "id": "ghidra", "name": "Ghidra", "version": "12.1.4" },
    "parameters": { "jump_table_evidence": "typed-case-default-blocks-v1", "import_mode": "ephemeral-source-immutable" },
    "digest": "9c7f6b24be69294e61da046e4583e3856cb9e40433b149c1bf8bb534d2fe03ef"
  },
  "operation": "analyze_function",
  "parameters": { "procedure": "grade" },
  "confidence": "observed",
  "authority": "shipped-artifact",
  "environment": null,
  "limitations": [
    "Default-space addresses use lowercase 0x-prefixed hexadecimal; other address spaces use <percent-encoded-space>:0x<hex>.",
    "Resolved reference metadata identifies computed, indirect, external, call, jump, and data edges; unresolved targetless flows remain unknown, and function classifications distinguish thunks and externals."
  ],
  "relationship_coverage": {
    "status": "complete",
    "diagnostics": [
      "Only resolved Ghidra call references are returned; unresolved computed or indirect calls remain unknown, while function classifications distinguish thunks and externals."
    ]
  },
  "locations": [],
  "evidence_links": []
}
```
The real `parameters` object of the profile has 25 keys. The real `limitations` list has ten sentences. Keep them. A limitation is part of the content, so dropping one changes the id, and your ledger would then reject the record.

Note what the record does not say. `environment` is `null` because Ghidra read a file and ran nothing. `locations` is empty because this operation reports addresses inside `normalized_result`. `relationship_coverage` has the status `complete`. Its diagnostic says that only resolved Ghidra call references are returned, and that unresolved computed or indirect calls stay unknown. So the caller and callee lists are complete for resolved calls only.

## The Id Is a Hash of Content, and the Path Is Not in It

rea computes `evidence_id` as `ev_` plus SHA-256 over the RFC 8785 canonical JSON of a projection of the record. The projection keeps the subject's `digest`, `format`, and `architecture` and drops `name` and `local_path`. It drops `relationship_coverage` when its value is `null`, so a record without call relationships keeps the same id as before the field existed. Everything else, including `raw_result` and every limitation, is hashed.

RFC 8785 sorts object keys, removes whitespace, and fixes the number and string forms. For records whose numbers are integers, Python's standard library produces the same bytes:
```python
def canonical_json(value):
    return json.dumps(value, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"), ensure_ascii=False, allow_nan=False)
```
`code/main.py` refuses floats before it hashes, because RFC 8785 and Python print some floats differently. The two rea records and the snapshot hold no floats, so the recipe reproduces every rea hash:

| rea value | Recomputed by `code/main.py` |
|---|---|
| `ev_67b6d3f992eaf49a…` for `grade` | equal |
| `ev_e88b10dc0c6400e5…` for `percent_change` | equal |
| profile digest `9c7f6b24be69294e…` over `{provider, parameters}` | equal |
| `query_26122aebe9d8abae…` for the `grade` snapshot entry | equal |
| `query_0f95ef38038d3666…` for the `percent_change` entry | equal |

Why exclude the path? The same observation of the same bytes gets the same id on any machine and in any folder. The `local_path` in the listing above names a folder on one Mac. The id does not change when you copy the fixture to `/home/you/re`. `rebind_subject_path()` lets you show a record under a new path. It refuses when `sha256`, `format`, or `architecture` differ. rea 6.5.0 does the same with `rebindEvidenceToTargetPath` when it replays a snapshot record for a target at a new path.

`validate_evidence()` recomputes the id and rejects a mismatch with rea's sentence, "Evidence semantic identifier does not match its record". It also rejects a record whose `analysis_profile.provider` differs from its `provider`. The test `test_tampered_id_and_mismatched_profile_are_rejected` edits one line of pseudocode inside the real `grade` record and watches the ledger refuse it.

## Observe the Object Yourself

Before any provider, the ledger reads the file. `observe_object()` parses the ELF64 section headers, `.symtab`, `.strtab`, and `.rela.text` with `struct.unpack_from`. It writes one `inspect_object` record and one `read_function_bytes` record per function symbol. All five are `observed` with authority `shipped-artifact`, because the source was the file on disk.

| Record | Content | Id |
|---|---|---|
| `inspect_object` | five sections with offsets, sizes, and hashes, four functions, three relocations | `ev_645e0a145f28bd5c…` |
| `read_function_bytes percent_change` | 16 bytes at `.text+0x00` | `ev_2572a7d254ad15cb…` |
| `read_function_bytes grade` | 46 bytes at `.text+0x10`, SHA-256 `ffcb75c2a7bb1104…` | `ev_a467c2427bfc0c56…` |
| `read_function_bytes total` | 31 bytes at `.text+0x40` | `ev_b1e845cea2543073…` |
| `read_function_bytes grade_label` | 63 bytes at `.text+0x60` | `ev_c50041be26e6b7f4…` |

`llvm-objdump -t` agrees: `grade` at `0000000000000010` with size `2e`. The three relocations in `.rela.text` are `R_X86_64_PC32` against `.rodata` at offsets `0x36`, `0x84`, and `0x93`, with addends `0x10`, `0x24`, and `-0x4`. Each record carries a `file-offset-range` location and one limitation: "Section bytes are read from the file on disk. The reader applies no relocation and runs no code."

Lesson 32 builds this reader in full. Here it is 60 lines, because this lesson is about what you record about the read.

## Derive the Table, and Say That You Derived It

The 46 bytes of `grade` contain four patterns that lesson 33 decoded:

| Bytes | Instruction | Offset in `grade` |
|---|---|---|
| `48 69 c0 67 66 66 66` | `imul rax, rax, 0x66666667` | 3 |
| `48 c1 f9 22` | `sar rcx, 34` | 13 |
| `83 c1 fa` | `add ecx, -6` | 23 |
| `83 f9 04 77 0c` | `cmp ecx, 4` then `ja` | 28 |

A multiply by `0x66666667` followed by a shift of 34 is a signed division by 10. The file holds no 10. `derive_grade_model()` writes that fact as a limitation: "The divisor 10 is a derivation from the multiplier 0x66666667 and the shift 34. The file holds no 10."

The `add ecx, -6` sets the first case to 6. The `cmp ecx, 4` with an unsigned jump admits five cases, 6 to 10.

The `lea` at `.text+0x33` carries the relocation with addend `0x10`. A PC32 relocation measures from the end of the 4-byte displacement, so the table starts at `.rodata+0x14`. Five little-endian words there read `1, 2, 3, 4, 4`. The switch in `ledger.c` returns 1 for 60 to 69, 2 for the seventies, 3 for the eighties, and 4 for 90 to 100. The compiler turned the switch into a lookup table of return values.

The resulting record `ev_605106bff2d9998f…` has `confidence` `derived`, and its `evidence_links` name the two observed records it rests on. Remove the bytes record from the ledger and the derived record has a dangling link. The figure above shows that state when you turn off `ev_a467c242…`.

Now compare with Ghidra. Its pseudocode for the same bytes:
```c
uint grade(int param_1)
{
  uint uVar1;
  uint uVar2;

  uVar2 = param_1 / 10 - 6;
  uVar1 = -(param_1 >> 0x1f) ^ (uint)((ulong)((long)param_1 * 0x66666667) >> 0x3f);
  if (uVar2 < 5) {
    uVar1 = *(uint *)(&DAT_001000b4 + (ulong)uVar2 * 4);
  }
  return uVar1;
}
```
Ghidra applied the relocation and named the table `DAT_001000b4`, which is `.rodata+0x14` after it placed `.text` at `0x100000`. It recovered the division by 10 and the five cases. For the default value it printed an expression that is always 0 and never says 0. The p-code in `native_value_flow` marks those operations `is_dead: true`. The record is a faithful observation of Ghidra. The meaning you read from it is derived, and the value you expect from a run is inferred.

The `percent_change` record shows the other failure. Ghidra's signature reads `undefined1 [16] percent_change(int param_1,int param_2,ulong param_3)`. The source says `int percent_change(int before, int after)`. `idiv` writes `EDX:EAX`, and the zero path leaves `EDX` untouched, so the decompiler inferred a 16-byte return and a third parameter. Its own `native_api.return_type.confidence` for `grade` is `"low"`. Treat a recovered signature as the provider's inference, and record it that way.

## Predictions Are Inferred Records

A prediction is a claim about behaviour that no observation has stated. `claim_suite()` builds eighteen of them from the derived models and from the source. `record_prediction()` stores each one as a record with `confidence` `inferred` and `authority` `analyst-inference`, linked to the records it rests on.

| Claim | Predicted value | Rests on |
|---|---|---|
| `percent_change(12400, 15500)` | 25, from 310000 / 12400 | division model `ev_076a9167…` |
| `percent_change(0, 5)` | 0, the zero guard | division model |
| `percent_change(100, 50)` | -50 | division model |
| `percent_change(-7, 3)` | -142, because `idiv` truncates toward zero | division model |
| `grade(55)` | 0, index -1 fails the unsigned compare | table model `ev_605106bf…` |
| `grade(60)`, `grade(69)` | 1, 1 | table model |
| `grade(70)`, `grade(85)` | 2, 3 | table model |
| `grade(95)`, `grade(100)`, `grade(105)` | 4, 4, 4 | table model |
| `grade(110)`, `grade(-5)` | 0, 0 | table model |
| `total(1, 2, 3)`, `total()` | 6, 0 | source record `ev_2f1e6d25…` |
| `grade_label(85)` | `"B"` | source record and table model |
| `grade(score)` for 90 to 100 | 4 for all eleven inputs | table model |

`predict()` uses C semantics, not Python semantics. `c_div()` truncates toward zero, and `wrap32()` folds every intermediate into 32 bits. Python's `//` rounds toward negative infinity, so `(3 - -7) * 100 // -7` gives -143 and the C program gives -142. Lesson 36 makes this grid much larger.

Each prediction opens one residual unknown. The unknown asks for `observed` evidence with authority `controlled-replay` and recommends one probe: `execute_function` on the host build. The next section produces that evidence. The question for the first grade claim reads "Does grade(95) == 4 hold when the compiled function runs?"

## Check Them Against a Run

`code/fixtures/harness.c` includes `ledger.c` and prints one result per invocation. `observe_runs()` compiles it with the first of `clang`, `cc`, or `gcc` on your PATH and runs every input in the grid once. Each run becomes one record:
```json
{
  "operation": "execute_function",
  "parameters": { "function": "grade", "args": [95] },
  "normalized_result": { "result": 4, "stdout": "4\n", "exit_code": 0 },
  "confidence": "observed",
  "authority": "controlled-replay",
  "environment": { "id": "host-process", "platform": "darwin", "architecture": "arm64", "isolation": "process" },
  "limitations": [
    "The run executed a host build of ledger.c, not the x86-64 object. The claim about the object rests on the shared source and on the compiler.",
    "One run observes one input. It proves nothing about other inputs."
  ]
}
```
The subject of a run record is the harness binary, a Mach-O arm64 file on this Mac, with its own SHA-256. The provider is `course-harness` with the compiler's version line, here `Apple clang version 17.0.0 (clang-1700.6.3.2)`. The `evidence_links` name the source record `ev_2f1e6d251543d017…`, because the run and the object share `ledger.c` and nothing else.

Read the first limitation twice. The x86-64 object never ran on this machine. What ran was a second build of the same source for another architecture. That is still an observation, and it is the strongest one available without an emulator, so the claim passes with that sentence attached. A report that omits it has lost information the reader needs.

The 17 single-input runs all agreed with the predictions. `code/fixtures/run-evidence.json` holds those 17 records and the source record, exported with `--record` on 2026-10-13. When no compiler is present, `build_ledger()` imports that bundle instead of running, and the report says so in its `runs` field.

## Promotion Rules

A claim moves from inferred to supported only through observed runs. `check_claim()` looks for `execute_function` records with the same function and arguments, compares each result with the prediction, and counts the covered inputs:

| Status | Condition | rea's completion ledger |
|---|---|---|
| `pass` | every input has an agreeing run and none disagrees | `pass` |
| `fail` | any run disagrees | `fail` |
| `unknown` | some inputs have runs, others have none | `unknown` |
| `unsupported` | no input has a run | `unsupported` |

`promote_claim()` is the strict form. It raises `ClaimError` when any id is `inferred` or `derived`. It raises when an id names a run of another function or of other arguments. It raises when the list is empty, and when the runs cover fewer inputs than the claim. The Ghidra pseudocode record and the table model both exist for `grade(55)`, and neither can promote it. Turn off `ev_7be90c0c…` in the figure and watch the claim fall to `unsupported` while two records about `grade` remain.

The range claim shows the partial case. Only two of its eleven inputs, 95 and 100, appear in the run grid. `check_claim()` returns `unknown` with `covered` 2 of 11, and `promote_claim()` refuses with "2 of 11 inputs have observed runs". The ledger does not round that up.

`completion_ledger()` mirrors rea's `EvidenceCompletionLedger`. Its id is `ecl_` plus the hash of its records, and `complete` is true only when `pass` equals `total`. The demo prints `ecl_da64933ea13befed…` with `complete: false`, because of that one range claim.

## Unknowns Are Records with a Hash Chain

rea stores a residual unknown as a strict record. `code/main.py` keeps the same fields and the same invariants.

The id is `unk_` plus SHA-256 over `{domain, question, scope_digest}`, with the question's whitespace collapsed to single spaces. Two analysts who ask the same question about the same file get the same id. The `scope_digest` is the SHA-256 of the object.

Every change is a new revision. Revision 1 has `previous_revision_digest` `null`. Every later revision names the `revision_digest` of the one before it, and the digest covers every field except itself. `verify_unknown_chain()` walks the list and recomputes each digest. It checks that each link points at the previous revision. It checks that the mutation evidence each revision names is in the ledger.

Each mutation is itself an evidence record, as rea does with provider `rea-unknown-registry`. Ours carries `confidence` `derived`, `authority` `analyst-inference`, and no subject. Its limitation reads "A registry mutation records what the analyst decided. It is not proof of the answer."

That is why the demo's 81 records include 36 derived mutation records: 18 openings and 18 updates.

Three invariants are enforced on every revision:

- Only a `resolved` unknown carries a `resolution`, and only revision 1 has no predecessor.
- A `contradicted` unknown names at least one contradicting id, and no id appears in both lists.
- A `verified` resolution names at least one evidence id with the required confidence and authority.

The third rule is where the ledger refuses most often. rea's workflow notes say "Only qualifying observed evidence can verify a resolution.". `resolve_unknown()` therefore rejects the table model, rejects an observed record with authority `shipped-artifact`, and accepts the run record `ev_f4ffbe8f922ec7fe…`. The resolved revision for `grade(95)` is revision 2, and its `previous_revision_digest` is `ffca840b55a8a188…`, the digest of revision 1.

`update_unknown()` takes `expected_revision` and raises `revision-conflict` when it is stale, as rea's `update_unknown` tool does. The right reaction is the one rea's notes give: reread the current revision and decide again.

One unknown stays open after the demo: `unk_f2eb0d7f84c80a19…`, "Does grade(score) == 4 for every score from 90 to 100 hold when the compiled function runs?". Its status is `investigating`, its supporting ids include the two runs, and its probe still names the nine inputs without a run.

## A Cache of Answers Is Not a Database of Analysis

rea has three things that look like a cache. The Ghidra target snapshot is a private copy of the input, imported with `-readOnly -deleteProject` and deleted on close. The in-memory `AnalysisSnapshotCache` holds up to 10,000 entries for one binary identity. The snapshot file holds `target`, `binding`, `entries`, `workflow_entries`, and an `evidence_bundle`.

The cache key is `query_` plus SHA-256 over `{target, binding, operation, parameters}`. `target` is `{sha256, kind, format, architecture}`, and a `raw-binary` target also has `entry_point`. `binding` is the provider and the whole analysis profile, digest included. Change any of the 25 profile parameters, for example `jump_table_evidence` from `typed-case-default-blocks-v1` to a `v2`, and the digest changes, so every key changes.

`code/fixtures/rea-snapshot.json` is the file rea wrote during the two runs, 142,690 bytes. rea wrote it with owner-only permissions, and the committed copy is readable by everyone. It has two entries and an evidence bundle with the same two records. `AnswerCache.import_snapshot()` recomputes each `query_id` and refuses the file when any differs. It refuses a snapshot whose `target` or `binding` differs from the active one, with rea's wording `profile_mismatch`. It refuses a snapshot whose `format_version` is not `course-answer-cache-1`.

Three measurements from this machine. The first `grade` query took 8.6 s, with a fresh Ghidra import. The `percent_change` query against the same snapshot took 8.5 s, because a different query is a cache miss. A third `grade` query took 2.1 s and returned the identical record with the identical `evidence_id`. The in-memory replay in rea adds the limitation "Loaded from a local REA analysis snapshot; this call did not re-run the provider.". Our `lookup()` adds a sentence of the same kind, so a reader can tell a replay from a fresh answer.

A mutation ends the cache. In rea 6.5.0, a rename or a comment clears the snapshot cache before rea sends the call to the provider. A failed reply cannot prove that the write rolled back, so a failed write also stops replay. A metadata import that changes the database does the same.

## Why an Agent Needs This

An agent that drives rea through MCP sees the full record on every call and can cite `evidence_id` in its report. The research from 2026 says where that goes wrong. Over-trust in tool output was one of the four weaknesses in the NDSS BAR study. In the planted-text study, showing binary content as data alone still left 15 unsafe proposals of 40, and provenance checks with tool authorization removed them. A third study watched an agent drive Ghidra through MCP ([arXiv 2606.06838](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06838)). In binaries with hundreds of functions, only 10 to 15 percent received real analysis before the agent produced stubs.

The ledger answers each of these with a record, and the agent reports only what the ledger holds. A claim without an observed run is `unsupported`. A claim with some runs is `unknown`. A provider text is `observed` about the provider and nothing more. Give the agent the skill file in `outputs/` and make the ledger the only place it writes conclusions. That holds for Claude, Cursor, Codex, OpenClaw, Hermes, or any agent that reads SKILL.md.

## Build It

Run the standard-library demo:
```bash
cd phases/13-tools-and-protocols/35-evidence-confidence-and-unknowns
python3 code/main.py
```
The demo reads the object, imports the two rea records, verifies the rea snapshot, and derives the two models. It then records 18 predictions, opens 18 unknowns, compiles and runs the harness, checks every claim, and resolves 17 unknowns. Expected shape:
```json
{
  "records": 81,
  "by_confidence": { "observed": 25, "derived": 38, "inferred": 18 },
  "rea_snapshot": { "entries": 2, "replay_hit": true, "stale_profile_refused": true },
  "grade_table": [1, 2, 3, 4, 4],
  "runs": "live: Apple clang version 17.0.0 (clang-1700.6.3.2)",
  "claims": [ { "claim_id": "grade(95)", "status": "pass", "covered": "1/1" }, { "claim_id": "grade(90..100)", "status": "unknown", "covered": "2/11" } ],
  "completion_ledger_id": "ecl_da64933ea13befed9483f8b00447bb3f4ceb74324c01e2515eff03f3af3ca750",
  "complete": false,
  "unknowns": { "resolved": 17, "investigating": 1 }
}
```
Without a C compiler, `runs` reads `imported 17 recorded run records from run-evidence.json` and the rest is the same.

Read `code/main.py` in this order:

1. `canonical_json()` and `compute_evidence_id()` hold the hash recipe and the semantic projection.
2. `create_evidence()` and `validate_evidence()` build and check a record.
3. `EvidenceLedger.record()` and `import_bundle()` store records and refuse conflicts.
4. `open_unknown()`, `update_unknown()`, and `resolve_unknown()` keep the revision chain.
5. `observe_object()` reads the ELF, and `derive_grade_model()` reads the table.
6. `claim_suite()`, `predict()`, and `record_prediction()` write the inferred tier.
7. `observe_runs()` turns each harness run into an observed record.
8. `check_claim()`, `promote_claim()`, and `completion_ledger()` apply the promotion rules.
9. `AnswerCache` keys answers like rea's snapshots and refuses stale ones.

## Use It

Keep one ledger per target and per investigation. Put the target's SHA-256 in every subject and the question's scope digest in every unknown. When you change tools, change the `provider` and let the ids diverge. When you rebuild the fixture, the subject digest changes and every old record becomes evidence about another file.

Write limitations at the moment you know them. The reader that applies no relocation says so. The run of a host build says so. The model that infers a divisor says so. A record written without its limitations looks stronger than the facts allow, and a later reader cannot repair that.

Treat every provider text as data. Strings and pseudocode from the target are text that the target controls. They never become instructions, and they never become observations of behaviour. rea 6.5.0 marks such results with `_meta.provenance.untrusted_content: true`. Its server instructions tell the model to treat target content as data and to report any request in it to run, install, download, or send something as a prompt-injection attempt. The marker helps, but your ledger must still keep target text out of the instructions.

## Interactive Lab

### Lab A: recompute a rea id

From the `code` directory, open Python:
```bash
cd phases/13-tools-and-protocols/35-evidence-confidence-and-unknowns/code
python3 -q
```
Run:
```python
from main import *
record = load_evidence_file(FIXTURES / "rea-evidence-grade.json")
record["evidence_id"] == compute_evidence_id(record)
record["subject"]["local_path"] = "/home/you/re/ledger-x86_64-O1.o"
record["evidence_id"] == compute_evidence_id(record)
record["limitations"].pop()
record["evidence_id"] == compute_evidence_id(record)
```
The first two comparisons are true. The path is not in the hash. The third is false, because a limitation is content.

### Lab B: refuse a promotion
```python
ledger, report = build_ledger(live_runs=False)
claim = [c for c in claim_suite(ledger.find(operation="derive_switch_model")[0], ledger.find(operation="derive_arithmetic_model")[0], ledger.find(operation="read_source")[0]) if c.claim_id == "grade(55)"][0]
promote_claim(ledger, claim, [ledger.find(operation="derive_switch_model")[0]["evidence_id"]])
```
The call raises `ClaimError` and names the derived id. Now pass the run id:
```python
run = run_records_for(ledger, "grade", [55])[0]
promote_claim(ledger, claim, [run["evidence_id"]])["status"]
```
The status is `pass`, and the returned `limitations` carry the host-build sentence.

### Lab C: refuse a stale snapshot
```python
import json
snapshot = json.loads(REA_SNAPSHOT_PATH.read_text())
target, binding = rea_snapshot_binding(snapshot)
AnswerCache(target, binding).import_snapshot(snapshot)
stale = dict(binding["analysis_profile"]["parameters"], jump_table_evidence="typed-case-default-blocks-v2")
AnswerCache(target, {"provider": binding["provider"], "analysis_profile": make_profile(binding["provider"], stale)}).import_snapshot(snapshot)
```
The first import returns 2. The second raises `CacheError` with `profile_mismatch`. One version string changed, and the whole snapshot is refused.

### Lab D: break the chain
```python
unknown_id = [u for u, r in ledger.unknowns.items() if r[-1]["status"] == "investigating"][0]
ledger.verify_unknown_chain(unknown_id)
ledger.unknowns[unknown_id][0]["severity"] = "critical"
ledger.verify_unknown_chain(unknown_id)
```
The first call returns 2. The second raises `EvidenceIntegrityError`, because revision 1 no longer matches its own digest and revision 2 points at a digest that no longer exists.

## Practice Lab

Close the open unknown and add a second provider.

Requirements:

- Extend `run_grid()` so the range claim's nine missing inputs run, then confirm the unknown moves to `resolved` at revision 3.
- Add `llvm-objdump -d` as a second provider with its own `provider` object and record its listing of `grade` as `observed`.
- Write a `derived` record that states the two listings, Ghidra's and llvm-objdump's, decode the same 14 instructions, and link both.
- Open an unknown for `grade_label(105)` with severity `high`, since the table index 4 reads `labels[4]`, and resolve it with a run.
- Export the ledger with `export_bundle()`, import it into a fresh ledger, and prove every chain still verifies.

Success means a report in which every sentence cites an id from the bundle and the one `unknown` claim is gone.

## Graded Lab

Five questions about the fixtures of this lesson. Find each answer with the code you built, then write it into `code/lab_answers.json`. Write numbers as numbers or as hex strings such as `"0x40"`, and lists as JSON lists.

1. `t1`: the evidence id that compute_evidence_id gives for rea-evidence-grade.json.
2. `t2`: the number of limitations in the grade record.
3. `t3`: the relationship_coverage status of the grade record.
4. `t4`: the confidence and the authority of the grade record, as a list of two strings.
5. `t5`: the SHA-256 of the subject of the grade record.

Check your answers:
```bash
cd phases/13-tools-and-protocols/35-evidence-confidence-and-unknowns
python3 code/lab.py
```
The checker computes each expected value from `code/main.py` on the committed fixtures. It prints `PASS`, `FAIL` or `TODO` for each task and a score, and it exits 0 only when all five pass. `python3 code/lab.py my-answers.json` checks another file. `code/tests/test_lab.py` proves that the checker accepts the right answers and rejects a wrong one.

### See it run

The [Inside a Decompiler](https://aiengineeringfromscratch.com/inside-a-decompiler?symbols=off) machine keeps an evidence ledger with four trays: observed, derived, inferred and unknown. This link opens the run with the symbol table switched off, so the name and the end of the function file as unknowns and the start files as inferred.

## Lesson Artifact

This lesson produces `outputs/skill-evidence-ledger.md`. It tells an agent how to write every finding as a record with confidence, authority, limitations, and links. It tells the agent how to keep unknowns as revisions, and when a claim is `pass`, `fail`, `unknown`, or `unsupported`.

## Verify It

Run the demo and the deterministic suite:
```bash
cd phases/13-tools-and-protocols/35-evidence-confidence-and-unknowns
python3 code/main.py
python3 -m unittest discover -s code/tests -v
```
The 28 tests prove:

- both rea `evidence_id` values, the profile digest, and both snapshot `query_id` values recompute from content
- a changed path keeps the id and a changed limitation changes it
- a tampered record, a mismatched profile provider, a float, and an unknown enum value are rejected
- a duplicate record returns `duplicate`, a conflicting record raises, and a bundle import is atomic
- the recorded run bundle imports with 18 records and no dangling links
- an unknown opens at revision 1, refuses a stale `expected_revision`, and resolves only with observed `controlled-replay` evidence
- an edited revision breaks the chain
- promotion refuses inferred, derived, empty, and unrelated evidence, and passes with an agreeing run
- partial coverage is `unknown` and a disagreeing run is `fail`
- the cache hits on the exact key and misses on other parameters
- the cache refuses a bumped profile version, a wrong target, a wrong format version, and a tampered key
- the ELF reader agrees with `llvm-objdump` on offsets, sizes, bytes, and relocations, and the table reads `1, 2, 3, 4, 4`
- the predictions use C division, and the recorded runs agree with all 17 single-input claims
- with a compiler present, the live runs agree too

## Production Failure Modes

| Failure | What the weak report says | What the ledger requires |
|---|---|---|
| Pseudocode read as behaviour | "grade returns 0 for failing scores" | an `execute_function` record for that input, or `unsupported` |
| Decompiler signature trusted | "percent_change returns 16 bytes" | the signature marked as the provider's inference with its `low` confidence |
| Empty list read as absence | "the function has no callers" | an `unknown` status, or a coverage field when the tool provides one |
| Path hashed into the id | "the record changed" after a copy | the semantic projection without `name` and `local_path` |
| Limitation dropped from a copy | a record that looks stronger than the source | id mismatch and rejection on import |
| Partial grid rounded up | "all scores from 90 pass" | `unknown` with `covered` 2 of 11 |
| Host run presented as the object's run | "the x86-64 object returned 25" | the host-build limitation carried on the claim |
| Unknown closed by a sentence | "resolved, see above" | a `verified` resolution with observed ids of the required authority |
| Stale revision overwritten | two analysts' edits collide | `revision-conflict` and a reread |
| Old snapshot replayed after a release | answers from a changed contract | `profile_mismatch` on import |
| Cache kept after a rename | a replay that hides a metadata write | invalidation before dispatch and a failed export |

## Operational Rule

Record what you read, what you computed, and what you expect as three kinds of record with three words. Close an unknown with an id, never with a sentence. Replay an answer only under the exact key it was stored with, and refuse it when one version string differs.

Source: [AI Engineering from Scratch, phase 13, 35-evidence-confidence-and-unknowns](https://github.com/rohitg00/ai-engineering-from-scratch/tree/3f9715c62a3bedcffb68a260f1a65ee2dd9cc10a/phases/13-tools-and-protocols/35-evidence-confidence-and-unknowns), with its code and notebook. MIT licence, (c) Rohit Ghumare and contributors.

## Check yourself

```recall
Q: rea gives every Evidence record a confidence value. Which set of values does the schema allow?
A: observed, derived, or inferred. Confidence is a three-value enum in src/domain/evidence.ts. Severity and completion statuses are different fields with their own values.
Q: Two people run the same rea query on the same object file in different folders on different machines. What happens to evidence_id?
A: It is the same because the hash excludes name and local_path. The semantic projection keeps the subject digest, format, and architecture and drops name and local_path. The same observation of the same bytes gets the same id anywhere.
Q: A claim says grade(55) == 0. The ledger holds the Ghidra pseudocode record and the derived table model. What is the claim's status?
A: unsupported, because no observed run states the result. The pseudocode is an observation of what Ghidra printed, not of what the function returns. Only an observed run of the function can promote a behaviour claim.
Q: A snapshot was saved under profile digest a04af771. A later rea release changes jump_table_evidence to a v2 contract. What does the cache do with the snapshot?
A: Refuses the import with profile_mismatch. The profile digest covers every contract version string. A changed version gives a new digest, and the snapshot no longer matches the active binding.
Q: What closes a residual unknown with the disposition verified?
A: At least one evidence id with the required confidence and authority. A verified resolution names evidence ids, and the ledger checks that each one is observed and carries the authority the unknown asked for.
Q: Runs of the host build showed grade(95) == 4 and grade(100) == 4. The claim covers every score from 90 to 100. Which status is correct?
A: unknown, because 2 of 11 inputs have observed runs. Partial coverage is unknown, not pass and not fail. The unknown record stays open until the other nine inputs have observed runs.
```

lessons.title: Rebuild and Prove Equal: Differential Tests, Byte Comparison, and the Evidence Loop
lessons.body:
> Passing your tests proves agreement on your tests, so equality needs a grid that reaches every edge and bytes that match after relocation masking.

**Type:** Build
**Languages:** Python, C
**Prerequisites:** Phase 13 · 34 (lifting to pseudocode), Phase 13 · 35 (evidence, confidence, and unknowns)
**Time:** ~110 minutes

## Learning Objectives

- Write a rebuild from the instruction listing and name the evidence record it came from.
- Build an input grid with one class per hazard: zero guard, negative values, truncating division, 32-bit overflow, and a divide trap.
- Run the original and the rebuild in one program and record every cell, including a trap.
- Recompile the rebuild with the original flags and compare function bytes after masking relocation fields.
- Read the constants a relocation points at and compare them, so a wrong literal cannot pass.
- Drive rea's MCP server from a small stdio client and record each step with its evidence id.
- Mint a fail-closed proof record whose id is a hash over its claims and evidence links.

## The Problem

You asked rea for the function dossier of `percent_change` in our `ledger-x86_64-O1.o` fixture. Ghidra 12.1.4 returned pseudocode, and the agent wrote this C from it:
```c
int percent_change(int before, int after) {
    if (before == 0) return 0;
    return (int)(((long)after - before) * 100 / before);
}
```
Four tests pass: `(100, 150)` gives 50, `(200, 100)` gives -50, `(0, 5)` gives 0, `(50, 100)` gives 100. The agent also rebuilt `grade` as four `if` statements on 90, 80, 70, and 60. Six more tests pass. The report says "verified".

That report answers none of these questions:

- What does the original return when `(after - before) * 100` does not fit in 32 bits?
- What does the original return for a score of 110?
- Does the rebuild compile to the same 16 bytes as the original?
- When two compiled functions hold the same bytes, do their relocations point at the same constants?
- Which evidence record did the rebuild come from, and did the agent read the listing or the pseudocode?
- What status does the proof get on a host without a C compiler?

Every target in this lesson is a program we wrote and compiled. The scope and law rules from lesson 32 apply unchanged.

## What the Evidence Says

The agent loop in `code/main.py` made six calls to rea 6.5.0 over stdio. The recorded run is `code/fixtures/runs/agent-run.json`. The server answered `initialize` with protocol version `2025-11-25`. Three calls returned Evidence records:

| Step | Tool | Time | Evidence id |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | `analyze_function percent_change` | 6.31 s | `ev_e88b10dc0c6400e51bb6f7fdc3eaea8d2c97cc02463f0db3e6afeefc273197cd` |
| 3 | `analyze_function grade` | 0.02 s | `ev_67b6d3f992eaf49a2e16de084b6ebfdd9884e8c5c7f75e175b7bb20f4f748ce1` |
| 4 | `read_bytes 0x1000b4, 20` | 0.00 s | `ev_c26146cfedf4c1ee146d8ff00cfa9a5d3f5335bdd9c97ccf4e1af5f6ea3ed6bc` |

The first call paid for the Ghidra import and auto-analysis. Each record carries `confidence: "observed"`, `authority: "shipped-artifact"`, and the SHA-256 of the object, `9a4a8082ba5e285a732552981a6935e0c5255725664f380e37c44ebfb04d803f`. Ghidra loads the relocatable object with `.text` at `0x100000`, so `percent_change` sits at `0x100000` and `grade` at `0x100010`.

The pseudocode for `percent_change` is where the `long` came from:
```c
undefined1  [16] percent_change(int param_1,int param_2,ulong param_3)
{
  long lVar1;
  undefined1 auVar3 [16];
  if (param_1 != 0) {
    lVar1 = (long)((param_2 - param_1) * 100);
    auVar3._0_8_ = lVar1 / (long)param_1 & 0xffffffff;
    auVar3._8_8_ = lVar1 % (long)param_1 & 0xffffffff;
    return auVar3;
  }
  ...
}
```
The decompiler saw `cltd` and `idivl` write both `edx` and `eax` and modelled a 16-byte return value with a 64-bit division. The listing in the same record says something plainer:
```
0x100000: TEST EDI, EDI
0x100002: JZ 0x0010000d
0x100004: SUB ESI, EDI
0x100006: IMUL EAX, ESI, 0x64
0x100009: CDQ
0x10000a: IDIV EDI
0x10000c: RET
0x10000d: XOR EAX, EAX
0x10000f: RET
```
Every operation is 32 bits wide. `IMUL EAX, ESI, 0x64` multiplies in 32 bits and keeps the low half. `CDQ` sign-extends `eax` into `edx`, and `IDIV EDI` divides the 64-bit pair by a 32-bit divisor. A rebuild that follows the listing is `100 * (after - before) / before` in `int`.

The `grade` record has the same shape. The pseudocode names a table, `*(uint *)(&DAT_001000b4 + (ulong)uVar2 * 4)`, and an unreadable default expression built from `0x66666667`. The listing shows the divide by 10 as `IMUL RAX, RAX, 0x66666667`, `SAR RCX, 0x22`, `SHR RAX, 0x3f`, `ADD ECX, EAX`. Then `ADD ECX, -0x6`, `CMP ECX, 0x4`, and `JA` keep tens from 6 to 10. `XOR EAX, EAX` before the compare is the default of 0. `LEA RCX, [0x1000b4]` and `MOV EAX, dword ptr [RCX + RAX*0x4]` read a table of five 4-byte entries.

Step 4 read those 20 bytes: `01000000 02000000 03000000 04000000 04000000`. The table is `1, 2, 3, 4, 4` for tens 6, 7, 8, 9, 10. That is the `switch` in `ledger.c`, with `case 10` and `case 9` sharing the value 4.

Both proofs in rea's own evidence pages started from the listing and from `read_bytes` of constants. The DX-Ball first pseudocode was `FUN_00406400(void)` with no stack input, and the instruction view corrected it. Read the listing first. Cite the record id, then write the C.

## Write the Candidates

The folder `code/fixtures/candidates/` holds eight rebuilds, one function per file. Four follow the listing or compile to the same code. Four are plausible and wrong, or wrong in a way one hand-written test finds.

| File | Source | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `percent_change_mul_first.c` | `100 * (after - before) / before` | the listing in C |
| `percent_change_split.c` | `(after * 100 - before * 100) / before` | different text, same bytes after clang folds it |
| `percent_change_wide.c` | `(int)(((long)after - before) * 100 / before)` | the pseudocode's `long`, divides before it wraps |
| `percent_change_div_first.c` | `(after - before) / before * 100` | divides first, so rounding differs |
| `grade_switch.c` | `switch (score / 10)` with the five cases | the original source |
| `grade_table.c` | `unsigned slot = score / 10 - 6; slot < 5 ? points[slot] : 0` | the listing in C |
| `grade_thresholds.c` | `if (score >= 90) return 4; ...` | no upper bound on the top band |
| `grade_case10_wrong.c` | `case 10: return 3;` | one table entry wrong |

Each file compiles with the fixture command, `clang -target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu -O1 -fno-asynchronous-unwind-tables -c`. The compiled objects are committed beside the sources so the tests run on a host without clang.

## Leg One: Execute and Compare

McKeeman's 1998 definition of differential testing needs "two or more comparable systems" fed "mechanically generated test cases", and treats a different result, a hang, or a crash as a bug candidate. He named the hard part: "The ugliest problem in testing is evaluating the result of a test." The original function is the oracle here. We do not need to know the right answer. We need the original and the rebuild to disagree nowhere on a grid that reaches every hazard.

### Design the grid

`input_grid()` in `code/main.py` builds 92 cells. For `percent_change` it takes every pair from ten `before` values and seven `after` values:
```
before: 0, 1, -1, 3, -3, 7, 100, -100, 2147483647, -2147483648
after:  0, 5, -5, 105, 536870911, 2147483647, -2147483648
```
For `grade` it takes 22 scores: both sides of each band edge, negatives, 0, 110, and the two `int` limits. `classify()` tags each cell. Overflow has 32 cells, negative 17, boundary 14, plain 12, and zero guard 7. Negative truncation has 5, rounding 2, beyond the switch 2, and trap 1.

Each class exists for one reason. The zero guard cells check the `TEST EDI, EDI` branch. Negative cells check truncating division: C and `idiv` round toward zero, so `-9 / 10` is 0 and `-10 / 10` is -1. Rounding cells check that the multiply happens before the divide, so `(105 - 100) * 100 / 100` is 5 and not 0. Overflow cells make `(after - before) * 100` exceed 32 bits. The one trap cell makes the wrapped product equal `INT_MIN` with `before` equal to -1.

Yang, Chen, Eide, and Regehr built Csmith to generate programs with no undefined behaviour. An oracle disagreement on undefined behaviour is noise and never a bug report. Signed overflow is undefined in C. Our oracle is a compiled object with one fixed behaviour, so overflow cells are in scope. The lesson is to know which cells rest on the standard and which rest on the compiled bytes.

### The driver and the trap

`code/driver.c` reads one cell per line from stdin and prints the inputs, the original result, and the rebuild result. `build_harness()` compiles the candidate with `-Dpercent_change=cand_percent_change -Dgrade=cand_grade`, so both versions link into one program under different names. On an x86-64 Linux host the original is the fixture object itself. On any other host it is `ledger.c` compiled natively, and the report records `original_kind: fixture-source`.

The driver installs a `SIGFPE` handler with `sigsetjmp` and `siglongjmp`. For `before = -1` and `after = 536870911`, the difference is 536870912 and the 32-bit product wraps to -2147483648. On x86-64, `idiv` with that dividend and a divisor of -1 raises the divide error exception. The quotient does not fit in 32 bits (Intel SDM Volume 2, IDIV). The handler turns that into the recorded value `trap`.

On AArch64, `sdiv` has no trap and returns -2147483648 for the same operands. Our run on an arm64 Mac recorded exactly that. The oracle depends on the architecture, and the report says which one ran.

### Results

`prove_behaviour(PLAUSIBLE)` builds the `long` rebuild and the threshold rebuild. The ten naive cases pass. The grid fails on 28 cells:

| Function | Inputs | Class | Original | Rebuild |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `percent_change` | 3, 2147483647 | overflow | -133 | -1431655899 |
| `percent_change` | 100, 2147483647 | overflow | -101 | 2147483547 |
| `percent_change` | 2147483647, 5 | overflow | 0 | -99 |
| `grade` | 110 | beyond the switch | 0 | 4 |
| `grade` | 2147483647 | beyond the switch | 0 | 4 |

All 26 `percent_change` failures are overflow cells with `|before| > 1`. For `before` equal to 1 or -1 the 64-bit quotient truncates back to the wrapped value, so those cells agree by accident. The threshold `grade` fails because the original switch has no case for tens of 11 and above, and `110 / 10` is 11.

`prove_behaviour(EQUAL)` builds `percent_change_mul_first.c` and `grade_switch.c`. All 92 cells agree. `percent_change_div_first.c` fails two of the four naive cases, which is the one case a hand-written test does find.

`oracle_disagreements()` checks a second thing. `percent_change_model()` and `grade_model()` are Python models of the listing, with `wrap32()` for the 32-bit multiply and `idiv32()` for the architecture rule. The report compares the model with the observed original on every cell. Zero disagreements means the model and the binary agree on every cell. The model is derived evidence and the run is observed evidence. The report keeps them in separate fields.

## Leg Two: Recompile and Compare

Behaviour on a grid is one leg. The second leg asks whether the rebuild, compiled with the same compiler and flags, produces the same bytes. The DX-Ball project reported "63 matching bytes" for its helper. The TH04 project reported a 2,139-byte match. Each used the compiler of its own period. rea itself cannot do this. Its `compare_functions` line-diffs provider text and attaches the limitation "Assembly is opaque provider text; relocation normalization is unavailable."

### Read the object

`ElfObject` in `code/main.py` reads one ELF64 relocatable object with `struct.unpack_from`. It checks the magic, the 64-bit class, little-endian data, `e_machine` 62, and `e_type` 1. Then it walks the section headers, the string table, `.symtab`, and every `.rela` section. In the fixture, `percent_change` starts at `.text` offset 0 with size 16 and `grade` at `0x10` with size 46. `total` starts at `0x40` with size 31 and `grade_label` at `0x60` with size 63.

The 16 bytes of `percent_change` are `85 ff 74 09 29 fe 6b c6 64 99 f7 ff c3 31 c0 c3`. The function has no relocations. `grade` has one: offset `0x26` inside the function, type `R_X86_64_PC32`, symbol `.rodata`, addend `0x10`. It belongs to the 7-byte `leaq` at offset `0x23`, whose last four bytes are the displacement field.

### Mask, then compare the records

In a RELA object the addend lives in the relocation record, and the four field bytes are zero. The candidate `grade_switch.o` also holds zero there. A plain byte compare passes while the two relocations name different places. `mask_relocations()` zeroes the field on both sides anyway, so the same method holds for REL objects and for Mach-O, where the field carries the addend.

Then `prove_bytes()` compares the relocation records by offset, type, and target section. The original says `.rodata+0x10` and the candidate says `.rodata-0x4`. The addend differs because the candidate object has no `labels.rel` table in front of its switch table. A different addend is a different offset, not a different function.

### Read the constants the relocation points at

For a PC-relative field that ends its instruction, the CPU adds the next instruction address, so the target is symbol plus addend plus 4. In the original that is `.rodata+0x14`, and in the candidate it is `.rodata+0x0`. `read_table()` reads five 4-byte entries there. Both hold `1, 2, 3, 4, 4`.

The count five comes from the listing: `CMP ECX, 0x4` with `JA` admits indexes 0 to 4, and `[RCX + RAX*0x4]` reads 4 bytes per index. `CLAIMS` in `code/main.py` records that shape for `grade` and records zero relocations for `percent_change`.

This step exists because of a bug the TH08 project documented. Its older comparison "replayed the target address into the instruction's relocation field, then compared instruction bytes without checking the floating-literal data at that address. Source `0.0` could therefore appear exact against target `128.0`." The fix audited 1,548 floating-literal references and corrected twelve more. `grade_case10_wrong.c` is our version of that bug. Its 46 code bytes equal the original, its relocation record has the same shape, and its table is `1, 2, 3, 4, 3`. Only the constant check fails it.

### Results

| Candidate | Size | Masked bytes | Relocation records | Table | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `percent_change_mul_first` | 16 vs 16 | equal | none | none | pass |
| `percent_change_split` | 16 vs 16 | equal | none | none | pass |
| `percent_change_wide` | 16 vs 26 | size differs | none | none | fail |
| `percent_change_div_first` | 16 vs 18 | size differs | none | none | fail |
| `grade_switch` | 46 vs 46 | equal | same shape | `1,2,3,4,4` both | pass |
| `grade_table` | 46 vs 46 | equal | same shape | `1,2,3,4,4` both | pass |
| `grade_thresholds` | 46 vs 39 | size differs | 1 vs 0 | none | fail |
| `grade_case10_wrong` | 46 vs 46 | equal | same shape | `1,2,3,4,4` vs `1,2,3,4,3` | fail |

Two results deserve a second look. `percent_change_split.c` has different source text and identical bytes, because clang treats signed overflow as undefined and folds `after * 100 - before * 100` into one multiply. `grade_table.c` also matches byte for byte, so the compiler reached the same table from an array index and from a `switch`. A byte match proves that this compiler, with these flags, produced the same code from the candidate. It does not prove the candidate is the original source text.

Size is a diagnostic and not an acceptance. rea's evidence pages record a 1,825-byte candidate with the right length and 467 differing bytes. The `wide` rebuild is 26 bytes because `movslq`, `imulq`, `cqto`, and `idivq` replaced the 32-bit forms. The listing had told us the width before any compile.

## The Agent Loop Over rea

Sixty-five of rea's MCP tools have no CLI command, and `verify_reconstruction` is one of them. `McpStdioClient` in `code/main.py` is the smallest client that reaches them. It starts `npx -y rea-agents@6.5.0 mcp`, writes one JSON-RPC request per line to stdin, and reads one JSON object per line from stdout on a thread. It sends `initialize` with protocol version `2025-11-25`, then `notifications/initialized`, then `tools/call`. The default deadline per call is 330 s, the same number rea allows for a Ghidra cold start.

`agent_loop()` makes the six calls and records each one:
```json
{
  "step": 2,
  "tool": "analyze_function",
  "arguments": {"procedure": "percent_change"},
  "seconds": 6.31,
  "is_error": false,
  "evidence_id": "ev_e88b10dc0c6400e51bb6f7fdc3eaea8d2c97cc02463f0db3e6afeefc273197cd",
  "confidence": "observed",
  "authority": "shipped-artifact",
  "limitations": ["Resolved reference metadata identifies computed, indirect, external, call, jump, and data edges; unresolved targetless flows remain unknown, and function classifications distinguish thunks and externals.", "..."],
  "result_sha256": "..."
}
```
The complete Evidence records are stored under their ids in the same file. The pseudocode and the listing the rebuild came from are part of the fixture. `table_address()` finds the `LEA` operand in the `grade` listing and feeds it to `read_bytes`. `open_binary`, `get_evidence_bundle`, and `close_binary` return no Evidence record and are recorded with a null id.

`run_agent(live=True)` drives rea when `npx` is on the path and `GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR` names a directory. Otherwise it replays the fixture and says so on stderr. The tests go one step further. `code/tests/fake_rea_server.py` is a stand-in server that answers each `tools/call` with the recorded record for the same tool and arguments. The client and the loop run against it on every test run, with no rea, Ghidra, or Java installed.

### What rea's verifier can and cannot say

rea's `verify_reconstruction` takes claims that point at comparison Evidence and returns pass, fail, or unknown per claim. Its fixed limitation reads "Pass means every declared claim passed; it does not establish global implementation equivalence." A claim about a function compares provider text from `compare_functions`. A behavioural claim compares two recorded process captures from `compare_process_captures`. When a source record has incomplete call coverage, a claim about calls is `unknown`. Nothing inside rea compiles a rebuilt function or runs it over your input grid. The two legs in this lesson are the part rea leaves to you.

rea's obligation ledger expects a proof record with `predicate_type: "rea.reconstruction-proof"`, `operation: "verify_reconstruction_obligations"`, `confidence: "observed"`, and `normalized_result.passed === true`. No public rea tool emits one. `build_proof()` in `code/main.py` mints it:
```json
{
  "predicate_type": "rea.reconstruction-proof",
  "operation": "verify_reconstruction_obligations",
  "confidence": "observed",
  "authority": "controlled-replay",
  "normalized_result": {
    "passed": true,
    "status": "pass",
    "claims": [
      {"claim_id": "percent_change.behaviour", "kind": "behavioral", "status": "pass", "evidence_ids": ["ev_e88b10dc..."]},
      {"claim_id": "grade.behaviour", "kind": "behavioral", "status": "pass", "evidence_ids": ["ev_67b6d3f9..."]},
      {"claim_id": "percent_change.bytes", "kind": "structural-function", "status": "pass", "evidence_ids": ["ev_e88b10dc..."]},
      {"claim_id": "grade.bytes", "kind": "structural-function", "status": "pass", "evidence_ids": ["ev_67b6d3f9..."]},
      {"claim_id": "grade.referenced-constants", "kind": "structural-function", "status": "pass", "evidence_ids": ["ev_67b6d3f9..."]}
    ]
  },
  "evidence_links": ["ev_e88b10dc...", "ev_67b6d3f9..."],
  "evidence_id": "ev_..."
}
```
The id is `ev_` plus the SHA-256 of the record without the id, over sorted-key compact JSON. `aggregate()` is fail-closed: `fail` wins, then `unknown`, and an empty claim list is `unknown`. On a host without a C compiler the two behaviour claims are `unknown`, so the record says `unknown` even when both byte claims pass. `authority` is `controlled-replay`, because the proof comes from our own harness and not from the object file alone.

## What the Research Says

Liu, Raff, and Micinski measured eight decompilation systems in nine configurations in 2026. Candidates that passed every test the benchmark includes still diverged on fuzzed inputs. The rate was 4.9 percent overall and up to 13 percent for one system. On 300 GitHub library functions and 287 CVE-grounded functions, the strongest refinement model raised Ghidra's build rate from 75 percent to 90 percent. Over the same functions the behavioural match rate fell from 74 percent to 62 percent. They traced the cause to invented fields, types, callees, and guards that replaced the visible unknowns a traditional decompiler leaves behind.

Our `percent_change_wide.c` is one of those invented types. The pseudocode offered a `long`, the rebuild kept it, and the result compiled, passed ten tests, and failed 26 overflow cells. The grade-threshold rebuild is an invented guard. Both would count as re-executable under the LLM4Decompile metric, which recompiles the output and runs the benchmark's assertions. Ghidra's own pseudo-C passed 20.12 percent of those assertions on HumanEval-Decompile.

DecompileBench measured 23,400 functions from 130 real programs. It found LLM methods 52.2 percent lower on functionality correctness than industrial decompilers, with higher understandability scores.

The three proofs the field uses are the three legs you can build. Phoenix and DREAM recompile the output and run the original program's tests. McKeeman and Csmith run generated inputs against the original with inputs kept inside defined behaviour. Ramos and Engler check two C functions with bounded symbolic execution, which proves equality on all explored paths up to an input size. This lesson builds the first two. The third is the practice lab in lesson 35's evidence ledger when a grid is too small to trust.

## Build It

Run the standard-library harness:
```bash
cd phases/13-tools-and-protocols/36-rebuild-and-prove-equal
python3 code/main.py
```
With clang on the path, the demo compiles both candidate pairs and runs 92 cells for each. It recompiles eight candidates, replays the agent run, and mints the proof record. Without clang it reads the committed objects and reports the behaviour claims as `unknown`.

Expected shape on an arm64 Mac:
```json
{
  "host": "aarch64 Darwin",
  "originalKind": "fixture-source",
  "gridCells": 92,
  "plausible": {"naivePassed": true, "gridMismatches": 28, "oracleDisagreements": 0},
  "equal": {"naivePassed": true, "gridMismatches": 0, "oracleDisagreements": 0},
  "legTwo": {
    "percent_change_mul_first": {"status": "pass", "reasons": []},
    "percent_change_wide": {"status": "fail", "reasons": ["size 16 vs 26 bytes"]},
    "grade_case10_wrong": {"status": "fail", "reasons": ["referenced constants differ: [1, 2, 3, 4, 4] vs [1, 2, 3, 4, 3]"]}
  },
  "agentRun": {"mode": "replayed fixture", "server": {"name": "rea", "version": "6.5.0", "protocolVersion": "2025-11-25"}},
  "proof": {"status": "pass", "evidence_id": "ev_..."}
}
```
Read `code/main.py` in this order:

1. `wrap32()`, `c_div()`, `idiv32()`, and the two `*_model()` functions hold the integer semantics of the listing.
2. `input_grid()` and `classify()` build and tag the 92 cells.
3. `build_harness()` and `execute()` compile one program from the original, the renamed candidates, and `driver.c`, then run the cells.
4. `prove_behaviour()` returns the leg-one report with mismatches and model disagreements.
5. `ElfObject` reads headers, symbols, and `.rela` records. `mask_relocations()` and `read_table()` prepare the compare.
6. `prove_bytes()` returns the leg-two report with sizes, masked ranges, relocation shape, and tables.
7. `McpStdioClient` and `agent_loop()` drive rea and record each step.
8. `build_proof()` and `aggregate()` mint the fail-closed record.

## Use It

To prove a new function equal, repeat these steps:

1. Fetch `analyze_function` for the function and record the evidence id. Read the listing before the pseudocode.
2. Write the candidate from the listing's operation widths. Keep the original's function name.
3. List every multiply, add, subtract, and divide in the listing. Add grid inputs that wrap each one at its width.
4. Add both sides of every compare constant in the listing. For `grade` those were 6 and 4 after the subtract.
5. Add every divisor that can trap on the target, and record which architecture ran the grid.
6. Run both legs and read the reasons before the status.
7. Keep the proof record beside the candidate. Its `evidence_links` tell a reader which records the claim rests on.

Rerun both legs after any compiler update. A byte match is a statement about one compiler with one set of flags.

## Interactive Lab

### Lab A: the model and the run

From the `code` directory, open Python:
```bash
cd phases/13-tools-and-protocols/36-rebuild-and-prove-equal/code
python3 -q
```
Run:
```python
from main import *
percent_change_model(3, INT_MAX)
percent_change_model(-1, 536870911, "x86_64")
percent_change_model(-1, 536870911, "aarch64")
report = prove_behaviour(PLAUSIBLE)
report.naive_passed, len(report.mismatches), report.mismatches[0]
```
The first call gives -133, the wrapped product divided by 3. The second gives `'trap'` and the third gives -2147483648. The report shows ten naive cases passed and 28 grid cells failed. Compare `report.oracle_disagreements` with an empty list.

### Lab B: read the object
```python
obj = ElfObject(ORIGINAL_OBJECT)
grade = obj.function("grade")
grade.size, grade.data[0x26:0x2a].hex(), grade.relocations
read_table(obj, grade.relocations[0], 5, 4)
```
The field bytes are `00000000`. The relocation names `.rodata` with addend `0x10`, and the table reads `[1, 2, 3, 4, 4]`.

### Lab C: break one constant
```python
report = prove_bytes("grade", CANDIDATES / "grade_case10_wrong.o")
report.masked_equal, report.relocations_match, report.tables_equal, report.reasons()
```
The bytes match, the records match, and the tables do not. Now edit `grade_case10_wrong.c` so `case 10` returns 4 again, recompile it with the fixture command, and watch the status change to `pass`.

### Lab D: drive rea

With rea 6.5.0 and Ghidra 12.1.4 installed:
```bash
GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR=/opt/homebrew/Cellar/ghidra/12.1.4/libexec \
JAVA_HOME=/opt/homebrew/opt/openjdk@21 \
python3 code/main.py --live
```
The first `analyze_function` takes several seconds while Ghidra imports the object. Compare the new evidence ids with the committed run. The same bytes under the same analysis profile give the same ids, because the id is a content hash that excludes the file path.

## Practice Lab

Extend both legs to `total` and `grade_label` from the same object.

Requirements:

- For `total`, the input is an array and a count. Build cells with count 0, a negative count, one element, and sums that wrap at 32 bits.
- For `grade_label`, the function calls `grade` inline and reads `labels.rel`, a table of five relative string offsets with their own relocations in `.rela.rodata`.
- Add a `CLAIMS` entry for `grade_label` with two relocations and a table of five 4-byte entries, and compare the strings the entries point at.
- Record which cells the model and the run disagree on, if any, and explain each one from the listing.
- Add one claim per leg per function to the proof record and keep the aggregate fail-closed.

Success means the proof record lists four functions, every claim carries an evidence id, and `grade_label` fails when one label string differs.

## Graded Lab

Five questions about the fixtures of this lesson. Find each answer with the code you built, then write it into `code/lab_answers.json`. Write numbers as numbers or as hex strings such as `"0x40"`, and lists as JSON lists.

1. `t1`: percent_change_model(3, 105) on x86_64.
2. `t2`: percent_change_model(0, 5) on x86_64.
3. `t3`: grade_model(100).
4. `t4`: the number of cells in input_grid().
5. `t5`: the number of grid cells where the x86_64 model traps.

Check your answers:
```bash
cd phases/13-tools-and-protocols/36-rebuild-and-prove-equal
python3 code/lab.py
```
The checker computes each expected value from `code/main.py` on the committed fixtures. It prints `PASS`, `FAIL` or `TODO` for each task and a score, and it exits 0 only when all five pass. `python3 code/lab.py my-answers.json` checks another file. `code/tests/test_lab.py` proves that the checker accepts the right answers and rejects a wrong one.

### See it run

The [Inside a Decompiler](https://aiengineeringfromscratch.com/inside-a-decompiler) machine ends with pseudocode and files it as inferred: the page does not prove it. This lesson is the step that turns that claim into a checked one.

## Output Skill

This lesson produces `outputs/skill-rebuild-and-prove-equal.md`. Use it to turn function evidence and a candidate rebuild into a two-legged proof and a proof record. The skill requires the listing before the pseudocode, a grid with every hazard class, relocation masking plus a constant check, and a fail-closed aggregate.

## Verify It

Run the demo and the test suite:
```bash
cd phases/13-tools-and-protocols/36-rebuild-and-prove-equal
python3 code/main.py
python3 -m unittest discover -s code/tests -v
```
The 35 tests prove:

- `c_div()` truncates toward zero and `wrap32()` follows two's complement
- the model gives -133 for `(3, INT_MAX)`, `trap` for the trap cell on x86-64, and -2147483648 on AArch64
- the grid has 92 cells and every hazard class, and the naive cases avoid every hard class
- the ELF reader finds four functions at the recorded offsets and sizes
- `percent_change` is 16 bytes with no relocations and `grade` has one `R_X86_64_PC32` at `0x26`
- the relocation field bytes are zero and masking changes nothing in this RELA object
- all eight committed candidates reach the expected status, with the recorded reasons
- `grade_case10_wrong` passes masked bytes and fails only the constant check
- the recorded leg-one runs show ten naive passes, 28 mismatches, and zero model disagreements
- with a compiler, both pairs rebuild and rerun with the same outcome
- the agent run targets the committed object by SHA-256, in order, with `ev_` ids on every Evidence step
- the `read_bytes` record equals the table the ELF reader finds
- the client drives the fake server and records the same evidence ids as the real run
- an error result from the server goes into the run record
- `aggregate()` is fail-closed and the proof id recomputes from its content

## Production Failure Modes

| Failure | What the weak report says | What the harness must prove |
|---|---|---|
| Rebuild keeps the decompiler's `long` | "ten tests pass" | 26 overflow cells differ from the original |
| Thresholds replace a switch | "every grade band passes" | 110 and larger return 0 in the original |
| Divide before multiply | "formula is algebraically equal" | rounding cells differ, naive cases fail |
| Trap cell skipped | "no crashes" | x86-64 raises `#DE`, AArch64 returns `INT_MIN`, the report names the host |
| Byte compare without masking | "bytes equal" | relocation records name different offsets |
| Masking without reading constants | "bytes equal after masking" | `1,2,3,4,3` differs from `1,2,3,4,4` |
| Size taken as acceptance | "same length" | differing bytes inside the same length |
| Different compiler or flags | "bytes differ, rebuild wrong" | the same source gives different bytes, so the compare is void |
| Model treated as observation | "model agrees" | the run is observed, the model is derived, disagreements are listed |
| Claim without evidence id | "verified" | every claim links an `ev_` record of the function it covers |
| No compiler on the CI host | "passed" | behaviour claims are `unknown` and the aggregate is `unknown` |
| Pseudocode read as source | "decompiler says long" | the listing shows `IMUL EAX`, `CDQ`, `IDIV EDI` |

## Operational Rule

Write the rebuild from the listing and name the record it came from. Run it against the original over a grid that wraps every intermediate and crosses every compare constant. Recompile it with the original flags, mask the relocation fields, compare the records, and read the constants they point at. Record each claim with its evidence id, and let an unverified claim stay unknown.

Source: [AI Engineering from Scratch, phase 13, 36-rebuild-and-prove-equal](https://github.com/rohitg00/ai-engineering-from-scratch/tree/3f9715c62a3bedcffb68a260f1a65ee2dd9cc10a/phases/13-tools-and-protocols/36-rebuild-and-prove-equal), with its code and notebook. MIT licence, (c) Rohit Ghumare and contributors.

## Check yourself

```recall
Q: A rebuilt percent_change passes four hand-written tests. What does that prove?
A: The rebuild agrees with the original on those four inputs and nothing more. A test set proves agreement on the inputs it contains. Zero, negative, rounding, and overflow cells are where rebuilds diverge.
Q: The original computes (after - before) * 100 / before in 32-bit int. The rebuild uses a 64-bit intermediate. Where do they differ?
A: On inputs where the 32-bit product wraps and before is not 1 or -1. The original divides the wrapped 32-bit product. The rebuild divides the exact 64-bit product and truncates afterwards. For before equal to 1 or -1 the two agree after truncation.
Q: Two x86-64 ELF objects hold the same 46 code bytes for grade, including zero bytes in the relocation field. Why is the byte compare still not enough?
A: The addend lives in the .rela.text record, and the table those records point at can differ. In a RELA object the field bytes are zero and the addend is in the relocation record. Mask the field, compare the record shape, then read and compare the constants at the target.
Q: The grid contains before = -1 and after = 536870911. The compiled x86-64 original executes idiv with INT_MIN / -1. What happens?
A: It raises a divide error and the process gets SIGFPE. x86-64 idiv raises #DE when the quotient does not fit. AArch64 sdiv returns INT_MIN for the same operands, so the oracle depends on the architecture.
Q: What did the 2026 study of LLM decompiler refinement measure when the build rate rose from 75% to 90%?
A: Behaviour match fell from 74% to 62%. Liu, Raff, and Micinski (arXiv 2609.05370) found that invented types, callees, and guards made more candidates compile while fewer matched the original on fuzzed inputs.
Q: Leg one could not run because the host has no C compiler. Leg two passed for both functions. What is the proof status?
A: unknown, because an unverified claim never aggregates to pass. fail wins, then unknown. A claim that was not checked stays unknown, and unknown never becomes pass.
```
