lessons.title: The Reverse Engineering Landscape: History, Tool Families, and How a Decompiler Is Built
lessons.body:
> Five tools read the same object and give four addresses, three block counts, and two answers for one switch, and this lesson builds the harness that shows which is which.

**Type:** Build
**Languages:** Python, C, x86-64 assembly, Java (one Ghidra script)
**Prerequisites:** Phase 13 · 32 (ELF from scratch), Phase 13 · 33 (disassembly and control flow), Phase 13 · 34 (lifting to pseudocode)
**Time:** ~150 minutes

## Learning Objectives

- Place the main tools of the field on a dated timeline from 1973 to 2026 and name the family each one belongs to.
- Name the eight stages of a decompiler and the term that Ghidra, Binary Ninja, Hex-Rays, radare2, rizin, and angr use for each stage.
- Lift one instruction into ESIL, RzIL, P-code, and VEX and explain which of them write flags eagerly and which store a thunk.
- Reduce the addresses of five tools to one `.text` offset and prove the reduction on one function.
- Build a comparison harness that reads captured tool outputs and reports agreement on instruction starts, blocks, edges, and function starts.
- Name, from captured evidence, where each tool invents code, misses code, or stops at an indirect jump.

## The Problem

You ask an agent to summarise what three reverse engineering tools say about `grade` in `ledger-x86_64-O1.o`. The agent runs each tool, reads three listings, and reports that the function sits at `0x08000050` in one tool, `0x400010` in another, and `0x100010` in the third. It concludes that the tools disagree about where the function is.

The tools agree. The object is relocatable and has no load address, so each tool chooses one. Subtract the address each tool gave `.text` and every answer is `0x10`. The agent compared raw addresses because nothing told it what the address meant in each tool.

Later the same agent reads `grade` in the `-O0` build and reports 3, 8, 8, and 9 basic blocks from four tools. All four numbers are real. One tool stopped at `jmp rax`. Two tools read the jump table through its relocations. One tool split a block at the jump to place a label. A block count without the reason behind it is a number without a claim.

This lesson is the map you need before you trust any of those numbers. Lessons 32 to 36 built one decoder, one lifter, one evidence record, and one rebuild. The second half of the track puts them next to the tools people use. To do that you need the history of the field, the families the tools fall into, the pipeline every decompiler runs, and a harness that compares what the tools say on objects you compiled yourself.

## Fifty-Three Years in Dated Steps

The field is older than most of its tools. Each date below has a primary source in Further Reading.

### 1973 to 1991: debuggers first, then disassemblers

The first decompilation theses are from 1973. Hollander at Stanford and Housel at Purdue wrote them, and both are known today through citations. The practical tools of the period were debuggers. Maranzano and Bourne wrote the `adb` tutorial at Bell Labs in 1977, and the debugger shipped with UNIX V7 in 1979. Tim Paterson's `DEBUG`, with an 8086 disassembler, shipped in PC-DOS 1.00 in August 1981. Richard Stallman's GDB entered distribution in 1986. SoftICE put a kernel debugger under DOS in 1987.

Batch disassemblers came next. Sourcer, from V Communications in 1988, ran multiple passes over a DOS program and wrote a commented listing. GNU binutils began with unnumbered snapshots in 1988, and `objdump` carries a 1990 copyright. Ilfak Guilfanov wrote the first line of IDA in January 1991 and released IDA 0.1 as shareware on 20 May 1991.

### 1991 to 2009: interactive disassemblers and the first decompilers

Cristina Cifuentes finished "Reverse Compilation Techniques" at QUT in July 1994. Her decompiler, `dcc`, took i80286 DOS programs to C, and her 1995 paper with Gough set the phases that every later decompiler kept. REC followed in 1997 and Boomerang in 2002, the first open-source decompiler, under a BSD licence.

IDA became a commercial product at DataRescue in 1996, gained a plugin SDK in 1999, and moved to Hex-Rays, founded in 2005. The Hex-Rays Decompiler 1.0 shipped on 17 September 2007. In the same year Mike Van Emmerik submitted "Static Single Assignment for Decompilation", the thesis that put SSA at the centre of decompiler data flow. Halvar Flake's "Structural Comparison of Executable Objects" (2004) started the diffing family, and BinDiff went on sale in August 2004.

radare started in February 2006 as a forensic hex editor with 64-bit offsets. radare2, the modular rewrite under LGPL-3.0, had its first release on 7 March 2009.

### 2009 to 2019: frameworks and intermediate representations

LLDB was announced as an LLVM subproject on 8 June 2010. BAP, the Binary Analysis Platform with its BIL intermediate language, appeared at CAV 2011. Google acquired zynamics, the makers of BinDiff, on 1 March 2011. Hopper appeared on the Mac App Store around the end of 2011. Matt Godbolt started Compiler Explorer in 2012 so that a C++ programmer could see the assembly a compiler produced.

angr received its first line of code in August 2013. The Phoenix paper (Schwartz, Lee, Woo, Brumley, USENIX Security 2013) showed semantics-preserving structuring with 40 `goto` statements across 8,676 functions. DREAM (Yakdan and others, NDSS 2015) removed the `goto` statements with pattern-independent structuring. Vector 35 was founded on 14 January 2015, and Binary Ninja went on sale on 23 July 2016 with its Low Level IL and a Python API. angr was released publicly in 2015 and placed third at the DARPA Cyber Grand Challenge in August 2016. BinDiff became free of charge in March 2016. Cutter 1.0 gave radare2 a Qt GUI in December 2017. In 2018 Guilfanov presented "Decompiler internals: microcode" at Recon, the first public description of the Hex-Rays IR.

### 2019 to 2026: open decompilers and the research turn

Ghidra 9.0 was released by the NSA at the RSA Conference on 5 March 2019 under Apache-2.0, with full source on GitHub a month later. angr 8.19.2.4 added a preliminary decompiler the same year. Binary Ninja 2.0 shipped its High Level IL decompiler on 20 May 2020. Rizin was announced as a fork of radare2 on 8 December 2020, and the Cutter team moved to it. IDA Freeware 7.6 added a cloud x64 decompiler in May 2021.

BinDiff 8 was open-sourced under Apache-2.0 on 25 September 2023. SAILR (Basque and others, USENIX Security 2024) became angr's default structurer and argued that only spurious `goto` statements should be removed, because Linux 6.1 has 3,754 of them in its source. Binary Ninja 4.0 added a Free edition in February 2024, and IDA 9.0 added `idalib` for headless use. The learned-decompiler papers run from SLaDe (2023) through LLM4Decompile (2024) to DecompileBench (2025) and two 2026 studies on agent-assisted readability and on decompilers that recompile more and preserve less.

The versions this lesson ran are the current ones on 14 October 2026: Ghidra 12.1.4 (21 September 2026), radare2 6.2.4 (5 October 2026), rizin 0.9.1 (29 June 2026), and angr 10.0.3 (10 October 2026). Binary Ninja 6.0 "Krypton" (3 September 2026) and IDA 9.4 (13 July 2026) are the current closed tools. This lesson did not run them.

## The Tool Families

A tool belongs to a family by what it produces. The families overlap in one program, and the overlap is where most confusion starts.

### Disassemblers

A linear sweep decodes from the first byte of a code section to the last. GNU `objdump -d` and `llvm-objdump -d` work this way, and neither builds a control-flow graph. GNU `objdump` treats symbols as instruction boundaries and sweeps between them. binutils 2.47 (26 July 2026) is GPL-3.0-or-later. LLVM 23.1.3 is Apache-2.0 with the LLVM exception. Apple's Command Line Tools ship `llvm-objdump` as "Apple LLVM version 17.0.0", and that is the copy this lesson captured.

An interactive disassembler runs recursive descent from known entries, adds heuristics for function starts, and keeps a database. IDA Pro (processor modules, autoanalysis queues, FLIRT signatures), Ghidra (`Disassembler` plus Auto Analysis analyzers), Binary Ninja (recursive descent, then linear sweep over unknown regions), Hopper, radare2 and rizin (`aa`, `aaa`, `af`), with Cutter and iaito as GUIs, are all in this family. Andriesse and others (USENIX Security 2016) measured nine of them on compiler-generated binaries. Instruction accuracy was close to 100 percent, and the hard primitive was function starts, with false negative rates of 20 percent or more.

### Decompilers

Commercial decompilers: the Hex-Rays Decompiler (twelve target families from x86 to RISC-V), Binary Ninja's HLIL with its Pseudo C rendering, and Hopper's pseudo-code view. Open decompilers: the Ghidra decompiler, a C++ engine under Apache-2.0 that r2ghidra and rz-ghidra reuse as a plugin and that pypcode reuses as a lifter; the angr decompiler on AIL with SAILR structuring under BSD-2-Clause; r2dec and jsdec in JavaScript; Boomerang and `dcc` as history. radare2 also has a built-in `pdc`, "pseudo disassembler output in C-like syntax". rizin has no built-in decompiler. The command `pdc` does not exist in rizin 0.9.1, and `pdg` needs the rz-ghidra plugin.

### Debuggers

GDB (1986) with the GEF and pwndbg front-ends, LLDB (2010), WinDbg with Time Travel Debugging (2017), OllyDbg (frozen in 2014), x64dbg (GPL-3.0, 2014), the Ghidra Debugger with its Python connectors, the Binary Ninja debugger, and the built-in debuggers of radare2 and rizin. Lesson 42 uses two of them on your own builds.

### Binary analysis frameworks

angr (VEX IR, symbolic execution, `CFGFast` and `CFGEmulated`, decompiler), BAP (BIL, OCaml), Dyninst, Jakstab, and ByteWeight are the frameworks that Andriesse named. Ghidra is a library through PyGhidra, Binary Ninja through `import binaryninja`, and IDA through `idalib`.

### Format and engine libraries

LIEF 1.0.0 (12 July 2026, Apache-2.0) parses ELF, PE, Mach-O, COFF, and the Android formats. CLE, "CLE Loads Everything", is angr's loader. Capstone 5.0.9 (28 May 2026, BSD-3-Clause) decodes; Keystone 0.9.2 (GPL-2.0) assembles; Unicorn 2.1.4 (GPL-2.0) emulates. radare2 6.2.4 bundles Capstone 5, and rizin 0.9.1 vendors Capstone, Zydis, and tree-sitter.

### Diffing tools and compiler-side viewers

BinDiff 8 (Apache-2.0) with its BinExport 12 plugin for IDA Pro, Binary Ninja, and Ghidra; Diaphora 3.4.3 (11 October 2026, AGPL-3.0) as an IDA plugin; `radiff2` and `rz-diff`. Compiler Explorer (BSD-2-Clause) shows the assembly a compiler emits for a source fragment, which is the forward direction of everything else in this list. Lesson 44 uses the diffing family.

## The Decompiler Pipeline, Stage by Stage

Cifuentes named the phases in 1994: syntax analysis, semantic analysis, intermediate code generation, control-flow graph generation, data-flow analysis, control-flow analysis, and code generation. She split them into a machine-dependent front end, a machine- and language-independent middle, and a language-dependent back end. Every decompiler since keeps that shape and renames the parts. The table below gives the eight stages this lesson uses and the name each tool gives them. The figure shows the same table with the tool columns selectable.

| Disassembly | `Disassembler`; SLEIGH `.slaspec` compiled to `.sla`; analyzers "Disassemble Entry Points", "Function Start Search" | architecture plugin; Recursive Descent, then linear sweep phases | processor module (`ana.cpp`, `emu.cpp`, `out.cpp`); autoanalysis queues; FLIRT | RArch plugin to `RAnalOp`; `aa`, `aaa`, `af` | RzAnalysis plugin; `aa`, `aaa`, `af` | Capstone blocks; `CFGFast` function start search |

### Loader

The loader parses the container, maps sections, and reads symbols and relocations. In a relocatable object nothing has an address yet, so the loader picks one. radare2 and rizin map the file at `0x08000000`, which puts `.text` at `0x08000040` because the section starts at file offset `0x40`. CLE places `.text` at `0x400000`. Ghidra's `ElfLoader` places it at `0x100000`. `llvm-objdump` prints section offsets and no base at all.

The loaders also differ on relocations. Ghidra processes them on import, and CLE applies them. radare2 prints a hint when it opens the object: relocations were not applied, and `bin.relocs.apply=true` changes that. What a loader does with relocations decides what every later stage can see, and you will meet the effect in the `-O0` jump table below.

### Disassembly

Lesson 33 built both methods. Every tool in the table except `llvm-objdump` runs recursive descent and then adds a search for function starts. Binary Ninja's documentation names the phases in order: Recursive Descent, Call Target Analysis, CFG Analysis as "linear disassembly of the unknown regions", and Tail Call Analysis. Ghidra runs its analyzers by priority, with "Disassemble Entry Points" and "Function Start Search" early. IDA keeps autoanalysis queues, each with a priority, and FLIRT signatures for library code. angr's `CFGFast` documents four sources of function starts: symbols, a prologue scan, call targets, and a complete scan of the remaining bytes. That last source is where angr invents functions at padding.

### CFG recovery

Each tool cuts blocks the way lesson 33 did, with one difference you will measure. angr ends a block at a `call`, because its IRSB is a single-entry, multiple-exit block and a call is an exit. Ghidra, radare2, and rizin run through a call. On `grade_label` at `-O0`, which calls `grade`, angr reports 2 blocks and the other three report 1. The instructions are the same.

### Lifting

Binary Ninja defines lifting as "translating from a lower level language to an intermediate language considered higher". The IRs differ in what they are for. P-code and VEX were built for analysis and decompilation. ESIL and RzIL were built for emulation, and neither has an SSA stage. Hex-Rays microcode starts as RISC-like code with 72 opcodes and passes through maturity levels from `MMAT_GENERATED` to `MMAT_LVARS`. Binary Ninja lifts to Lifted IL, then folds flags into conditions in LLIL, and MLIL "translates registers and memory accesses into variables". The next section puts four of these IRs side by side on one instruction.

### SSA

Van Emmerik's thesis lists what SSA buys a decompiler: expression propagation, parameter and return identification without an ABI assumption, preservation analysis, type analysis as a sparse data-flow problem, and the analysis of indirect jumps and calls. Ghidra calls its SSA construction `Heritage` and adds two operations that exist only in the graph, `MULTIEQUAL` for the phi and `INDIRECT` for side effects. Binary Ninja exposes an SSA form at every IL level. angr has two SSA stages inside `Clinic`. Hex-Rays does not name an SSA form and does use-def data flow in its global optimisation passes. ESIL and RzIL have none.

### Data flow and types

Ghidra's main simplification loop runs "Eliminate Dead Code", "Propagate Local Types", and "Perform Term Rewriting" until nothing changes, with the rewriting done by a pool of `Rule` objects. Hex-Rays transforms microcode, detects call arguments at `MMAT_CALLS`, and allocates local variables at `MMAT_LVARS`. angr runs `CallingConventionAnalysis`, `VariableRecoveryFast`, and `Typehoon`, an implementation of Noonan, Loginov, and Cok's polymorphic type inference. Lesson 41 is about this stage.

### Structuring

Ghidra's `CollapseStructure` searches for sub-graphs that match a structure, collapses them to one node, and when it gets stuck removes an edge and marks it unstructured. Hex-Rays reduces the CFG to `if`, `while`, `do`, and `switch` and leaves the rest as goto regions. angr identifies single-entry, single-exit regions and structures them with `SAILRStructurer` by default, with `PhoenixStructurer` and `DreamStructurer` as alternatives. Lesson 34 wrote one structurer by hand.

### Emission

Ghidra emits C tokens through `PrintC` with an Oppen pretty-printer after `ActionNameVars` and `ActionSetCasts`. Hex-Rays beautifies and prints the ctree. Binary Ninja renders HLIL as Pseudo C, Pseudo Rust, or Pseudo Python. angr returns `codegen.text`. radare2 prints `pdc`, `pdd`, or `pdg`.

## One Instruction in Four IRs

Take `48 83 ec 10`, `subq $0x10, %rsp`. Decode it on paper with the rules from lesson 33.

1. `48` is REX with `W = 1`. The operand is 64 bits.
2. `83` is the group-1 arithmetic opcode with an 8-bit immediate. The ModRM reg field picks the operation.
3. `ec` is ModRM `11 101 100`. `mod = 11` is the register form. `reg = 101` is `/5`, which is `sub`. `r/m = 100` is `%rsp`.
4. `10` is the immediate, 16.

Four lifters were given those four bytes. The fixtures hold the exact commands and the full text.

ESIL from radare2 6.2.4 is one comma-separated string of 30 tokens:
```text
16,0x8000000000000000,-,!,16,rsp,-=,63,$o,^,of,:=,63,$s,sf,:=,$z,zf,:=,$p,pf,:=,64,$b,cf,:=,4,$b,af,:=
```
It is a stack machine. `16,rsp,-=` subtracts in place. Every flag is then written with an internal operator: `$o` overflow, `$s` sign, `$z` zero, `$p` parity, `$b` borrow.

RzIL from rizin 0.9.1 is an S-expression with 14 `set` effects:
```text
(seq (set op1 (var rsp)) (set op2 (bv 64 0x10)) (set sub (- (var op1) (var op2))) (set rsp (var sub))
     (set _result (var sub)) (set pf (! (lsb (let _val (cast 8 false (var _result)) ...))))
     (set zf (is_zero (var _result))) (set sf (msb (var _result))) ... (set cf (|| ...)) (set of (|| ...)) (set af (|| ...)))
```
Every flag is a boolean expression over bitvectors. The parity flag alone is a four-level `let`.

P-code from the SLEIGH specification `x86:LE:64:default` through pypcode 4.0.1 is nine operations after the `IMARK`:
```text
CF = RSP < 0x10
OF = sborrow(RSP, 0x10)
RSP = RSP - 0x10
SF = RSP s< 0x0
ZF = RSP == 0x0
unique[58300:8] = RSP & 0xff
unique[58400:1] = popcount(unique[58300:8])
unique[58500:1] = unique[58400:1] & 0x1
PF = unique[58500:1] == 0x0
```
Register transfers with temporaries in the `unique` space. The flags are computed at the instruction, eagerly, and `CF` and `OF` are computed before the subtraction overwrites `RSP`.

VEX from pyvex 10.0.3 is seven statements after the `IMark`:
```text
t2 = GET:I64(offset=48)
t0 = Sub64(t2,0x0000000000000010)
PUT(offset=144) = 0x0000000000000008
PUT(offset=152) = t2
PUT(offset=160) = 0x0000000000000010
PUT(offset=168) = 0x0000000000000000
PUT(offset=48) = t0
```
No flag appears. VEX names registers by their offset in the guest state, and offset 48 is `rsp`. Offsets 144 to 168 are `cc_op`, `cc_dep1`, `cc_dep2`, and `cc_ndep`. The lifter stores the operation code 8, which is the 64-bit subtraction, and the two operands. A later branch that reads a flag computes it from the thunk. That is why `pcode.writesFlags` is true and `vex.computesFlags` is false in the harness report, and why VEX is the shortest of the four.

The same four lifters on `48 63 c7`, `movslq %edi, %rax`, the first instruction of `grade` at `-O1`, give 5 ESIL tokens (`32,edi,~,rax,=`), 1 RzIL `set`, 1 P-code operation (`RAX = sext(EDI)`), and 4 VEX statements. No lifter writes a flag, because the instruction has none. Ghidra's own listing of that instruction, captured through the headless script, prints the same operation as `(register, 0x0, 8) INT_SEXT (register, 0x38, 4)`: register offset 0 is `RAX`, offset `0x38` is `RDI`, and the sizes are 8 and 4 bytes.

`83 f9 04`, `cmpl $0x4, %ecx`, from the bounds check in `grade`, gives 30 ESIL tokens, 13 RzIL `set` effects, 10 P-code operations, and 7 VEX statements with `cc_op` 7, the 32-bit subtraction. Nothing writes `%ecx`. The two subtraction widths you will meet in VEX are 7 for 32 bits and 8 for 64 bits, and the translator you build carries that table.

## Four Address Bases for One Function

Before the harness can compare anything it has to agree with itself about where a function is. Do the arithmetic once by hand for `grade` in `ledger-x86_64-O1.o`.

| Tool | Address of `.text` | Address of `grade` | Offset |
|---|---|---|---|
| `llvm-objdump` | `0x0` | `0x10` | `0x10 - 0x0 = 0x10` |
| radare2, rizin | `0x08000040` | `0x08000050` | `0x08000050 - 0x08000040 = 0x10` |
| angr | `0x400000` | `0x400010` | `0x400010 - 0x400000 = 0x10` |
| Ghidra | `0x100000` | `0x100010` | `0x100010 - 0x100000 = 0x10` |

The symbol table says `grade` is at `.text + 0x10` with size 46. Every tool agrees once the base is removed. The harness reads the base from each capture: `iSj` in radare2 and rizin, the `.text` section entry in the angr capture, the `.text` memory block in the Ghidra capture, and zero for the sweep. The test `test_every_tool_places_grade_at_offset_0x10_from_its_own_base` fixes that fact.

## Where the Tools Agree and Where They Split

The harness in `code/main.py` reads the captures, reduces every address, and compares. These are the numbers it reports, and the tests assert each of them.

### The agreement case: ledger at -O1

Four functions, 56 instructions in the sweep, 54 inside the symbols and 2 in padding. Every tool reports the same instruction starts in every function: 9, 14, 13, and 18. The four graph builders report 3, 3, 5, and 4 blocks and 2, 3, 5, and 4 edges, and the edge sets are identical, pair for pair, across radare2, rizin, angr, and Ghidra. The five blocks and five edges of `total` are the ones lesson 33 drew by hand.

The one difference is at the padding. The 3 bytes between functions (`66 90` after `grade`, `90` after `total`) are decoded by the sweep, which has no reason to stop, and by angr, which creates `sub_40003e` and `sub_40005f` with no symbol. radare2, rizin, and Ghidra claim none of them.

### The vectorised case: ledger at -O2

`total` is 41 instructions in 10 blocks with 13 edges, in every one of the four graph builders. The SSE2 loop and the scalar remainder loop from lesson 33 are cut the same way everywhere. angr again adds two functions at padding.

### The jump table: grade at -O0

Here the tools split, and the split is the lesson.

| Tool | Blocks | Edges | What the capture says |
|---|---|---|---|
| radare2 | 3 | 2 | the block at `0x62` has no successor; bytes `0x76` to `0x9a` are never reached; 8 instruction starts missing |
| rizin | 8 | 11 | the block at `0x62` carries a `switch_op` with 5 cases and 4 distinct targets |
| angr | 8 | 7 | the case blocks exist, and the transfer at `0x62` goes to an unresolvable target node |
| Ghidra | 9 | 12 | `switchD` label at `0x74` splits the block; four `COMPUTED_JUMP` flows to `0x76`, `0x7f`, `0x88`, `0x91` |

All four decoded the same 33 instructions when they reached them. radare2 stopped at `jmp rax` and left 36 bytes unclaimed, and the harness names that range as missed code. rizin and Ghidra found the four distinct targets that lesson 33 read from the five relocations in `.rela.rodata`. angr lists the case blocks inside `grade` and still has no edge from the jump block to them; its capture records the transfer at `0x62` as leading to an unresolvable target node, and its decompiler printed a computed `goto`. Ghidra has one block and one edge more than rizin for the same control flow because its switch analysis placed a label on the `jmp rax` and the block model starts a new block at a label.

The lesson-33 graph had 8 blocks and 11 edges. rizin matches it exactly. The point is to see that 9 and 11 and 7 and 2 are not four measurements of code found. They are four answers to how far a tool followed one indirect jump and where it chose to cut.

### Data in code: sweep-trap

`lookup` is 24 bytes with the 4 table bytes `31 c0 90 48` at `0x10`. The sweep reports 8 instruction starts in that range. The harness lists its differences from the majority: extra starts at `0x10`, `0x12`, and `0x13`, and a missing start at `0x14`. That is the `addq $0x1, %rax` from lesson 33 one byte early. radare2, rizin, and Ghidra report 6 starts, 2 blocks, 1 edge, and leave `0x10` to `0x14` unclaimed. angr reports the same 2 blocks and 1 edge for `lookup` and then invents `sub_400010` on the table bytes: 2 instructions in a 4-byte block that ends at `0x14`, where the second block of `lookup` starts, so the REX byte at `0x13` belongs to no instruction. The harness's last finding for this object is that no graph builder decodes `0x10` to `0x14`, so those bytes sit inside a function and are data.

### Invented and missed, by tool

Across the four objects the harness names 9 functions that angr invents with no symbol, every one at padding or at the trap table. It names one range that radare2 misses, the 36 case bytes of `grade` at `-O0`. It names 9 ranges that the linear sweep decodes and no graph builder treats as code: the eight padding gaps plus the trap table. It names no missed function in any tool.

## Three Decompilers on grade

Three of the captured tools emit C-like text for `grade` at `-O1`. The source is `switch (score / 10)` with five cases, compiled to a bounds check and a table of return values.

Ghidra 12.1.4:
```c
uint grade(int param_1)
{
  uint uVar1;
  uint uVar2;

  uVar2 = param_1 / 10 - 6;
  uVar1 = -(param_1 >> 0x1f) ^ (uint)((ulong)((long)param_1 * 0x66666667) >> 0x3f);
  if (uVar2 < 5) {
    uVar1 = *(uint *)(&DAT_001000b4 + (ulong)uVar2 * 4);
  }
  return uVar1;
}
```
angr 10.0.3:
```c
extern unsigned int g_4000b4[4];

unsigned int grade(int a0)
{
    unsigned int v1;  // ecx
    unsigned int v2;  // eax

    v1 = (unsigned int)((long long)(a0 * 1717986919) >> 0x22) + (unsigned int)(a0 * 1717986919 >> 63) - 6;
    v2 = 0;
    if (v1 <= 4)
        v2 = g_4000b4[v1];
    return v2;
}
```
radare2 6.2.4, `pdc`:
```c
void sym.grade (int64_t arg1) {
    rax = edi
    rax = rax * 0x66666667
    rcx = rax
    rcx >>= 0x22
    rax >>>= 0x3f
    ecx += eax
    ecx += 0xfffffffa
    eax = 0
    v = ecx - 4
    if (((unsigned) v) <= 0) {
        eax = ecx
        rcx = rip
        eax = dword [rcx + rax*4]
    }
    return
}
```
Read the three against the pipeline. Ghidra's term rewriting folded the multiply by `0x66666667` and the shift by 34 back into `param_1 / 10`, which is lesson 34's idiom. angr lifted the same bytes and left the arithmetic as `a0 * 1717986919 >> 0x22`. radare2's `pdc` is ESIL emulation plus pseudo syntax: register names, no variables, no types, and the bounds check printed as `<= 0` after an unsigned subtraction. Ghidra typed the table load through `DAT_001000b4`; angr declared `g_4000b4[4]`, four elements where the source has five. Neither Ghidra nor angr recovered the enumeration of cases, because at `-O1` there is no switch left in the bytes. At `-O0`, where the jump table exists, Ghidra printed `switch(param_1 / 10)` with cases 6 to 10 and a default, and angr printed a computed `goto`.

rizin has no decompiler of its own, and the capture records that `pdc` does not exist there. Binary Ninja's HLIL and the Hex-Rays ctree are the two outputs this lesson could not capture.

## Build It

Run the demo:
```bash
cd phases/13-tools-and-protocols/37-the-reverse-engineering-landscape
python3 code/main.py
```
The output is one JSON report. It opens with the tool versions recorded at capture time and with the tools present on your machine, which may all be absent. Then for each of the four objects it gives the symbol extents, the padding gaps, the base each tool used, the function starts each tool found or invented, and for each function the instruction-start agreement, block counts, edge counts, and the edges each tool lacks. It ends with byte accounting per tool, the tools' own notes, a list of findings in plain sentences, and the IR section: the translator's output for the three instructions next to the counts measured on the captured lifts.

Expected shape:
```json
{
  "captureTools": {"llvm-objdump": "Apple LLVM version 17.0.0", "radare2": "radare2 6.2.4 ...", "rizin": "rizin 0.9.1 ...", "angr": "10.0.3", "ghidra": "12.1.4"},
  "localTools": {"radare2": "absent", "...": "..."},
  "fixtures": {
    "ledger-x86_64-O0.o": {
      "bases": {"llvm-objdump": "0x0", "radare2": "0x8000040", "angr": "0x400000", "ghidra": "0x100000", "...": "..."},
      "functions": {"grade": {"blocks": {"radare2": 3, "rizin": 8, "angr": 8, "ghidra": 9}, "edges": {"radare2": 2, "rizin": 11, "angr": 7, "ghidra": 12}, "...": "..."}},
      "findings": ["radare2 never reaches bytes 0x76-0x9a inside grade that the other graph builders decode", "..."]
    }
  },
  "ir": {"translator": [{"text": "subq $0x10, %rsp", "flags": {"pcodeLike": "eager", "vexLike": "thunk"}, "...": "..."}], "observed": {"...": "..."}}
}
```
Read `code/main.py` in this order:

1. `read_text_symbols()` reads the section headers and the `STT_FUNC` symbols of `.text`. The symbol table is the only ground truth the harness has, and `TextSection.gaps()` derives the padding from it.
2. `parse_objdump()`, `parse_r2_family()`, `parse_angr()`, and `parse_ghidra()` each turn one capture into a `ToolView`: a base, the instructions as offset to length, and one `FunctionView` per function with blocks, edges, and any decompiled text. Each parser knows one tool's vocabulary and nothing else.
3. `majority()` and `ranges()` are the two helpers every comparison uses.
4. `function_report()` compares instruction starts against the majority of the graph builders, then block counts, then edge sets, and lists what each tool lacks.
5. `byte_report()` accounts for every byte as code inside a symbol, padding, unclaimed, invented, or missed, and names the bytes inside symbols that no graph builder decodes.
6. `findings()` turns those into sentences, and `compare()` assembles one report per object.
7. `decode_small()`, `to_pcode_like()`, and `to_vex_like()` are the translator: three encodings in register form, one eager style, one thunk style.
8. `observed_ir()` measures the captured lifts, and `figure_data()` assembles the timeline, the stage table, and the evidence the figure shows.

Three more commands exist. `python3 code/main.py compare FIXTURE.o` prints one object's report. `python3 code/main.py ir 4883ec10` prints the translator's two forms for one instruction. `python3 code/main.py figure-data` prints the data embedded in the figure.

The captures were made once by `code/fixtures/capture_tools.py`, which records every command and version in `captures.json`. The harness and the tests never start a tool. If you have the tools, run the capture script to refresh the files, and read the fixtures README for the environment it needs.

## Use It

Use the harness on a new object in this order.

1. Build the object yourself and keep the compiler command. Read its symbol table before you open any tool, so you know how many functions there are and where the padding is.
2. Capture each tool once in headless mode. Store the raw output and the exact command beside the object. A disagreement you cannot re-read is not a finding.
3. Check the base. Pick one function and confirm that every tool places it at the same offset after you subtract its `.text` address. If one does not, stop and find out what that tool loaded.
4. Compare instruction starts first. If the graph builders disagree here, the rest of the comparison is about decoding and not about analysis.
5. Compare blocks and edges, and read each tool's notes before you judge a count. A `switch_op`, a `COMPUTED_JUMP`, or an unresolvable target node explains most differences.
6. Account for bytes. Padding that a tool claims is a heuristic at work. Symbol bytes that a tool leaves are a stopped walk. Symbol bytes that no graph builder claims are data.
7. Write down which tools you did not run. A description from documentation is useful and is a different kind of evidence from a capture.

## Practice Lab

Add a fifth capture and extend the harness.

Requirements:

- Pick one tool this lesson did not capture and that you can run on your machine: GNU `objdump`, LIEF with Capstone, a Binary Ninja Free session exported by hand, or Ghidra with a different analyzer set. Capture its output on all four objects with the exact command and version in `captures.json`.
- Write one parser that turns the capture into a `ToolView` with the tool's base, instructions, functions, blocks where the tool has them, and edges where it has them.
- Add the tool to `TOOLS` and, if it builds a graph, to `DESCENT_TOOLS`. Run the demo and read what changed in the majority sets.
- Write a test that asserts the tool's block counts on `ledger-x86_64-O1.o` and a test that asserts what it does with the trap table.
- Write one paragraph for the lesson that says, in the tool's own words, what it calls the loader, the disassembler, and the CFG.

Success means `python3 code/main.py` reports the new tool in `captureTools`, every function in `ledger-x86_64-O1.o` keeps `allDescentToolsAgree` true, and the findings for `sweep-trap.o` say what the new tool did with bytes `0x10` to `0x14`.

## Lesson Artifact

This lesson includes `outputs/skill-the-reverse-engineering-landscape.md`. Use it to run several tools on one object you built, reduce their addresses to one base, and report, per function, where they agree on instruction starts, blocks, and edges, and which bytes each tool invents or misses. It requires captures with recorded commands and versions, a symbol table read from the file, and a statement of which tools were described from documentation only.

## Verify It

Run the demo and the deterministic suite:
```bash
cd phases/13-tools-and-protocols/37-the-reverse-engineering-landscape
python3 code/main.py
python3 -m unittest discover -s code/tests -v
```
Verification should prove:

- the ELF reader finds four function symbols in `ledger-x86_64-O1.o` with sizes 16, 46, 31, and 63, and two padding gaps
- the sweep captures hold 86, 56, 84, and 11 instructions for the four objects
- radare2 and rizin report the same instructions, blocks, and edges on `ledger-x86_64-O1.o`, and only radare2 has `pdc` text
- angr marks `sub_40003e` and `sub_40005f` as functions with no symbol
- Ghidra's blocks for `total` are the five blocks of lesson 33 and its call flows are not graph edges
- every tool places `grade` at offset `0x10` after its base is removed
- every tool agrees on every instruction start in every function of `ledger-x86_64-O1.o`
- the four graph builders report 3, 3, 5, 4 blocks and 2, 3, 5, 4 edges there, with identical edge sets
- `total` at `-O2` has 10 blocks and 13 edges in every graph builder
- `grade` at `-O0` has 3, 8, 8, and 9 blocks and 2, 11, 7, and 12 edges in radare2, rizin, angr, and Ghidra, with the reasons in each tool's notes
- `grade_label` at `-O0` is one block everywhere except angr, which ends a block at the call
- angr invents one function per padding gap plus one on the trap table, and no other tool invents or misses a function
- the sweep gains starts `0x10`, `0x12`, `0x13` and loses `0x14` on the trap, and no graph builder decodes `0x10` to `0x14`
- the findings name the missed range in radare2 and every invented function in angr
- the manifest records a version and a command for all 21 capture files
- three tools decompile `grade`, and only Ghidra folds the division idiom
- the translator writes CF, OF, SF, ZF, PF eagerly in one style and a `cc_op` thunk in the other, writes no register for `cmp`, and no flag for `movslq`
- the translator refuses memory forms, other opcodes, extra REX bits, and wrong lengths
- the translator's `cc_op` numbers 8 and 7 equal the ones in the captured VEX
- the captured lifts give 9, 1, 10 P-code operations and 7, 4, 7 VEX statements for the three instructions
- the timeline runs from 1973 to 2026 in order, the pipeline has eight stages and six tools with a term in every cell, and the two closed tools are marked as not run
- the interactive figure embeds the same data the harness produces

## Production Failure Modes

| Failure | What the weak report says | What the harness must prove |
|---|---|---|
| Raw addresses from different tools | "the tools disagree about where grade is" | one offset after each base is removed, checked on one function |
| Block count as a measure of code found | "Ghidra found the most code" | the same instruction starts, with the extra block explained by a label |
| One tool as the oracle | "objdump shows the table bytes are instructions" | the sweep is a linear sweep; three graph builders leave the bytes unclaimed |
| Padding functions counted as discoveries | "angr found seven more functions" | every one sits in a padding gap or on data, and none has a symbol |
| A stopped walk reported as dead code | "the four case blocks are unreachable" | 36 bytes missed by one tool and reached by three |
| Edge counts compared without the notes | "rizin and Ghidra disagree on grade" | the same four computed targets, one extra split at a label |
| A decompiler's arithmetic read as the program | "the function multiplies by 1717986919" | the idiom from lesson 34, folded by one tool and left by another |
| A closed tool described as if run | "Binary Ninja reports five blocks" | the figure and the table mark it as documentation only |
| Captures without commands | "we ran radare2" | the manifest with version, command, and date for every file |
| An IR with no flags read as a lossy lift | "VEX dropped the flags" | the thunk in `cc_op`, `cc_dep1`, `cc_dep2`, evaluated at the branch |

## Operational Rule

Capture every tool once with its command and version, reduce every address to one base, and compare instruction starts before blocks and blocks before edges. Account for every byte as claimed, padding, data, or missed. Read a tool's own note before you judge its count, and say which tools you only read about.

Source: [AI Engineering from Scratch, phase 13, 37-the-reverse-engineering-landscape](https://github.com/rohitg00/ai-engineering-from-scratch/tree/3f9715c62a3bedcffb68a260f1a65ee2dd9cc10a/phases/13-tools-and-protocols/37-the-reverse-engineering-landscape), with its code and notebook. ## Check yourself

```recall
Q: radare2, rizin, angr, and Ghidra all open ledger-x86_64-O1.o and report four functions, yet grade sits at 0x08000050, 0x400010, and 0x100010 in three of them. What explains the three addresses?
A: Each tool chooses its own base address for a relocatable object, so the same function keeps its .text offset 0x10 under three different bases. A relocatable object has no load address. radare2 and rizin map the file at 0x08000000, angr at 0x400000, Ghidra at 0x100000. Subtracting the .text base gives the same offset 0x10 in every tool.
Q: On ledger-x86_64-O0.o the harness reports 3 blocks for grade in radare2, 8 in rizin and angr, and 9 in Ghidra. Which statement matches the captured evidence?
A: Ghidra split the switch block at the jmp rax to place its switchD label, rizin resolved five cases as a switch_op, and radare2 stopped at the indirect jump with 36 bytes never reached. The counts come from the same bytes. The difference is how far each tool follows jmp rax: radare2 stops, rizin and Ghidra read the table through its relocations, angr keeps the case blocks but routes the jump to an unresolvable node.
Q: pypcode lifts sub rsp, 0x10 into nine operations that write CF, OF, SF, ZF, and PF, and pyvex lifts it into seven statements with PUT(cc_op) = 0x8 and no flag at all. What does the difference mean?
A: P-code writes every flag eagerly; VEX stores a condition-code thunk (operation and operands) and computes a flag only when a later instruction reads it. Both lifts are complete. SLEIGH writes the flags at the instruction. VEX records cc_op, cc_dep1, cc_dep2, cc_ndep and evaluates a flag lazily at the branch that uses it.
Q: On sweep-trap.o llvm-objdump lists 8 instruction starts inside lookup and radare2, rizin, and Ghidra list 6. Where do the two extra starts come from?
A: The linear sweep decodes the four table bytes 31 c0 90 48 as xorl, nop, and a REX prefix that swallows the real addl, so it gains starts at 0x10, 0x12, and 0x13 and loses the start at 0x14. The harness reports extra starts 0x10, 0x12, 0x13 and a missing start at 0x14 for the sweep. The three graph builders leave 0x10 to 0x14 unclaimed, and the harness names that range as data inside a function.
Q: Ghidra decompiles grade at -O1 to param_1 / 10 - 6 and angr decompiles the same bytes to (a0 * 1717986919) >> 0x22. Which pipeline stage produced the difference?
A: Term rewriting in the data-flow stage: Ghidra's Rule pool folds the multiply-and-shift idiom back into a division, angr's simplifier leaves the arithmetic as lifted. Both tools decode the same imul by 0x66666667 and sar by 34. Ghidra's simplification loop rewrites that idiom into a division; angr's AIL simplification does not, so the lifted arithmetic reaches the emitter.
Q: A teammate proposes to trust whichever tool reports the most basic blocks, because more blocks means more code was found. Which captured result argues against that rule?
A: Ghidra reports 9 blocks for grade at -O0 where rizin reports 8 for the same edges, and angr adds a block with no symbol at every padding gap, so block count measures block boundaries and heuristics rather than code found. Ghidra's extra block is a label split at jmp rax, and angr's extra functions are alignment bytes. Agreement on instruction starts, edges, and byte accounting is the evidence; a single count is not.
```

lessons.title: Calling Conventions and Stack Frames: System V, Windows x64, and AArch64
lessons.body:
> A disassembly shows which registers a function reads. Only the ABI says what those registers mean, and the ABI is chosen by the object header, so this lesson reads the header first and then checks every register against the rule that put it there.

**Type:** Build
**Languages:** Python, C, x86-64 and AArch64 assembly
**Prerequisites:** Phase 13 · 32 (ELF from scratch), Phase 13 · 33 (disassembly and control flow)
**Time:** ~140 minutes

## Learning Objectives

- Pick the calling convention from the object header: ELF x86-64 is the System V psABI, COFF AMD64 is Microsoft x64, ELF AArch64 is AAPCS64, Mach-O arm64 is Apple's variant.
- Decode the prologue of one function byte by byte for each ABI and place every saved register, the return address, and the frame pointer at its offset from the entry stack pointer.
- Infer the parameter registers of a function from the registers it reads before it writes them, and the stack argument slots from the loads above the entry stack pointer.
- Tell the independent register sequences of System V from the positional slots of Microsoft x64, and both from the NGRN and NSRN counters of AAPCS64.
- Check every inference against the source signature, the rule in the specification, and the compiler's own unwind data in `.pdata`, `.xdata`, and `.eh_frame`.
- Compare how Ghidra, IDA, Binary Ninja, radare2, rizin, and angr name and recover the same facts, and record where their output disagrees with the source.

## The Problem

You compiled `convention.c` for Linux x86-64 at `-O2` and asked radare2 6.2.4 for the arguments of `eight_args`. It answered with seven: `rdi`, `rsi`, `rdx`, `r8`, `r9`, `rsp+0x8`, and `rsp+0x10`. The C source has eight parameters. The bytes read `%rcx` exactly once, in `leaq (%rdx,%rcx), %rax`, and the tool's variable recovery did not count a register that only appears inside an address.

You then opened the Windows build of the same file in rizin 0.9.1. It reported the convention as `amd64` and found `r8`, `rcx`, `rdx`, and three stack slots. The object is COFF, so the convention is Microsoft x64, the fourth register argument is `r9`, and there are four stack slots. The two tools miss different registers in the same source.

A listing is a sequence of instructions. A calling convention is a contract that lives outside the listing: which registers carry arguments, which the callee must preserve, where the return address and the stack arguments sit, and what the caller must leave above the stack pointer. Four documents define the contracts that matter here. The System V AMD64 psABI (Version 1.0, build dated 12 March 2025) sections 3.2.1 to 3.2.3. The Microsoft x64 calling convention, stack usage, and prolog and epilog pages (page dates from 2018-12-17 to 2025-03-19). The Arm AAPCS64 release 2025Q4 (23 January 2026) sections 6.1 to 6.9. Apple's arm64 platform notes. This lesson reads those rules, applies them to one C file compiled three ways, and builds the analyzer that turns a listing into a checked list of parameter locations, saved registers, and frame offsets.

## One Header Picks the Rulebook

`convention.c` has twelve functions: `leaf_add`, `eight_args`, `mixed`, `by_value`, `big_ret`, `sum_varargs`, `keeps`, and five callers of `extern` functions with the same shapes. The structs use `long long`, because `long` is 4 bytes on the MSVC target and 8 bytes on the others, and a struct that changes size changes convention. Apple clang 17.0.0 compiled it seven times from this machine: `-target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`, `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`, and `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` at `-O0` and `-O2`, and `arm64-apple-macos` at `-O2`. No Linux or Windows headers are installed, so the file declares what it needs and includes only clang's own `stdarg.h` and `stddef.h`.

`describe_object()` in `code/main.py` reads the 4-byte magic number and one machine field and names the contract:

| Header | Field | Value | Rulebook |
|---|---|---|---|
| `7f 45 4c 46` ELF | `e_machine` at offset 0x12 | 62 | System V AMD64 psABI |
| `64 86` COFF | `Machine` at offset 0 | 0x8664 | Microsoft x64 |
| `7f 45 4c 46` ELF | `e_machine` | 183 | AAPCS64 |
| `cf fa ed fe` Mach-O 64 | `cputype` at offset 4 | 0x0100000c | AAPCS64 with Apple differences |

The three contracts disagree on almost every row of the table that follows. Every value is quoted from the document named in the header row, and every one is checked by a test against the fixtures.

| Rule | System V psABI | Microsoft x64 | AAPCS64 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Integer arguments | `%rdi %rsi %rdx %rcx %r8 %r9`, next free register | `RCX RDX R8 R9`, by position | `x0` to `x7`, by NGRN |
| Floating-point arguments | `%xmm0` to `%xmm7`, next free register | `XMM0` to `XMM3`, by position | `v0` to `v7`, by NSRN |
| Integer result | `%rax`, then `%rdx` | `RAX` | `x0`, then `x1` |
| Floating-point result | `%xmm0`, then `%xmm1` | `XMM0` | `v0` |
| Result too large for registers | address passed in `%rdi` "as if it were the first argument", returned in `%rax` | pointer in `RCX`, arguments shifted right, returned in `RAX` | address in `x8`, `x0` to `x7` untouched |
| Callee-saved | `%rbp %rbx %r12` to `%r15` | `RBX RBP RDI RSI RSP R12` to `R15`, `XMM6` to `XMM15` | `r19` to `r29`, `SP`, low 64 bits of `v8` to `v15` |
| First stack argument on entry | `8(%rsp)` | `40(%rsp)`, above a 32-byte shadow store | `0(sp)` |
| Below the stack pointer | 128-byte red zone | "considered volatile" | no red zone (Apple: 128 bytes) |
| Alignment at the call | `(%rsp + 8)` multiple of 16 on entry | 16-byte aligned outside prolog and epilog | `SP mod 16 = 0` |
| Variadic marker | `%al` holds an upper bound on vector registers used | floats duplicated in the integer register | none in registers; Apple uses 8-byte stack slots |

## System V: Two Independent Register Sequences and a Red Zone

psABI 3.2.3 classifies every eightbyte of every argument as INTEGER, SSE, or MEMORY and then assigns registers from two lists that do not interact. "INTEGER" takes "the next available register of the sequence %rdi, %rsi, %rdx, %rcx, %r8 and %r9". SSE takes `%xmm0` to `%xmm7`. "If there are no registers available for any eightbyte of an argument, the whole argument is passed on the stack", and memory arguments "are pushed on the stack in reversed (right-to-left) order".

`eight_args(a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h)` at `-O2` is 27 bytes:
```text
      10: 48 01 fe                     	addq	%rdi, %rsi
      13: 48 8d 04 0a                  	leaq	(%rdx,%rcx), %rax
      17: 48 01 f0                     	addq	%rsi, %rax
      1a: 4c 01 c0                     	addq	%r8, %rax
      1d: 4c 01 c8                     	addq	%r9, %rax
      20: 48 03 44 24 08               	addq	0x8(%rsp), %rax
      25: 48 03 44 24 10               	addq	0x10(%rsp), %rax
      2a: c3                           	retq
```
Six registers, then two loads at `8(%rsp)` and `16(%rsp)`. Figure 3.3 of the psABI puts "memory argument eightbyte 0" at `16(%rbp)` when `%rbp` is the frame base, which is `8(%rsp)` on entry before any push. `g` is at 8, `h` at 16.

`mixed(int i, double d, long long l, float f)` shows the two lists. The ints take `%edi` and `%rsi`, the first and second INTEGER registers. The double and the float take `%xmm0` and `%xmm1`, the first and second SSE registers. The first instruction is `cvtsi2sd %edi, %xmm2`, and `%xmm2` is a scratch register that the function writes before it reads. An analyzer that treats the destination of `cvtsi2sd` as a read invents a third floating-point argument. radare2 did exactly that and reported `mixed` as `(double arg1, double arg2, double arg3)` in `xmm0`, `xmm1`, `xmm2`.

`by_value(struct pair p)` passes a 16-byte struct as two INTEGER eightbytes in `%rdi` and `%rsi`, and returns it the same way: `leaq 0x1(%rdi), %rax; leaq -0x1(%rsi), %rdx; retq`. `big_ret(long long seed)` returns 32 bytes, which is class MEMORY, and the psABI says "the caller provides space for the return value and passes the address of this storage in %rdi as if it were the first argument". `seed` moves to `%rsi`, and the function starts with `movq %rdi, %rax` because "On return %rax will contain the address that has been passed in by the caller in %rdi".

The red zone is the other System V signature. psABI 3.2.2: "The 128-byte area beyond the location pointed to by %rsp is considered to be reserved and shall not be modified by signal or interrupt handlers." At `-O0`, `eight_args` is `pushq %rbp; movq %rsp, %rbp` and then six stores to `-0x8(%rbp)` through `-0x30(%rbp)` with no `subq`. The stores sit 48 bytes below the stack pointer. The `-O2` build of `sum_varargs` allocates 88 bytes with `subq $0x58, %rsp` and then writes the register save area at `-0x58(%rsp)` down to `-0x80(%rsp)`: 128 bytes below the stack pointer, the whole red zone. Build the same file with `-mno-red-zone` and `leaf_add` gains a `pushq %rax` and an `addq $0x8, %rsp` to hold its 8 bytes of locals above the stack pointer.

Variadic calls add one register. "%al is used as hidden argument to specify the number of vector registers used", an upper bound from 0 to 8. `call_varargs` sets it with `xorl %eax, %eax` at `-O2` and `movb $0x0, %al` at `-O0`. `sum_varargs` reads it first: `testb %al, %al; je` skips eight `movaps %xmmN` saves when no vector register was used.

## Microsoft x64: Positions, a Shadow Store, and No Red Zone

The Microsoft rules are positional. "Integer arguments are passed in registers RCX, RDX, R8, and R9. Floating point arguments are passed in XMM0L, XMM1L, XMM2L, and XMM3L." and "Any floating-point and double-precision arguments in the first four parameters are passed in XMM0 - XMM3, depending on position." The same `mixed` arrives as `%ecx`, `%xmm1`, `%r8`, `%xmm3`: slot 0 is an int, so `RCX`; slot 1 is a double, so `XMM1`; slot 3 is a float, so `XMM3`. `XMM0` and `XMM2` stay empty.

The caller must also leave room. "The caller must always allocate sufficient space to store four register parameters, even if the callee doesn't take that many parameters." The pages call it the shadow store or the home addresses, and the four slots are "effectively owned by the called function". On entry `0(%rsp)` is the return address, `8(%rsp)` to `39(%rsp)` are the four homes, and the first stack argument is at `40(%rsp)`. `eight_args` at `-O2` reads `0x28(%rsp)`, `0x30(%rsp)`, `0x38(%rsp)`, `0x40(%rsp)`: 40, 48, 56, 64.

The caller side shows the arithmetic. `call8` at `-O2` is `subq $0x48, %rsp` and then stores of 5, 6, 7, 8 at `0x20(%rsp)` to `0x38(%rsp)` before `movl $1, %ecx` and friends. 72 bytes is 32 for the shadow store, 32 for four stack arguments, and 8 so that the return address is on a 16-byte boundary. `call_varargs` has only register arguments and still allocates `subq $0x28, %rsp`: 32 for the shadow store and 8 for alignment. `keeps` pushes three nonvolatile registers (24 bytes) and then `subq $0x20, %rsp`, so that `ext` finds its 32-byte shadow store below the return address.

Structs follow their own rule. "Any argument that doesn't fit in 8 bytes, or isn't 1, 2, 4, or 8 bytes, must be passed by reference." and "16-byte arguments are passed by reference." `by_value` therefore receives a pointer to a copy in `%rdx`, after a hidden result pointer in `%rcx`: "the caller must allocate memory for the return value and pass a pointer to it as the first argument. The remaining arguments are then shifted one argument to the right." `call_pair` builds the copy at `0x20(%rsp)` with `movaps`, passes `leaq 0x20(%rsp), %rdx`, passes the result buffer with `leaq 0x38(%rsp), %rcx`, and reads `.b` back from `0x40(%rsp)`.

There is no red zone. "All memory beyond the current address of RSP is considered volatile: The OS, or a debugger, may overwrite this memory during a user debug session, or an interrupt handler." The `-O0` `leaf_add` needs 8 bytes of locals and gets them with `pushq %rax` at entry and `popq %rcx` before `retq`, two single-byte instructions instead of a `subq` and an `addq`. The stack-usage page defines the leaf that may do this: "A leaf function is one that does not require a function table entry. It can't make changes to any nonvolatile registers, including RSP".

Variadic callees home their registers. "For vararg or unprototyped functions, any floating point values must be duplicated in the corresponding general-purpose register." `sum_varargs` at `-O2` stores `%rdx`, `%r8`, `%r9` to `0x18(%rsp)`, `0x20(%rsp)`, `0x28(%rsp)` after one `pushq %rax`, which is entry offsets 16, 24, 32: the homes of the second, third, and fourth register parameters. Its `va_list` is `leaq 0x18(%rsp), %rax`, the home of `%rdx`, the first unnamed argument.

## AAPCS64, and What Apple Changes

AAPCS64 6.8.2 walks a list of rules with two counters. C.9: an integral argument "is copied to the least significant bits in x[NGRN]" and NGRN increments. C.1 does the same for floating-point arguments with NSRN. C.12: a composite of at most `8 - NGRN` double-words is "copied into consecutive general-purpose registers". C.13 sets "The NGRN is set to 8" once an argument goes to the stack, so nothing returns to registers afterwards. `eight_args` uses `x0` to `x7` and never touches the stack. `mixed` is `w0`, `d0`, `x1`, `s1`. `by_value` is `x0` and `x1` in and out.

6.9 says a result that would be passed in registers "is returned in the same registers", otherwise "The address of the memory block shall be passed as an additional argument to the function in x8". `big_ret` writes `str x0, [x8]`, `stur q0, [x8, #0x8]`, `str x9, [x8, #0x18]` and never writes `x0`. `call_big` sets `mov x8, sp`, and `seed` stays in `x0`, because 6.9 adds "there is no requirement for the callee to preserve the value stored in x8" and `x8` is not one of the argument registers.

6.1.1: "A subroutine invocation must preserve the contents of the registers r19-r29 and SP." 6.4.5.2: at a public interface "SP mod 16 = 0". The stack is full-descending and "No thread is permitted to access (for reading or for writing) the inactive region" below it, so the Linux `-O0` `leaf_add` emits `sub sp, sp, #0x10` for 8 bytes of locals where System V used the red zone.

6.4.6 defines the frame record: "a frame record of two 64-bit values on the stack ... The lowest addressed double-word shall point to the previous frame record and the highest addressed double-word shall contain the value passed in LR on entry to the current function." and "The location of the frame record within a stack frame is not specified." clang shows both positions in this one file. `keeps` at `-O2` on Linux puts the record at the bottom with `stp x29, x30, [sp, #-0x30]!; mov x29, sp`. The same function at `-O0` puts it at the top with `sub sp, sp, #0x20; stp x29, x30, [sp, #0x10]; add x29, sp, #0x10`.

Apple's arm64 notes keep the registers and the alignment and change the frame, the red zone, and variadic calls. "The frame pointer register (x29) must always address a valid frame record. Some functions, such as leaf functions or tail calls, may opt not to create an entry in this list." The Apple build of `keeps` saves `x22, x21, x20, x19` first and puts the record on top: `stp x29, x30, [sp, #0x20]; add x29, sp, #0x20`. "The platforms reserve register x18. Don't use this register." "The ARM64 red zone consists of the 128 bytes immediately below the stack pointer", and clang still emitted `sub sp, sp, #0x10` for the `-O0` leaf, so the compiler does not use it by default. Variadic arguments are assigned "to the appropriate number of 8-byte stack slots" and "the type va_list is an alias for char*". `call_varargs` on Apple stores 10, 20, 30 to `[sp]`, `[sp, #8]`, `[sp, #0x10]` and passes only `w0`; the Linux build passes `w1`, `w2`, `w3` and tail-calls with `b extva`. The Apple `sum_varargs` reads `add x8, sp, #0x10`, the caller's stack pointer, as its `va_list`; the Linux `sum_varargs` saves `x1` to `x7` and `q0` to `q7` into a 224-byte frame and initialises the structure fields `__gr_offs` to -56 and `__vr_offs` to -128 with one `mov x8, #-0x38; movk x8, #0xff80, lsl #32`.

Symbols differ too. Mach-O prefixes every C symbol with `_`, so the listing shows `_keeps` and the first function appears under the private label `ltmp0`. The analyzer renames labels through the symbol table.

## Decode One Prologue by Hand, Three Times

`keeps(int n)` calls `ext(i)` in a loop and keeps `n`, `i`, and `acc` across the call, so every ABI must save registers. Read the first bytes of the `-O2` build for each target.

System V, 4 bytes:

1. `55` is `push r64` with the register in the low three bits: `50 + 5`, `%rbp`. Depth 8, `%rbp` saved at entry offset -8.
2. `41 56`: `41` is REX with `B` set, `56` is `50 + 6`. REX.B extends 6 to 14: `pushq %r14` at -16.
3. `53` is `50 + 3`: `pushq %rbx` at -24.

Three pushes are 24 bytes. The return address adds 8, and 32 is a multiple of 16, so the `callq ext` inside the loop is aligned without a `subq`. There is no `movq %rsp, %rbp`, so this build has no frame pointer. The body uses `%rbp` as the callee-saved register that holds `acc` (`xorl %ebp, %ebp`, `addl %eax, %ebp`). The epilogue is the mirror: `5b 41 5e 5d c3`.

Microsoft x64, 7 bytes:

1. `56` is `pushq %rsi` at -8. `57` is `pushq %rdi` at -16. `53` is `pushq %rbx` at -24. All three are nonvolatile here, and `RDI` and `RSI` were argument registers under System V.
2. `48 83 ec 20`: REX.W, opcode `83 /5` with an 8-bit immediate, ModRM `ec` is `11 101 100`: `subq $0x20, %rsp`. Depth 56.

56 plus the return address is 64, aligned. The 32 bytes are the shadow store that `ext` is owed. The epilog page allows only "an add RSP,constant or lea RSP,constant[FPReg], followed by a series of zero or more 8-byte register pops and a return or a jmp", and the bytes are `48 83 c4 20 5b 5f 5e c3`.

AArch64, 16 bytes in four words, little-endian:

1. `a9bd7bfd` is `stp` with pre-index. Bits 31:30 `10` select 64-bit registers, bits 25:23 `011` select pre-index, bit 22 is 0 for store. imm7 at bits 21:15 is `1111010`, which is -6, scaled by 8: -48. Rt2 at 14:10 is 30, Rn at 9:5 is 31 (`sp`), Rt at 4:0 is 29. `stp x29, x30, [sp, #-0x30]!`: the stack pointer drops 48, `x29` goes to -48 and `x30` to -40.
2. `f9000bf5` is `str` with an unsigned 12-bit offset scaled by 8: imm12 at 21:10 is 2, Rn is `sp`, Rt is 21. `str x21, [sp, #0x10]`, entry offset -32.
3. `910003fd` is `add` immediate: imm12 is 0, Rn is `sp`, Rd is 29. `mov x29, sp`: the frame pointer points at the record at -48.
4. `a9024ff4` is `stp` with a signed offset: imm7 is 4, scaled to 32. Rt2 is 19, Rt is 20. `stp x20, x19, [sp, #0x20]`: `x20` at -16, `x19` at -8.

The frame is 48 bytes: `x29` at 0, `x30` at 8, `x21` at 16, 8 bytes of padding at 24, `x20` at 32, `x19` at 40. The lowest word of the record points to the previous record and the next word holds LR, as 6.4.6 requires. `cmp w0, #0x1` sits between the first and second store; the scheduler moved it into the prologue, and the analyzer tolerates a compare or an arithmetic instruction between stack operations.

## The Compiler Wrote the Same Facts Twice

A prologue parse is one derivation. The compiler emits a second one for the unwinder, and the two must agree.

On Windows the second derivation is `.pdata` and `.xdata`. Build the `-O2` object without `-fno-asynchronous-unwind-tables` and `llvm-objdump -h` shows `.xdata` of 0x34 bytes and `.pdata` of 0x48 bytes. 0x48 is 72, six `RUNTIME_FUNCTION` entries of 12 bytes with three `IMAGE_REL_AMD64_ADDR32NB` relocations each. The six are `sum_varargs`, `keeps`, `call8`, `call_varargs`, `call_pair`, and `call_big`. The other six functions are leaves, and the exception handling page says "If the search doesn't find a function table entry, the code is assumed to be part of a leaf function, and RSP directly addresses the return pointer."

The `.xdata` bytes for `keeps` are `01 07 04 00 07 32 03 30 02 70 01 60`. `UNWIND_INFO` starts with Version in 3 bits and Flags in 5 bits: version 1, no flags. SizeOfProlog is 7, CountOfCodes is 4, FrameRegister and FrameOffset are 0. Each `UNWIND_CODE` is an offset in the prolog and a byte of opcode and info. `07 32`: at offset 7, op 2 is `UWOP_ALLOC_SMALL`, info 3 means `3 * 8 + 8 = 32` bytes. `03 30`: op 0 is `UWOP_PUSH_NONVOL`, register 3 is `rbx`. `02 70`: `rdi`. `01 60`: `rsi`. The codes are stored in reverse order of execution, and they name the same three pushes and the same 32-byte allocation as the bytes `56 57 53 48 83 ec 20`. The `sum_varargs` entry is `01 01 01 00 01 02 00 00`: a 1-byte prolog with one code, `UWOP_ALLOC_SMALL` of 8 bytes. That is how the unwinder sees `pushq %rax`: an allocation, because `%rax` is volatile and nothing is being saved.

On Linux the second derivation is `.eh_frame`, which psABI 4.2.4 defines and DWARF 5 section 6.4 encodes. `llvm-dwarfdump --eh-frame` on the relocatable object prints one FDE per function and resolves the `R_X86_64_PC32` relocations, so the ranges are usable. For `keeps`:
```text
  DW_CFA_def_cfa_offset: +16
  DW_CFA_def_cfa_offset: +24
  DW_CFA_def_cfa_offset: +32
  DW_CFA_offset: RBX -32
  DW_CFA_offset: R14 -24
  DW_CFA_offset: RBP -16
```
The CFA is the stack pointer before the call, 8 above the entry stack pointer, so `RBP -16` is entry offset -8, `R14 -24` is -16, `RBX -32` is -24, and the deepest CFA offset of 32 is the 24-byte frame plus the return address. The AArch64 FDE for `keeps` says `DW_CFA_def_cfa: W29 +48` with `W29 -48`, `W30 -40`, `W21 -32`, `W20 -16`, `W19 -8`. There the CFA is the entry stack pointer itself, so the offsets are the frame offsets without conversion, and the CFA is defined from `x29` while the frame record is live. `eh_frame_cross_check()` runs this comparison for all 12 FDEs of both objects. One entry needed care: `call8` under System V pushes two outgoing arguments mid-body, so its deepest CFA offset is 32 while its prologue frame is 8, and the check compares the deepest stack pointer the body reaches, 24, plus 8.

## What the Tools Call This

Every tool in this field has a data structure for the calling convention and a pass that assigns one to a function. The names differ and the gaps differ. The closed tools are described from their documentation; the open ones were run on the fixtures and their output is captured beside the objects.

**Ghidra 12.1.4 (Apache-2.0).** The rules live in compiler specification files, `.cspec`, next to the SLEIGH language. `x86-64-gcc.cspec` declares a `<default_proto>` named `__stdcall`, "Derived from System V Application Binary Interface AMD64 Architecture Processor Supplement April 2016", with `<pentry>` lists for `XMM0_Qa` to `XMM7_Qa` and `RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9`, a stack entry at offset 8, a `join_dual_class` rule for types up to 16 bytes, outputs `XMM0_Qa, XMM1_Qa, RAX, RDX`, and `hidden_return` for the rest. `x86-64-win.cspec` declares `__fastcall` with four `<group>` elements that pair `XMM0_Qa` with `RCX`, `XMM1_Qa` with `RDX`, and so on, which is the positional rule, a stack entry at offset 40, `convert_to_ptr` for structs of 3, 5, 6, or 7 bytes with the comment "only structs of size 8,16,32,64 bits can be packed to register", `unaffected` listing `RBX RBP RDI RSI RSP R12` to `R15` and `XMM6` to `XMM15`, and a `localrange` of stack 8 to 39, which is the shadow store. `AARCH64.cspec` declares `__cdecl` whose first entry is `x8` with `storage="hiddenret"`, then `q0` to `q7` and `x0` to `x7`, `convert_to_ptr` for structs of 17 bytes or more, and `killedbycall` including `x8` with the comment "indirect result location register, which is not reflected in the pentry list". The decompiler's final stage is named "Establish Function's Prototype"; the analyzers are "Call Convention ID" and "Decompiler Parameter ID"; the program option "Prototype Evaluation" picks the default model.

**IDA Pro and IDA Free (Hex-Rays, commercial; current release 9.4, build 9.4.260714).** The function type is a C declaration set through SetType, and "IDA will use the type information to comment the disassembly with the information about function arguments." Locations that no standard convention produces are written in IDA's own convention: `int __usercall func@<ebx>(int x, int y@<esi>)` puts the result in `EBX` and `y` in `ESI`, and `@<^12.4>` names a stack location by offset and size. `__userpurge` is the same with callee stack cleanup. The same page lists `__spoils` for the clobbered set, `__hidden`, `__return_ptr`, and `__struct_ptr` for the implicit arguments this lesson recovers by hand. The decompiler's "Decompile as call" action accepts a `__usercall` prototype for one instruction. IDA Free supports x86 and x86-64 only.

**Binary Ninja 6.0 "Krypton" (Vector 35, commercial, with a Free edition that decompiles x86, x86_64, ARMv7, and AArch64).** A `Platform` "contains all information related to the execution environment of the binary, mainly the calling conventions used, the operating system, and the architecture", and the list includes `linux-x86_64`, `windows-x86_64`, `linux-aarch64`, and `mac-aarch64`, each with a `default_calling_convention`. A `CallingConvention` has `int_arg_regs`, `float_arg_regs`, `callee_saved_regs`, `caller_saved_regs`, `int_return_reg`, `high_int_return_reg`, `float_return_reg`, and two flags that encode the differences in this lesson directly: `arg_regs_share_index`, "When True, the Nth argument consumes the Nth slot of both the integer and float register lists regardless of its type", and `stack_reserved_for_arg_regs`, "the shadow/home space used by the Windows x64 calling convention". `eligible_for_heuristics`, `required_arg_regs`, and `required_clobbered_regs` drive its heuristic convention detection. Platform types are C headers under `types/platform/`, one per platform name.

**radare2 6.2.4 (LGPL-3.0, run here).** `afcl` lists the conventions the architecture plugin knows: `amd64 amd64syscall dlang golang golang_abi0 ms p9 reg swift` for x86-64 and `arm64 dlang golang p9 reg swift` for AArch64. `afc` reports the convention of the current function, `afcr` prints `cc.amd64.arg0: rdi` through `arg5: r9` and `ret0: rax`, and the profiles are SDB files named `cc-ARCH-BITS.sdb`. radare2 picked `amd64` for the ELF object and `ms` for the COFF object, which is the correct split. `afv` lists arguments and variables, and `afs` prints a signature. On the Linux `-O2` object `afv` found seven arguments for `eight_args` and dropped `rcx`; on the Windows object it found `rcx, rdx, r8` and four stack slots and dropped `r9`. Both missing registers appear only inside a `lea`. On `mixed` it reported `double arg1 @ xmm0, arg2 @ xmm1, arg3 @ xmm2` on Linux and no arguments at all on Windows. On AArch64 it found `x0` to `x7` for `eight_args`, and for `big_ret` it listed `x0` and `double arg2 @ d1` where the function reads `x8` and loads a constant into `q1`. Every `afs` signature starts with `void`, because the return type is not inferred. At `-O0`, where every argument is stored to the frame, `afv` found all eight arguments of `eight_args` with `rbp+0x10` and `rbp+0x18` for the stack pair.

**rizin 0.9.1 (LGPL-3.0, run here) and Cutter 2.5.0.** `afcl` lists `amd64 amd64syscall ms reg swift`. `afc` returned `amd64` for the COFF object, so the Microsoft profile exists and was not selected from the format. `afi` listed seven arguments for `eight_args` on Linux, again without `rcx`, and on Windows `r8, rcx, rdx` with three stack slots, without `r9` and without the slot at `0x40`. `afv` does not exist; the listing command is `afvl`. Cutter is the graphical front end over rizin.

**angr 10.0.3 (BSD-2, run here).** `CFGFast` followed by `CompleteCallingConventions(recover_variables=True)` sets `function.calling_convention` to `SimCCSystemVAMD64`, `SimCCMicrosoftAMD64`, or `SimCCAArch64`, by binary format, and `function.prototype` to a signature. It recovered all eight arguments of `eight_args` on all three targets, the hidden pointer of `big_ret` on x86-64 as `(BOT*, long long) -> BOT*`, the by-reference struct of the Windows `by_value` as `(BOT*, BOT*) -> BOT*`, and the System V variadic `sum_varargs` as `(long long, ...)`. Its gaps are different from radare2's: `mixed` came back as `(long long, long long, double, float)` on System V and AArch64, the right registers in the wrong order, because the integer list is printed before the float list; the AArch64 `big_ret` came back as `(long long) -> double`, so the `x8` convention was missed and the vector stores were read as a result; and the AArch64 `sum_varargs` came back with 16 parameters, the whole register save area.

**Others.** Hopper 6.6.0 is a commercial disassembler and decompiler for macOS and Linux; its convention handling was not run or documented for this lesson. lldb 1703 and gdb show the live frame with `frame info` and `register read`, which is lesson 42's dynamic view of the same offsets. Compiler Explorer shows the three listings side by side from source, which is the fastest way to confirm a rule before you look for it in bytes.

## Build It

Run the demo:
```bash
cd phases/13-tools-and-protocols/38-calling-conventions-and-stack-frames
python3 code/main.py
```
The output is one JSON report. For each of the seven objects it names the format, the machine, and the ABI, and for each of the twelve functions it gives the prologue bytes, the saved registers with entry offsets, the frame size, the frame pointer, the parameter registers, the stack argument offsets, the spills, the return register or hidden pointer, the call depths, and the outgoing registers and stores of the callers. Every function ends with its checks: the rule, the expected value from the signature, the observed value from the bytes, and whether they agree. The report ends with the two unwind cross-checks and the tool captures. Across the 84 function analyses, 489 checks run and all 489 agree.

Expected shape:
```json
{
  "objects": {
    "convention-x86_64-windows-O2": {
      "format": "COFF", "machine": "AMD64", "abi": "Microsoft x64", "checks": "73/73 agree",
      "functions": {
        "keeps": {
          "prologue": ["56  pushq %rsi", "57  pushq %rdi", "53  pushq %rbx", "48 83 ec 20  subq $0x20, %rsp"],
          "frameBytes": 56,
          "savedRegisters": [{"register": "rsi", "entryOffset": -8}, {"register": "rdi", "entryOffset": -16}, {"register": "rbx", "entryOffset": -24}],
          "parameterRegisters": ["rcx"],
          "returnRegisters": ["rax"],
          "calls": [{"callee": "ext", "depth": 56}],
          "checks": [{"rule": "Microsoft x64: the caller must always allocate ...", "expected": "at least 32 bytes ...", "observed": [56], "agree": true}, "..."]
        }
      }
    }
  },
  "sehCrossCheck": ["..."],
  "ehFrameCrossCheck": {"...": "..."}
}
```
Read `code/main.py` in this order:

1. `describe_object()` reads the ELF, COFF, or Mach-O header and the symbol table and returns the ABI and the function list.
2. `parse_listing()` splits the `llvm-objdump -d -r` text into functions, keeps the relocation target of every call and jump, and strips comments with the marker of the right syntax: `#` for AT&T, `//` and `;` for AArch64, where `#` introduces an immediate.
3. `effect_x86()` and `effect_arm()` turn one instruction into reads, address reads, writes, loads, stores, and a stack pointer delta. The last AT&T operand is the destination; the first AArch64 operand is the destination except in stores, compares, and branches. `lea` reads an address and loads nothing. The destination of `mov`, `cvtsi2sd`, `setcc`, and the zero idiom `xor r, r` is a write only. A call writes the whole volatile set. A pre-indexed store moves `sp` before the access and a post-indexed load moves it after.
4. `analyze_function()` walks the body once up to the first `ret` or tail jump. It tracks the depth of the stack pointer below its entry value, so a memory operand `disp(%rsp)` is at entry offset `disp - depth` and `disp(%rbp)` is at `frame_pointer + disp`. It records argument-class registers that are read before they are written, loads at or above the first stack argument offset of the ABI, stores of argument registers into the frame, accesses below the current stack pointer, and the depth at every call.
5. `_return_registers()` keeps a result register when its last access before the exit is a write. A read as a data operand kills the candidate; a read as an address base does not, which is what keeps `rax` alive in `big_ret` under Microsoft x64, where `movq %rcx, %rax` is followed by stores through `(%rax)`.
6. `expected_locations()` applies the three rulebooks to a C signature: the two System V lists with eightbyte classes, the Microsoft positional slots with by-reference structs, and the AAPCS64 counters with `x8` for results above 16 bytes.
7. `run_checks()` compares the two and adds the frame rules: callee-saved registers written must be saved, `(rsp + 8) % 16 == 0` or `sp % 16 == 0` at every call, 32 bytes of shadow at every Microsoft call, no access below the stack pointer under Microsoft and AAPCS64 and at most 128 bytes under System V, and an epilogue that mirrors the prologue with the stack pointer back at its entry value.
8. `seh_cross_check()` and `eh_frame_cross_check()` read the unwind data of the objects built without `-fno-asynchronous-unwind-tables` and compare it with the prologue parse.

Three more commands exist. `python3 code/main.py analyze convention-x86_64-windows-O2 keeps` prints one function. `python3 code/main.py object FILE` prints the header's verdict. `python3 code/main.py seh` prints the decoded `UNWIND_INFO` of every function that has one.

## Use It

Use the analyzer in this order on a new object you built.

1. Run `python3 code/main.py object FILE.o` and write down the ABI it names. If the header and your build command disagree, stop; one of them is wrong.
2. Capture `llvm-objdump -d -r FILE.o` next to the object and run the analysis. Read the prologue bytes and the saved registers before anything else, and compare the frame size with the pushes and the `sub`.
3. Read the parameter registers and the stack offsets against your source signature. A register that the signature does not explain is a hidden pointer, a variadic marker, or a scratch register that the analyzer mistook for an argument. The last case is a bug in the effect table. Fix it with a general rule for that instruction.
4. Read the checks that disagree, if any. Each names the rule it rests on, so the first thing to check is the rule, then the bytes, then the analyzer.
5. When the object has unwind data, run the cross-check. Two derivations that agree are the strongest evidence this lesson produces.
6. When another tool is installed, capture its output with the exact command and compare. Where it agrees you have three derivations. Where it differs you have a specific register and a specific instruction to look at, and that is a finding for lesson 35.

## Production Failure Modes

| Failure | What the weak tool reports | What the analysis must prove |
|---|---|---|
| COFF object read as System V | `rdi` and `rsi` as arguments that the function never reads | The header says 0x8664; the convention is Microsoft x64 |
| Register read only inside a `lea` | Seven arguments for an eight-argument function | Base and index registers are reads |
| `cvtsi2sd` destination counted as a read | A third double argument in `xmm2` | The first write to `xmm2` is a write; `mixed` has two SSE arguments |
| Positional slots read as sequences | `xmm0` named as the double argument on Windows | Slot 1 is `XMM1`, slot 3 is `XMM3` |
| `push rbp` taken as a frame pointer | A frame pointer in an `-O2` function that uses `rbp` as an accumulator | Only `mov %rsp, %rbp` after the push creates one |
| Red zone measured from the entry stack pointer | 216 bytes "below the stack pointer" | 128 bytes below the current stack pointer after an 88-byte `sub` |
| Shadow store treated as locals | Stack arguments at 8 to 32 | Microsoft stack arguments start at 40 |
| `lea` treated as a load | A stack argument at `0x60(%rsp)` in a variadic callee | `lea` computes `overflow_arg_area`; it loads nothing |
| Hidden pointer read as a normal argument | `big_ret(void *, long long)` | The pointer is stored through and copied to `rax`, `rax`, or stays in `x8` |
| Deepest CFA compared with the prologue frame | A mismatch on a caller that pushes outgoing arguments | Compare with the deepest stack pointer the body reaches |
| Convention asserted from the ISA | `amd64` for a COFF object | The format picks the rulebook, then the ISA picks the registers |
| Prototype trusted from one tool | Three doubles, or sixteen variadic parameters | The source signature or a second derivation must agree |

## Operational Rule

Read the header before the first instruction, and name the rulebook. Place every saved register and every argument at an offset from the entry stack pointer, and check it against the rule that put it there and against the unwind data the compiler wrote for the same frame. Treat a tool's prototype as a claim until the bytes or the source confirm it.
