courses.blurb: How software actually ships, runs, and survives in production — the delivery pipeline, the release, the signals you watch, and what you do when it breaks.

chapters.title: Containers & delivery
chapters.summary: How code gets from a commit to a running artifact — pipelines, containers, orchestration, and reproducible infrastructure.

lessons.title: CI/CD: the pipeline from commit to prod
lessons.body:
Continuous Integration (CI) and Continuous Delivery/Deployment (CD) turn "it works on my machine" into "it works, verifiably, every time we merge."

**CI** means every push is automatically built and tested against the shared mainline. The point is to catch integration problems within minutes of introducing them, while the change is still small and fresh in your head — not weeks later during a painful merge.

**CD** is the extension: an artifact that passes CI is automatically prepared for release. *Continuous Delivery* keeps a deployable build ready at all times and ships on a button press; *Continuous Deployment* removes the button and ships every green build to production automatically.

A typical pipeline runs stages in order, and a failure at any stage stops the line:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev
    participant CI as CI runner
    participant Reg as Artifact registry
    participant Prod
    Dev->>CI: push commit
    CI->>CI: build + unit tests
    CI->>CI: lint + integration tests
    CI->>Reg: publish versioned artifact
    Reg->>Prod: deploy (auto or gated)
```

Principles that make it work: keep the pipeline **fast** (developers won't wait 40 minutes), keep it **trustworthy** (a red build must mean a real problem, or people start ignoring it), and make every build produce **one immutable, versioned artifact** that is promoted unchanged through environments — you test the exact thing you ship.

```recall
Q: Why is catching integration problems within minutes the point of CI?
A: The change is still small and fresh in the author's head, so it is cheap to fix. Catching it weeks later forces a painful merge after many changes have piled on top.
Q: What distinguishes Continuous Delivery from Continuous Deployment?
A: Continuous Delivery keeps a deployable build ready and ships on a button press; Continuous Deployment removes the button and ships every green build to production automatically.
Q: Why must a red build mean a real problem?
A: If red builds are often false alarms, people start ignoring them and a genuine failure slips through. A trustworthy pipeline is one whose red state always warrants stopping.
Q: Why promote one immutable versioned artifact unchanged through environments?
A: So you test the exact thing you ship. Rebuilding per environment risks differences, whereas promoting the identical artifact guarantees prod runs what passed the tests.
```

lessons.title: Docker: packaging the runtime
lessons.body:
A container packages your application **together with everything it needs to run** — libraries, runtime, system tools — into one image. That image runs identically on a laptop, in CI, and in production, which is what kills "works on my machine."

The mental model: an **image** is a read-only, layered blueprint built from a `Dockerfile`; a **container** is a running instance of that image. Layers are cached and shared, so two images built on the same base share those bytes.

```steps
Dockerfile | Write the layered recipe: base image, dependencies, your app
Build | Build the read-only image; each instruction becomes a cached, shareable layer
Push | Store the versioned image in a registry
Run | Start a container, a running instance of that image, on any host
Dispose | Treat the container as throwaway; the next deploy replaces it
```

Containers are **not** virtual machines. A VM ships a whole guest OS and boots in seconds-to-minutes; a container shares the host kernel and starts in milliseconds, using isolation primitives (namespaces, cgroups) rather than hardware virtualization. That lightness is why you can pack many containers on one host and start them on demand.

Two habits that matter in practice:

- **Small images**: start from a slim base, copy only what you need, and use multi-stage builds so compilers and build tools don't ship to production.
- **Immutable and stateless**: treat a container as disposable. State (files, sessions) belongs in a database or object store, not inside the container's writable layer — because the next deploy throws that container away.

```recall
Q: How does a container differ from a virtual machine?
A: A VM ships a whole guest OS and boots in seconds to minutes. A container shares the host kernel and uses namespaces and cgroups for isolation, starting in milliseconds, so many pack onto one host.
Q: Why does containerizing an app kill "works on my machine"?
A: The image bundles the app with its libraries, runtime, and system tools, so the same image runs identically on a laptop, in CI, and in production rather than depending on each host's setup.
Q: Why use a slim base and multi-stage builds?
A: To keep images small. A slim base and multi-stage builds leave compilers and build tools out of the final image, so they do not ship to production, shrinking size and attack surface.
Q: Why must container state live in a database or object store?
A: Containers are disposable and the next deploy throws the current one away along with its writable layer. State kept inside would be lost, so it belongs in external durable storage.
```

lessons.title: Kubernetes and Helm: running containers at scale
lessons.body:
One container is easy. Hundreds of containers across many machines — restarted when they crash, rescheduled when a node dies, load-balanced, rolled out gradually — is what **Kubernetes (k8s)** manages.

The core idea is **declarative desired state**. You don't tell Kubernetes "start this container here." You declare "I want 5 replicas of this image," and a control loop continuously works to make reality match. A crashed pod is replaced; a dead node's pods are rescheduled elsewhere. You describe the *what*; the system owns the *how*.

```flow
dir: LR
you: You | actor
desired: Desired state, 5 replicas | store
loop: Control loop | gate
pods: Running pods | store
svc: Service, stable IP | store
you -> desired : declare
desired -> loop : reconcile
loop -> pods : create or reschedule
pods -> loop : report actual state
loop -> pods : replace crashed pod
svc -> pods : route to healthy pods
```

Objects you'll name in an interview:

- **Pod** — the smallest unit; one (or a few tightly-coupled) containers sharing a network address.
- **Deployment** — declares how many replicas of a pod to keep running and manages rollouts/rollbacks.
- **Service** — a stable virtual IP / DNS name in front of a changing set of pods, so callers don't chase individual pod addresses.
- **ConfigMap / Secret** — configuration and credentials injected at runtime, kept out of the image.

**Helm** is the package manager on top. A **chart** is a templated, versioned bundle of these manifests with values you fill in per environment — so "deploy the payments service to staging with 3 replicas" is one command against one chart, not a folder of hand-edited YAML. It gives you versioned, repeatable, parameterized deploys and a clean rollback to a previous release.

```recall
Q: What does "declarative desired state" mean in Kubernetes?
A: You declare the end state you want, such as 5 replicas of an image, and a control loop continuously works to make reality match, replacing crashed pods and rescheduling those on dead nodes.
Q: Why does a Service exist in front of pods?
A: Pods come and go and their addresses change. A Service is a stable virtual IP and DNS name in front of the changing set, so callers do not have to chase individual pod addresses.
Q: What does a Deployment manage that a bare Pod does not?
A: A Deployment declares how many replicas to keep running and manages rollouts and rollbacks, whereas a Pod is just the smallest run unit with no self-healing replica count of its own.
Q: What does Helm add on top of raw manifests?
A: A chart is a templated, versioned bundle of manifests with per-environment values, giving one-command parameterized deploys and clean rollback instead of hand-edited YAML.
```

lessons.title: Infrastructure as Code and Terraform
lessons.body:
Infrastructure as Code (IaC) means your servers, networks, databases, and DNS are defined in **version-controlled files**, not clicked into existence in a console. The payoff: infrastructure becomes reviewable, repeatable, and recoverable. You can stand up an identical environment from scratch, diff a proposed change before it happens, and roll back by reverting a commit.

**Terraform** is the common declarative tool. You describe the desired end state; Terraform figures out the create/update/delete actions to reach it:

- **`terraform plan`** shows exactly what will change before anything happens — the single most valuable habit, because it turns "hope this works" into a reviewable diff.
- **`terraform apply`** executes that plan.
- **State file** — Terraform records what it currently manages so it knows the delta next time. This state is shared and must live in a locked remote backend (not on one laptop), or two engineers applying at once will corrupt it.

```steps
Write | Describe the desired end state in version-controlled config files
Plan | Run terraform plan to see the exact create, update, delete diff before anything happens
Review | Treat the plan as a reviewable diff and approve it like code
Apply | Run terraform apply to execute the planned changes
Record state | Terraform updates the locked remote state so it knows the delta next time
```

Two disciplines separate mature IaC from a mess: prefer **immutable infrastructure** (replace servers rather than mutating them in place, so drift can't accumulate) and never make **out-of-band manual changes** — a console edit that Terraform doesn't know about causes confusing "drift" the next plan tries to undo.

```recall
Q: Why is terraform plan called the single most valuable habit?
A: It shows exactly what will create, update, or delete before anything happens, turning "hope this works" into a reviewable diff you can approve like code.
Q: Why must the state file live in a locked remote backend?
A: State records what Terraform currently manages so it can compute the delta. If it sits on one laptop, two engineers applying at once corrupt it, so a shared locked backend serializes changes.
Q: What problem do out-of-band manual changes cause?
A: A console edit Terraform does not know about creates drift. The next plan sees a mismatch and tries to undo the manual change, producing confusing and unwanted diffs.
Q: Why prefer immutable infrastructure over mutating servers in place?
A: Replacing servers rather than editing them stops configuration drift from accumulating, so every instance matches its declared definition and environments stay reproducible.
```

chapters.title: Deployment & release
chapters.summary: Getting a new version into production safely — release strategies, flags, health signals, scaling, and schema changes.

lessons.title: Deploy strategies and rollbacks
lessons.body:
A deploy is a moment of risk: the new version might be broken in a way tests missed. Deployment strategies exist to **shrink the blast radius** and make going back easy.

- **Rolling** — replace instances a few at a time. Old and new run side by side during the transition; no extra fleet needed. Simple and common, but rollback is slow (you have to roll *back* the same way), and both versions serve traffic at once.
- **Blue-green** — stand up a full second environment (green) alongside the live one (blue), test it, then flip all traffic at once. Rollback is instant — flip back. The cost is running two full environments during the cutover.
- **Canary** — release to a small slice of traffic (say 1%), watch the metrics, and only widen if it's healthy. This catches problems real tests can't, with minimal user impact.

A canary with an automated health gate:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant CD as Deploy system
    participant Canary as Canary (1%)
    participant Mon as Monitoring
    participant Fleet as Full fleet
    CD->>Canary: route 1% of traffic to new version
    Canary->>Mon: error rate, latency
    Mon-->>CD: within thresholds?
    CD->>Fleet: promote to 100%
    Note over CD,Fleet: if unhealthy: auto-rollback
```

**Rollback** is the safety net under all of this. The rule: you should always be able to get back to the last known-good version *fast* and without thinking. This is far easier when releases are **immutable versioned artifacts** (roll back = redeploy the previous artifact) and when database changes are **backward compatible** — a schema the old code can't read makes rollback impossible.

```recall
Q: Why is blue-green rollback faster than rolling rollback?
A: Blue-green keeps the previous full environment live, so rollback is a single traffic flip. Rolling must replace instances a few at a time in reverse, so going back is as slow as the original deploy.
Q: What does a canary catch that pre-prod tests cannot?
A: Problems that only show up under real production traffic and data. A small slice is exposed while metrics are watched, so a bad version is caught with minimal user impact before it is widened.
Q: Why do immutable versioned artifacts make rollback safe?
A: Rolling back is just redeploying the previous known-good artifact unchanged, instead of trying to reverse mutations in place, so you return to a state you have already run.
Q: How can a database change make rollback impossible?
A: If the schema changes so the old code can no longer read it, flipping back to the old version breaks. That is why schema changes must stay backward compatible during a deploy.
```

lessons.title: Feature flags: decoupling deploy from release
lessons.body:
A feature flag is a runtime switch that decides whether a piece of behaviour is active — without a redeploy. Its deepest value is **separating deployment from release**: you can ship code to production with the feature turned off, then turn it on for users when you (or product) choose. Deploy becomes a low-risk technical event; release becomes a business decision.

```flow
dir: LR
deploy: Deploy code, flag off | step
prod: In production, dark | store
flag: Feature flag | gate
on: Release to users | step
kill: Flip off, kill switch | gate
deploy -> prod : ship
prod -> flag : evaluated at runtime
flag -> on : turn on, 1% to 100%
on -> kill : misbehaves
kill -> prod : feature dark again
```

What that unlocks:

- **Progressive rollout** — enable a feature for 1% → 10% → 100% of users, or for internal staff first, watching metrics as you widen.
- **A kill switch** — if a new feature misbehaves, flip it off in seconds instead of rushing an emergency rollback.
- **Trunk-based development** — merge incomplete work behind an off flag, avoiding long-lived branches and painful merges.

The discipline flags demand: they are **temporary debt**. Every flag is a branch in your code and a state to test. Remove a flag once its feature is fully rolled out and stable, or you accumulate a maze of dead conditionals and combinatorial test paths that nobody dares delete.

```recall
Q: What is the core thing a feature flag decouples, and why does it matter?
A: It decouples deployment from release. Code can ship to production turned off, so deploy is a low-risk technical event while turning the feature on becomes a business decision made when ready.
Q: Why is a kill switch preferable to an emergency rollback?
A: Flipping a flag off disables the bad behavior in seconds without a redeploy, whereas an emergency rollback is slower and riskier under pressure.
Q: How do flags enable trunk-based development?
A: Incomplete work can be merged behind an off flag, so there are no long-lived branches and the painful merges they cause are avoided.
Q: Why are flags described as temporary debt?
A: Each flag is a branch in the code and extra state to test, multiplying combinatorial test paths. Left in after rollout they become dead conditionals nobody dares delete, so they must be removed once stable.
```

lessons.title: Health checks: liveness and readiness
lessons.body:
An orchestrator and a load balancer need to know two *different* things about your instance, and conflating them causes outages.

- **Liveness** — "is this process alive, or is it wedged and needs a restart?" A failing liveness check tells Kubernetes to **kill and restart** the container. Use it for unrecoverable states like a deadlock.
- **Readiness** — "is this instance ready to *serve traffic right now*?" A failing readiness check tells the system to **stop sending requests** to this instance, but leave it running. Use it during startup (still loading a cache, warming a connection pool) or when a dependency is temporarily unavailable.

Why the distinction matters:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant K8s as Orchestrator
    participant Pod
    participant LB as Load balancer
    K8s->>Pod: readiness probe
    Pod-->>K8s: 503 — still warming up
    K8s->>LB: keep this pod OUT of rotation
    Pod->>Pod: finishes warming
    K8s->>Pod: readiness probe
    Pod-->>K8s: 200 OK
    K8s->>LB: add pod to rotation
```

The classic mistake is using a liveness probe that checks a downstream dependency: when that dependency has a blip, *every* instance fails liveness, gets **restarted at once**, and you turn a small dependency hiccup into a full self-inflicted outage. Liveness = "am I healthy?"; readiness = "can I serve *right now*?"

```recall
Q: Why should a liveness probe not check a downstream dependency?
A: A blip in that dependency fails liveness on every instance at once, so the orchestrator restarts the whole fleet simultaneously and turns a small hiccup into a self-inflicted outage.
Q: An instance is still warming its cache. Which probe should fail, and what happens?
A: Readiness should fail. The load balancer takes the pod out of rotation but leaves it running, so no traffic is sent until it reports ready.
Q: What goes wrong if you only have a liveness probe and no readiness probe?
A: Traffic is routed to instances that are up but not yet able to serve, so users hit errors during startup or while a dependency is temporarily unavailable.
Q: When is killing and restarting the container the right response?
A: For unrecoverable states like a deadlock, where the process is wedged and only a restart recovers it. That is what liveness is for.
```

lessons.title: Autoscaling: horizontal vs vertical
lessons.body:
Load isn't constant, so capacity shouldn't be either. Autoscaling adjusts resources to match demand — saving money at the trough and preventing meltdown at the peak.

Two axes:

- **Vertical scaling (scale up)** — give one instance more CPU/RAM. Simple, no distribution needed, but bounded by the biggest machine you can buy, and resizing usually means downtime or a restart.
- **Horizontal scaling (scale out)** — add more instances behind a load balancer. This is the cloud-native default: near-limitless headroom and fault tolerance (one instance dies, others carry on). The requirement it imposes is that instances be **stateless**, so any request can hit any instance.

**Horizontal autoscaling** watches a signal — CPU, request rate, queue depth — and adds or removes instances to keep it near a target.

```flow
dir: LR
signal: Watch signal | store
target: Compare to target | gate
up: Add instances | step
down: Remove instances | step
warm: Warm-up time | gate
lb: Load balancer | store
signal -> target : CPU, queue depth
target -> up : above target
target -> down : below target
up -> warm : wait to be ready
warm -> lb : join rotation
down -> lb : leave rotation
``` Two cautions: scale on the metric that actually reflects *your* bottleneck (a queue-backed worker should scale on queue depth, not CPU), and account for **warm-up time** — if a new instance takes 90 seconds to be ready, you must scale *ahead* of the load, not after it has already arrived.

```recall
Q: Why is horizontal scaling the cloud-native default over vertical?
A: It offers near-limitless headroom and fault tolerance, since one instance dying leaves others serving. Vertical scaling is bounded by the biggest machine and usually needs downtime to resize.
Q: What requirement does horizontal scaling impose on instances?
A: They must be stateless, so any request can hit any instance behind the load balancer. State kept in one instance would break when requests are spread across many.
Q: Why should a queue-backed worker scale on queue depth, not CPU?
A: You must scale on the metric that reflects the real bottleneck. A worker can be backlogged with a deep queue while CPU looks fine, so CPU would miss the overload.
Q: Why account for warm-up time when autoscaling?
A: If a new instance takes, say, 90 seconds to be ready, scaling only after load arrives leaves you overwhelmed during warm-up. You must scale ahead of the load.
```

lessons.title: Serverless: cold starts and limits
lessons.body:
Serverless (AWS Lambda and friends) runs your code without you managing servers: you deploy a function, the platform spins up an execution environment on demand, runs it, and scales instances up and down with traffic — to zero when idle. You pay per invocation, not for idle capacity.

The signature trade-off is the **cold start**. When a request arrives and no warm environment is waiting, the platform must create one — download your code, start the runtime, initialize — before your function even begins. That added latency (tens of milliseconds to seconds, worst on heavy runtimes and large dependencies) hits the *first* request to a new instance. Once warm, the environment is reused for a while, so subsequent requests are fast. Mitigations: keep the deployment package small, keep expensive setup outside the handler, and use provisioned/warm concurrency for latency-sensitive paths.

```steps
Request arrives | No warm environment is waiting, so the platform must build one
Download code | Fetch your deployment package into a fresh execution environment
Start runtime | Boot the language runtime, worse on heavy runtimes and large dependencies
Initialize | Run module-level setup before the handler, then invoke your function
Reuse warm | The environment is kept for a while, so later requests skip all of the above
```

The other reality is **limits**. Serverless functions are meant to be small and short: there are caps on execution time, memory, package size, and payload size, and each invocation is stateless (nothing persists between calls — state goes to a database or cache). Serverless shines for spiky, event-driven, bursty workloads; it fits long-running, stateful, or steady-high-throughput work far less well.

```recall
Q: Why does a cold start hit only the first request to a new instance?
A: The platform must build an execution environment (download code, start the runtime, initialize) only when none is warm. Once warm, it is reused for subsequent requests, so they skip that work.
Q: Why keep expensive setup outside the handler?
A: Code outside the handler runs once during initialization and is reused across invocations on a warm environment, so the setup cost is not paid on every request.
Q: When is serverless a poor fit?
A: For long-running, stateful, or steady high-throughput workloads. Execution-time, memory, and payload caps plus statelessness fight those, and steady load loses the pay-per-use benefit.
Q: Why must each invocation be treated as stateless?
A: Nothing persists between calls and environments are created and destroyed on demand, so any state must live in a database or cache, not in process memory.
```

lessons.title: Database migrations and scheduled jobs
lessons.body:
Two operational tasks that quietly cause outages when done naively.

**Database migrations and schema versioning.** Your schema evolves — new columns, new tables, changed types — and those changes must be **versioned, ordered, and repeatable**, exactly like code. Migration tools apply numbered scripts in sequence and track which have run, so every environment converges to the same schema.

The hard part is applying a migration to a live system without downtime, especially since a deploy may need to **roll back**. The rule is **expand, then contract**:

1. **Expand** — make an additive, backward-compatible change (add the new column). Old and new code both still work.
2. **Migrate** — deploy code that writes to both old and new, backfill data.
3. **Contract** — only after the new code is stable everywhere, remove the old column.

A destructive change in one step (rename or drop a column the running code still uses) breaks either the old version during rollout or the new version on rollback.

```steps
Expand | Make an additive, backward-compatible change like adding the new column; old and new code both work
Dual-write | Deploy code that writes to both old and new locations
Backfill | Copy existing data into the new column so it is complete
Verify | Confirm the new code is stable everywhere before removing anything
Contract | Only now remove the old column, since no running code depends on it
```

**Cron jobs / scheduled tasks.** Recurring work — nightly reports, cleanup, billing runs — needs three properties people forget: **idempotency** (a job that runs twice, because of a retry or overlap, must not double-charge or double-send), **monitoring** (a silent cron that stops firing is invisible until something downstream is missing — alert on *absence* of the expected run), and **overlap handling** (decide what happens if a run starts before the previous one finished).

```recall
Q: Why does a one-step rename or drop break a zero-downtime deploy?
A: During rollout old and new code run together, and a rollback may revert to the old code. A destructive change breaks whichever version still expects the removed column, so it must be split into expand then contract.
Q: Why must the contract step wait until the new code is stable everywhere?
A: Removing the old column while any running code or a possible rollback still reads it would break that code. Waiting until the new code is stable removes the last dependency on the old column.
Q: Why must a cron job be idempotent?
A: Retries or overlapping runs can execute it more than once. Without idempotency that could double-charge or double-send, so running twice must produce the same result as running once.
Q: Why alert on the absence of a scheduled run?
A: A silent cron that stops firing is invisible until something downstream is missing. Alerting on a missing expected run catches the failure before the gap causes damage.
```

chapters.title: Observability & reliability
chapters.summary: Knowing what your system is doing and whether it is meeting its promises — signals, tracing, alerting, and the SLO framework.

lessons.title: Metrics, logs, and the three pillars
lessons.body:
You cannot operate what you cannot see. **Observability** is the property of being able to ask *new* questions about your system's behaviour from the outside, without shipping new code to answer them. It rests on three complementary signals — the "three pillars."

- **Metrics** — numeric measurements aggregated over time: request rate, error rate, latency, CPU, queue depth. Cheap to store, ideal for dashboards and alerts, and they answer *"is something wrong, and how bad?"* But they're aggregates — they lose per-request detail.
- **Logs** — timestamped records of discrete events, ideally **structured** (JSON with fields, not free-text) so you can search and filter them. They answer *"what exactly happened for this request/user?"* Powerful but voluminous and costly at scale, so sample and set retention deliberately.
- **Traces** — the path of a single request across services (next lesson). They answer *"where did the time go / where did it fail?"*

```flow
dir: LR
sys: System behaviour | store
metrics: Metrics | store
logs: Logs | store
traces: Traces | store
what: Is something wrong | gate
why: What happened here | gate
where: Where did it fail | gate
sys -> metrics : aggregate numbers
sys -> logs : discrete events
sys -> traces : request path
metrics -> what : how bad
logs -> why : per-request detail
traces -> where : slow or failing hop
```

The distinction that matters: **monitoring** is watching known signals for known failure modes (dashboards, thresholds); **observability** is having enough rich, correlated data to debug problems you *didn't* anticipate. Metrics tell you the *what*; logs and traces let you find the *why*. A useful default is Google's "Four Golden Signals" to instrument first: **latency, traffic, errors, and saturation**.

```recall
Q: What distinguishes observability from monitoring?
A: Monitoring watches known signals for known failure modes via dashboards and thresholds. Observability means having rich correlated data to ask new questions and debug problems you did not anticipate, without shipping new code.
Q: When do you reach for logs instead of metrics?
A: When you need per-request detail: exactly what happened for one request or user. Metrics are aggregates and lose that detail, so they tell you something is wrong but not the specifics.
Q: Why sample logs and set retention deliberately?
A: Logs are voluminous and costly at scale, so keeping everything forever is expensive. Sampling and deliberate retention control cost while preserving enough detail to debug.
Q: Which question does each pillar answer?
A: Metrics answer whether something is wrong and how bad; logs answer what exactly happened for a request; traces answer where across services the time went or the failure occurred.
```

lessons.title: Distributed tracing
lessons.body:
In a monolith, a slow request is one stack trace. In a system of many services, a single user action fans out into a chain of internal calls, and "the checkout is slow" could be any hop. **Distributed tracing** reconstructs that chain.

The mechanism: when a request enters the system it's assigned a **trace id**; every service it touches records a **span** (its own slice of work, with start/end time) tagged with that trace id and its parent span. Propagating the trace id across every service call is what lets you stitch the spans back into one timeline.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Gateway
    participant Orders
    participant Payments
    participant DB
    Gateway->>Orders: request (trace-id abc)
    Orders->>Payments: charge (trace-id abc)
    Payments->>DB: write (trace-id abc)
    DB-->>Payments: ok
    Payments-->>Orders: ok
    Orders-->>Gateway: ok
```

The result is a waterfall view: you see each span's duration and can point at the exact service and call that dominated the latency or threw the error. This is the pillar that answers **"where"** in a microservice system, and it's why teams standardize on a propagation format (OpenTelemetry) — a trace is only as good as its weakest, un-instrumented hop.

```recall
Q: What is the role of the trace id versus a span?
A: The trace id identifies one request across the whole system; each service records a span for its own slice of work tagged with that trace id and its parent span, so the spans can be stitched into one timeline.
Q: Why does an un-instrumented hop degrade the whole trace?
A: If a service does not propagate the trace id, its spans are lost and the timeline has a gap, so you cannot see where the time went or the failure occurred at that hop. A trace is only as good as its weakest hop.
Q: What question does distributed tracing answer that a monolith stack trace does not?
A: Where in a chain of many services a request spent its time or failed. In a monolith one stack trace suffices, but a fanned-out request needs spans stitched across services to localize the slow or failing hop.
Q: Why do teams standardize on a propagation format like OpenTelemetry?
A: So every service passes the trace context the same way, ensuring spans from different services and languages can be correlated into a single coherent trace.
```

lessons.title: Alerting: paging on symptoms, not causes
lessons.body:
An alert's job is to get a human's attention when — and *only* when — action is genuinely needed. The failure mode isn't too few alerts; it's too many. **Alert fatigue** is when so many alerts fire (many noisy or non-actionable) that on-call engineers start ignoring them, and the one that mattered is lost in the noise.

Principles for alerts worth waking someone for:

- **Alert on symptoms, not causes.** Page on *"users are seeing errors / latency is above the SLO,"* not on *"CPU is at 90%."* High CPU may be totally fine; a served-error rate is what actually hurts users. Cause-based alerts fire constantly and often don't correspond to real user pain.
- **Every page must be actionable.** If the recipient can't do anything about it right now, it shouldn't page — make it a ticket or a dashboard, not a 3 a.m. wake-up.
- **Tie alerts to your SLOs (next lesson).** The strongest signal to page on is *"we are burning our error budget fast enough to breach the objective."*
- **Use severity tiers.** A page (immediate human action) is different from a ticket (handle during business hours) is different from an FYI. Route them differently.

The test for any alert: *"if this fires and the human does nothing, was that the right outcome?"* If yes often enough, delete or downgrade it.

```flow
dir: TB
cond: Condition fires | step
symptom: Hurts users now | gate
actionable: Human can act now | gate
page: Page on-call | step
ticket: Make a ticket | step
drop: Delete or downgrade | gate
cond -> symptom : evaluate
symptom -> drop : no user pain
symptom -> actionable : user pain
actionable -> ticket : act later
actionable -> page : act now
```

```recall
Q: Why alert on symptoms rather than causes?
A: Symptoms like a served-error rate above the SLO reflect real user pain, while causes like 90% CPU may be harmless. Cause-based alerts fire constantly and often do not correspond to anyone being hurt.
Q: What is alert fatigue and why is it the dangerous failure mode?
A: It is when so many noisy or non-actionable alerts fire that on-call starts ignoring them, so the one that mattered is lost in the noise. Too many alerts is worse than too few.
Q: What test decides whether a condition should page?
A: If it fires and the human does nothing, was that the right outcome? If doing nothing is often fine, the alert is not actionable and should be deleted or downgraded to a ticket or dashboard.
Q: Why is burning the error budget fast the strongest thing to page on?
A: It ties the page directly to the risk of breaching the objective users care about, so it fires on genuine, SLO-relevant danger rather than on an internal metric that may not matter.
```

lessons.title: SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets
lessons.body:
This is the framework (from Google's SRE practice) that turns "reliable" from a vibe into a number you can manage.

- **SLI — Service Level Indicator.** A *measured* quantity of your service's behaviour: e.g. the proportion of requests served successfully in under 300 ms. It's the raw signal.
- **SLO — Service Level Objective.** Your *target* for an SLI over a window: e.g. "99.9% of requests succeed under 300 ms, measured over 28 days." This is an internal goal you hold yourselves to.
- **SLA — Service Level Agreement.** A *contract* with customers, with financial consequences if breached. Your SLO should be **stricter** than your SLA, so you notice trouble before a customer can invoke the contract.

The powerful idea is the **error budget**. If your SLO is 99.9% success, then 0.1% of requests are *allowed* to fail — that 0.1% is a budget you get to spend:

- **Budget remaining** → you can take risks: ship features faster, run experiments, do a bold migration.
- **Budget exhausted** → you stop shipping risky changes and spend engineering effort on reliability until you're back in budget.

```flow
dir: LR
sli: Measure SLI | store
slo: Compare to SLO | gate
budget: Error budget | store
ship: Ship features, take risks | step
freeze: Freeze risky changes | gate
sli -> slo : success ratio
slo -> budget : spend or remaining
budget -> ship : budget remaining
budget -> freeze : budget exhausted
freeze -> sli : fix reliability
ship -> sli : keep measuring
```

This dissolves the classic dev-vs-ops fight ("ship faster" vs "stay stable") into a shared, data-driven rule. 100% reliability is the wrong target — it's impossible, ruinously expensive, and users can't tell the difference between 99.9% and 100% anyway. The error budget makes the *right* amount of unreliability an explicit, spendable resource.

```recall
Q: Why should your SLO be stricter than your SLA?
A: So you notice and react to trouble before a customer can invoke the contract. The SLA has financial consequences; the tighter internal SLO gives you headroom to fix things first.
Q: What does the team do differently when the error budget is exhausted versus remaining?
A: With budget remaining they can take risks: ship faster, run experiments, do bold migrations. When it is exhausted they freeze risky changes and spend effort on reliability until back in budget.
Q: Why is 100% reliability the wrong target?
A: It is impossible and ruinously expensive, and users cannot tell 99.9% from 100%. The error budget names the right amount of unreliability instead of chasing a target with no payoff.
Q: How does the error budget resolve the dev-versus-ops conflict?
A: It replaces "ship faster" versus "stay stable" with a shared, data-driven rule: budget remaining permits risk, budget spent forces a reliability focus.
```

lessons.title: Latency, throughput, and tail (P99)
lessons.body:
Two different performance questions, and the statistic that separates good engineers from ones who quote averages.

- **Latency** — how long *one* request takes (a duration).
- **Throughput** — how many requests you handle *per unit time* (a rate, e.g. QPS).

They trade off: pushing throughput toward saturation causes queuing, which drives latency up sharply. You optimize for one or the other depending on the workload (an interactive API cares about latency; a batch pipeline cares about throughput).

The crucial move on latency is to **stop looking at the average**. The mean hides pain: if 1 in 100 requests takes 5 seconds and the rest take 20 ms, the average looks fine while some users have a terrible experience. So measure **percentiles**:

```bars
title: Why the average hides tail pain (illustrative)
unit: ms
P50 typical request | 20
Slow 1 in 100 request | 5000
```

- **P50 (median)** — the typical experience.
- **P99 / P99.9 — tail latency** — the slowest 1% / 0.1%. This is where timeouts, retries, and angry users live.

Tail latency matters more than it seems because of **fan-out**: if one user action makes 100 internal calls in parallel and waits for all of them, the odds that *at least one* hits the slow P99 are high — so your user-facing latency is effectively governed by your backend's *tail*, not its median. Set SLOs and alerts on the tail, not the average.

```recall
Q: Why do latency and throughput trade off near saturation?
A: Pushing throughput toward saturation causes requests to queue, and queuing drives latency up sharply, so you optimize for one or the other depending on the workload.
Q: Why is the average latency a misleading number?
A: The mean hides the tail. If 1 in 100 requests takes 5 seconds and the rest take 20 ms, the average still looks fine while a slice of users has a terrible experience.
Q: Why does fan-out make tail latency govern user-facing latency?
A: If one action makes many parallel calls and waits for all, the chance that at least one hits the slow P99 is high, so the slowest hop sets the response time, not the median.
Q: For an interactive API versus a batch pipeline, which metric do you optimize?
A: An interactive API optimizes latency (per-request duration); a batch pipeline optimizes throughput (requests per unit time), because that is what each workload is judged on.
```

chapters.title: Resilience & incidents
chapters.summary: Surviving failure — recovery, geographic redundancy, deliberately injected chaos, cost control, and how to run and learn from an incident.

lessons.title: Disaster recovery, backups, and failover
lessons.body:
Everything fails eventually — a disk, a datacenter, a bad deploy that corrupts data. Disaster recovery (DR) is planning for the bad day so it's a controlled event, not a company-ending one.

Two numbers frame every DR plan:

- **RPO — Recovery Point Objective**: how much *data* you can afford to lose, measured in time. "RPO of 5 minutes" means backups/replication must be at most 5 minutes behind, so a disaster loses at most 5 minutes of writes.
- **RTO — Recovery Time Objective**: how long you can afford to be *down* while recovering. "RTO of 1 hour" means you must be back within an hour.

Tighter targets cost more, so set them per system by business impact.

**Backups** are the foundation — but an untested backup is a *hope*, not a plan. The single most important discipline is to **regularly test restores**; teams routinely discover their backups are incomplete or unrestorable only during a real disaster. Also keep backups off the primary system (a ransomware event or a fat-fingered delete that hits your live data shouldn't reach your backups).

**Failover** is switching to a standby when the primary fails — a replica database promoted to primary, or traffic rerouted to a healthy region. It can be automatic (fast, but risks flapping and split-brain) or manual (slower, safer). Whichever you choose, **rehearse it** before you need it.

```flow
dir: LR
disaster: Disaster hits | step
detect: Detect primary down | gate
failover: Promote standby | step
restore: Restore from backup | step
rpo: Data loss within RPO | gate
rto: Back up within RTO | gate
disaster -> detect : alarm
detect -> failover : reroute traffic
detect -> restore : if data lost
failover -> rto : service recovered
restore -> rpo : accept data gap
```

```recall
Q: What is the difference between RPO and RTO?
A: RPO is how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time, so it bounds how far behind backups may be. RTO is how long you can afford to be down while recovering.
Q: Why is an untested backup only a hope, not a plan?
A: Teams routinely discover their backups are incomplete or unrestorable only during a real disaster. Regularly testing restores is what proves the backup actually works.
Q: Why keep backups off the primary system?
A: A ransomware event or a fat-fingered delete that hits live data must not also reach the backups. Keeping them separate ensures a recovery source survives the same incident.
Q: What is the tradeoff between automatic and manual failover?
A: Automatic failover is fast but risks flapping and split-brain; manual is slower but safer. Either way you must rehearse it before a real incident so it works when needed.
```

lessons.title: Multi-region deployments
lessons.body:
Running in more than one geographic region buys two things: **lower latency** (serve users from a nearby region) and **disaster survival** (an entire region can go down and you stay up). It also introduces the hardest problem in distributed systems — keeping data consistent across long distances — so it's a deliberate trade-off, not a default.

Common shapes, increasing in cost and complexity:

- **Active-passive** — one region serves all traffic; a second stands by with replicated data, ready to take over on failover. Simpler; the standby's capacity is mostly idle.
- **Active-active** — multiple regions serve live traffic simultaneously. Best latency and utilization, but now writes can happen in two places at once, forcing you to confront conflict resolution and cross-region replication lag head-on.

```flow
dir: LR
users: Users | actor
r1: Region 1 | store
r2: Region 2 | store
passive: Standby, idle | store
conflict: Conflict resolution | gate
users -> r1 : active-passive
r1 --> passive : replicate data
passive --> r1 : failover
users -> r2 : active-active
r1 --> conflict : concurrent writes
r2 --> conflict : concurrent writes
```

The physics you can't escape: the speed of light makes a synchronous, strongly-consistent write across continents slow (a round trip of ~100 ms+). So multi-region systems usually accept **eventual consistency** for most data and reserve synchronous cross-region coordination for the few things that truly need it. Data residency and regulatory rules (where user data is legally allowed to live) often drive the design as much as performance does.

```recall
Q: What two benefits justify running in multiple regions?
A: Lower latency by serving users from a nearby region, and disaster survival since an entire region can go down while you stay up.
Q: Why is active-active harder than active-passive?
A: In active-active, writes can happen in two regions at once, forcing you to handle conflict resolution and cross-region replication lag. Active-passive sends all traffic to one region with a standby, avoiding concurrent writes.
Q: Why do multi-region systems usually accept eventual consistency?
A: The speed of light makes a synchronous strongly-consistent write across continents slow, around 100 ms or more per round trip, so most data is kept eventually consistent and synchronous coordination is reserved for the few things that need it.
Q: Besides performance, what often drives multi-region design?
A: Data residency and regulatory rules about where user data is legally allowed to live, which can dictate the design as much as latency does.
```

lessons.title: Cost optimization
lessons.body:
In the cloud, architecture decisions are spending decisions — every running resource has a meter. Cost optimization is treating money as a first-class operational metric, alongside latency and reliability, rather than a surprise on the monthly bill.

```flow
dir: LR
idle: Idle, over-provisioned | store
model: Wrong purchasing model | store
storage: Hot data on fast tier | store
egress: Cross-region egress | store
visible: Tag and dashboard spend | gate
cut: Lower bill | step
idle -> cut : right-size, autoscale
model -> cut : reserved, spot
storage -> cut : tier cold data
egress -> cut : cut transfer
visible -> cut : attribute spend
```

Where the waste usually hides:

- **Idle and over-provisioned resources** — instances sized for a peak that rarely comes, or left running with nothing to do. **Right-sizing** (match capacity to actual usage) and **autoscaling** (shed capacity at the trough) recover most of this.
- **The right purchasing model** — on-demand for spiky/unpredictable load, reserved or committed-use pricing for steady baseline load (big discount for a commitment), and spot/preemptible instances for fault-tolerant, interruptible work (deep discount, can be reclaimed).
- **Storage tiering** — hot data on fast expensive storage, cold/archival data on cheap slow tiers, with lifecycle rules that move it automatically.
- **Data transfer** — cross-region and egress traffic is often a silently large line item.

The discipline that makes it stick is **visibility**: tag resources by team/service so cost is attributable, and put spend on a dashboard people actually look at. You can't optimize a bill you can't attribute. The trade-off is always cost *versus* performance and resilience — cheaper is a valid choice only when you've named what reliability you're giving up.

```recall
Q: Which purchasing model fits steady baseline load, and why?
A: Reserved or committed-use pricing. You trade a usage commitment for a large discount, which pays off precisely because the baseline load is predictable and always present.
Q: When are spot/preemptible instances the right choice?
A: For fault-tolerant, interruptible work. They are deeply discounted but can be reclaimed, so only workloads that tolerate being killed mid-run should use them.
Q: Why is visibility the discipline that makes cost optimization stick?
A: You cannot optimize a bill you cannot attribute. Tagging resources by team or service and surfacing spend on a dashboard makes waste visible and gives it an owner.
Q: What must you name before choosing the cheaper option?
A: The reliability or performance you are giving up. Cost always trades against those, so a cheaper choice is only valid once that tradeoff is explicit.
```

lessons.title: Incidents, on-call, and postmortems
lessons.body:
An incident is any unplanned disruption that needs an urgent response. How a team handles the live event — and what it does afterward — is the clearest signal of operational maturity.

**During the incident**, structure beats heroics:

- **Roles.** An **Incident Commander (IC)** coordinates and decides — they don't fix, they run the response. Others investigate and mitigate. This prevents ten people debugging in ten directions.
- **Mitigate first, diagnose later.** The priority is stopping user pain — roll back, fail over, flip a feature flag — *before* hunting the root cause. Recovery is the goal; understanding can wait.
- **Communicate.** Keep a running timeline and update stakeholders; a silent incident channel breeds a dozen "is it fixed yet?" interruptions.

Escalation when the first responder is stuck:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Alert as Alerting
    participant P as Primary on-call
    participant IC as Incident Commander
    participant SME as Service expert
    Alert->>P: page (SLO burn / errors)
    P->>P: assess + attempt mitigation
    P->>IC: escalate (impact is broad)
    IC->>SME: pull in owning team
    IC->>IC: coordinate until resolved
```

**On-call** is the rotation that makes someone responsible for responding. Healthy on-call is *sustainable*: reasonable rotations, alerts that are actually actionable (see the alerting lesson), and enough runbooks that the responder isn't starting from zero.

**Postmortems** are how you convert an outage into a permanent improvement. The non-negotiable principle is **blameless**: the goal is to fix the *system and process*, never to punish a person — because in a blameful culture people hide mistakes and the same failure recurs. A good postmortem records the timeline, the real (often multi-layered) root cause, the customer impact, and — most importantly — **action items with owners** that make this class of failure less likely or less severe. Human error is almost never the root cause; it's a symptom of a system that made the error easy to make and hard to catch.

```recall
Q: Why does the Incident Commander coordinate rather than fix?
A: A single person deciding and directing prevents ten people debugging in ten directions. The IC runs the response while others investigate and mitigate, keeping the effort coherent.
Q: Why mitigate before diagnosing the root cause?
A: The priority is stopping user pain. Rolling back, failing over, or flipping a flag restores service now, whereas hunting the root cause first prolongs the outage. Understanding can wait.
Q: Why must postmortems be blameless?
A: In a blameful culture people hide mistakes, so the same failure recurs. A blameless postmortem fixes the system and process, which is what actually prevents recurrence.
Q: Why is human error almost never the real root cause?
A: It is usually a symptom of a system that made the error easy to make and hard to catch. Fixing the system, not punishing the person, is what reduces the chance of the failure class returning.
```
